Cassidyite

Cassidyite (IMA 1966-024) is an IMA-accepted hydrated calcium-nickel phosphate mineral of the fairfieldite-collinsite group, the nickel analogue of collinsite, with IMA September 2026 Master List formula Ca2Ni(PO4)2(H2O)2 and solid-solution composition Ca2(Ni,Mg)(PO4)2·2H2O (with Ni:Mg ranging from 3:2 to 3:7). Described by White, Henderson, and Mason (1967) from weathered meteoritic iron shale at the Wolf Creek meteorite crater (19°18'S, 127°46'E), Western Australia, Australia (type specimen USNM 119553), where it forms pale green to bright green crusts and small spherules in cracks and cavities alongside lipscombite, pecoraite, and reevesite via weathering of schreibersite (Fe,Ni)3P. Electron microprobe analysis (pp. 1194–1195) gives mean CaO = 32.3 wt% and P2O5 = 39.2 wt%, with NiO 6.4–16.2 wt% and MgO 5.7–2.2 wt% (Fe not detected; CoO-equivalent ~0.4 wt%), spanning nickelian collinsite to magnesian cassidyite. Triclinic (space group P-1), with nominal unit-cell dimensions a = 5.71 Å, b = 6.73 Å, c = 5.41 Å, alpha = 96°49', beta = 107°22', gamma = 104°35', V = 190 Å3, Z = 1, density 3.1–3.2 g/cm3 inferred from calculated endmembers (2.96 g/cm3 for the Mg endmember and 3.26 g/cm3 for the Ni endmember; direct measurement precluded by admixtures and fine grain size), and refractive indices alpha = 1.64–1.65 and gamma = 1.67–1.68.

Catapleiite

Catapleiite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2Zr(Si3O9)(H2O)2. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records grandfathered status and the year 1850, not a numbered approval accession. It is distinct from calciocatapleiite, elpidite, elemental zirconium and mixed zirconium-bearing rocks. An ideal species formula does not establish the composition or symmetry of every natural grain. Cegiełka and colleagues (2022) assigned catapleiite from microscopy and electron-microprobe data in a loose Dyrnaes River block that they attributed to the Ilímaussaq Green Granite, south Greenland. Figure 3B, Figure 6 and Table 5 document their catapleiite assignment in zircon-bearing aggregates associated with elpidite. This is the same heterogeneous block already described in the elpidite record, not independent sampling or a pure catapleiite feed. The paper does not provide sample-specific diffraction confirmation. Its proposed late-magmatic formation and subsequent hydrothermal sodium loss are geological interpretations, not controlled transformation assays. The detailed analytical appendix and Supplementary Table 1 remain unavailable. Figure 3C labels material SZR while its caption calls it catapleiite; Table 4 and Table 6 repeat IL-356 under different material headings. Main-text and Table 5 sodium ranges also disagree. These unresolved source differences are retained without importing whole-dataset composition ranges or calculating alteration yields. Zubkova and colleagues (2020) distinguish natural catapleiite from the zirconosilicate produced by annealing it at 1000 degrees C. Their silver-exchange experiment used that thermally transformed derivative, whose framework differs from hydrated catapleiite. Its silver-bearing product is not a demonstrated exchange product of the unheated mineral. Figure 1 reuses earlier structural models for the starting mineral and thermal derivative; the new structure determination concerns the silver-exchanged derivative. This study supplies material-boundary context, not a catapleiite recovery yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Cavansite

Cavansite is a hydrated calcium vanadyl silicate mineral, Ca(V4+O)(Si4O10)(H2O)4, approved as IMA 1967-019 and retained in the September 2026 IMA list. It is a distinct species from pentagonite despite their related composition. The primary Oregon description and later natural-crystal work support a porous silicate framework containing vanadyl groups, calcium and water. Pcmn in the original description and Pnma in the 2012 study are different settings of the same orthorhombic space-group type, with the a and c axes interchanged. The 2009 proposed H3O+/OH-bearing formula is disputed by the 2012 hydrogen-bond refinement, and is not substituted for the current IMA formula. Natural-crystal heating experiments support protocol-dependent abiotic dehydration, without a microbial mechanism, mineral-specific recovery yield or industrial deployment. No criticality designation is inherited from vanadium or other constituents.

IMA:1967-019
Caysichite-(Y)

A natural yttrium- and calcium-bearing silicate-carbonate mineral. The September 2026 IMA list retains (Ca,Yb,Er)4Y4(Si8O20)(CO3)6(OH)(H2O)5·2H2O and records a 1987 special-procedure renaming; that year is not an approval accession. The 1974 original described Evans-Lou mine material from Quebec, Canada, formerly labelled UN-11 and UN-16, with type material deposited as Geological Survey of Canada collection 10402. Most analyses used hand-picked colourless crusts; a separate yellow grain contained an interstitial Y-rich material and a rim tentatively identified as synchysite-(Y), so its chemistry is not pooled with the colourless material. The 1978 refinement on a specimen supplied by Hogarth established orthorhombic Ccm21 symmetry and double-crankshaft silicate chains. Its Y/Ca/REE site assignments and OH/water distribution were model-based; hydrogen atoms were not located. A 2025 study of separate Ploskaya Mountain, Russia, material supports a related structure but explicitly leaves its species equivalence to the Canadian material unresolved: proposed dominant cations differ between sites. It proposes vacancy and carbonate-protonation models, without locating hydrogen, and requests renewed study of the type locality material. Its proposed formula does not replace the current IMA formula here. Published numerical formula and reflection-count discrepancies are retained in the source dossier rather than silently reconciled. Geological formation by alteration of hellandite remains an interpretation from textures and associations, not a demonstrated microbial process. No criticality-list designation, extraction yield or industrial deployment is asserted.

Childrenite

Childrenite is the Fe2+-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+Al(PO4)(OH)2(H2O), distinct from the Mn2+-dominant endmember eosphorite and oxidized related phases. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1823. Toupal et al. (2024) characterized two natural grains in granite collected on 11 July 2020 from two outcrops near the southern boundary of the Homolka granite, Czech Republic. Twenty electron-microprobe spots across those two grains gave Fe/(Fe+Mn) from 0.51 to 0.86; these are analytical spots, not twenty independent specimens. Single-crystal diffraction and Raman measurements on Grain A support an orthorhombic Cmca childrenite structure with divalent-cation bond valence at the mixed Fe site. This is specimen-specific structural evidence, not a direct oxidation-state assay of every natural childrenite. It improves on the older Handbook's Bba2 assignment and possible monoclinic interpretation without treating all historical specimens as identical. The crystals show patchy Fe/Mn zoning and probable uraninite inclusions; the inclusions are not independently confirmed as a uranium mineral here. Calculated water raises all microprobe totals above 100 wt%, which the authors attribute to beam-induced partial dehydration; this is not a controlled dehydration experiment. The chemical and structural observations distinguish the investigated grains from a merely compositionally similar ferric phase. The official CIF and main Table 2 disagree on temperature, 273(2) versus 293(2) K, and measured-reflection count, 5429 versus 5682; neither disputed value is adopted as a resolved condition. The CIF's Fe/Ca scattering-site model and formula-sum field are not treated as the measured Fe/Mn/Ca chemistry, and its analytical Si0.04 differs from the main formula's approximately Si0.01. These source limits do not remove the agreement on the unit cell, Cmca symmetry and the 602 observed reflections underlying R1=0.0295. This record establishes natural-mineral identity only, without an experimentally demonstrated formation, extraction, microbial transformation or recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

The September 2026 IMA list marks it renamed with 2010 s.p.; this special-procedure notation is not a new-mineral accession. The accepted experiment used a characterized synthetic analogue as a bacterial nutrient-source comparison. Its findings are not inherited from the pyromorphite dissolution arm or from elemental phosphorus criticality.

Chlorite denotes a hydrous phyllosilicate group with a hydroxide interlayer, not a single species or the dissolved chlorite anion. Chromite beneficiation tailings

Mixed residual mineral solids from physical beneficiation of chromite-bearing ore. The curated 2018 case is fresh superficial tailings collected in May 2017 at a beneficiation plant in Sukinda valley, Odisha, India, with a separate stockpiled-tailings core used for chemical extraction comparisons. The source describes comminution, desliming and gravity concentration, rather than chromate manufacture. These solids are distinct from the chromite mineral species, unprocessed ore, lateritic overburden, the plant's chromite concentrate and chemically processed chromite ore residues. Reported XRD phases include chromite, goethite, hematite, gibbsite and chlorite; Cr also occurs in nonchromite phases. Table 1 reports 56.7 wt% Fe2O3 and 18.1 wt% Cr2O3 on an XRF oxide-equivalent basis, not quantitative mineral fractions. A separate 2025 fungal study uses two Eti Krom enrichment-tailings feeds labelled olivine and serpentine; both are mixed mineral materials, distinct from the Odisha samples and from pure olivine or serpentine minerals. Neither constituent criticality nor industrial microbial processing is inferred from these feeds' compositions or industrial origins.

Chromite ore processing residue

Chromium-bearing waste from chemical processing of chromite ore, distinct from the chromite mineral species and physical-beneficiation tailings. The curated case is a cementitious, high-lime-process residue from a Glasgow waste-fill site that received material from the Rutherglen Chromite Processing Works. High-lime processing oxidized ore Cr(III) to soluble Cr(VI), followed by aqueous extraction. The 2015 study sampled field-moist material from an exploratory borehole during the M74 motorway project and initially identified it tentatively as COPR from its pale granular appearance and high-pH yellow leachate. Subsequent XRF and XRD characterized a mixed residue rather than proving a pure feed. XRD identified cementitious and hydrated phases, including calcite, portlandite, brownmillerite, pyroaurite, hydrogarnet and brucite; remnant chromite was not detected by that assay. Table 4 reports 3.8 wt% Cr in the XRF composition, without loss-on-ignition correction; this is neither a mineral fraction nor a field-wet feed concentration. This record does not confer a constituent element's criticality designation on the residue or assert commercial microbial processing.

Cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts

Naturally occurring layered iron-manganese oxide and oxyhydroxide deposits on exposed marine rock surfaces, commonly seamounts. This resource identity covers the cobalt-bearing, predominantly hydrogenetic crusts formed by accumulation from seawater; it does not denote every hydrothermal encrustation. The heterogeneous crust material is distinct from sediment-hosted polymetallic nodules, constituent cobalt or manganese elements, a pure mineral species, and a processing residue. Maciąg et al. characterize crusts and their altered basalt interfaces from Dirck Hartog Ridge; their sample-specific mineral mixtures are not a universal formula or grade. Collection and physical preparation do not make this geological resource secondary. The laboratory mechanism below records conditional redistribution of cobalt and nickel in whole-crust microcosms; it does not establish a specific receiving phase, a purified metal product or industrial deployment. The resource inherits no constituent criticality.

Coconinoite

Coconinoite (IMA 1965-003) is an IMA-accepted hydrated iron-aluminum uranyl phosphate-sulfate mineral with IMA September 2026 Master List formula Fe3+2Al2(UO2)2(PO4)4(SO4)(OH)2·20H2O. Described by Young, Weeks, and Meyrowitz (1966) from the oxidized zone of Colorado Plateau uranium deposits at the Sun Valley mine (Coconino County, Arizona, USA), Blackwater No. 4 and Huskon No. 7 mines (Apache County, Arizona, USA), and the Jomac mine (White Canyon district, San Juan County, Utah, USA), where it forms light creamy-yellow microcrystalline aggregates of lath-shaped grains (6 x 2 um) in seams with gypsum, jarosite, limonite, quartz, clay, and coalified wood. Microchemical analyses in Table 2 (p. 656) report for Blackwater No. 4 sample 1715 Fe2O3 9.7, Al2O3 6.6, UO3 34.9, P2O5 18.3, SO3 5.4, H2O- 18.2, H2O+ 5.8 (total H2O 24.0), CaO 0.1, CO2 < 0.1, Na2O < 0.1, acid-insol. 0.5, total 99.5 wt%, and for Jomac sample T-J2-53 Fe2O3 10.3, Al2O3 6.5, UO3 34.2, P2O5 17.7, SO3 6.1, total H2O 23.4, CaO < 0.1, CO2 0.7, Na2O 0.1, acid-insol. 1.0, total 100.0 wt%. Coffinite

Coffinite is the uranium-bearing silicate mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as U(SiO4)·nH2O, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1956. That year is not a numbered mineral approval. Coffinite is distinct from uraninite, dissolved uranium, uranium-bearing ores and synthetic mixtures that merely contain uranium and silicon. The variable water term is not a measured hydration number for every specimen. Suzuki et al. (2016) identified natural coffinite nanoparticles in the L3 calcium-carbonate layer of a fracture-filling vein from borehole 07MI07 at the Mizunami Underground Laboratory, Japan. Elemental mapping, selected-area electron diffraction and lattice imaging support their assignment; the particles occur with aluminosilicate and contain other elements including phosphorus, zirconium and yttrium. The authors' proposed microbial origin is an interpretation of a natural setting, not a controlled organism-specific formation experiment. The separate laboratory mechanism below concerns newly formed coffinite on a prepared UO2 pellet, not bioleaching of that natural vein or testing of irradiated spent fuel. No criticality designation is inherited from elemental uranium, and no isolated-metal yield or industrial operation is asserted.

Coking coal

Coal suitable for making coke, treated as an end-use commodity rather than a mineral species, the carbon element, coke itself or all coal. The EIA glossary defines coking coal as suitable bituminous coal. Its separate metallurgical-coal definition includes both coking coal and pulverized coal consumed in steelmaking, whereas the USGS 2026 fact sheet uses coking and metallurgical coal interchangeably in its coke-production scope. This record follows the narrower coke-making identity and records the original EU 2024 coking-coal designation without silently equating all metallurgical-coal uses. The experiment concerns beneficiation of selected Tabas feeds described by the authors as suitable for coking; retained coke-making performance after treatment was not demonstrated.

Coquimbite

Coquimbite is a trigonal aluminium-ferric-iron sulfate mineral, ideally AlFe(III)3(SO4)6(H2O)12·6H2O. IMA-CNMNC proposal 19-F, approved in October 2019, redefined the species to recognize essential aluminium; the September 2026 mineral list retains that formula and redefined status. The older Al-free formula Fe2(SO4)3·9H2O is not the current species definition. Coquimbite and paracoquimbite have related structures and form the coquimbite group; aluminocoquimbite has a different topology and is not a member of that group. In Mauro et al. 2020, a natural Monte Arsiccio specimen was characterized by electron microprobe, spectroscopy and single-crystal diffraction. Twenty microprobe spots gave the empirical formula Al0.96Fe3.11S5.97O24·18H2O, with water calculated from the structure rather than directly measured. Table 3 and the associated CIF model an Al-dominant site with occupancy Al0.946(7)Fe0.054(7). These sample-specific chemical and structural results support the revised identity without implying an exactly ideal bulk composition. The study establishes mineral identity and structure; it does not test microbial formation, extraction or recovery.

Cordylite-(Ce)

A natural barium-rare-earth fluorocarbonate mineral with the IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula (Na,Ca,□)BaCe2(CO3)4(F,O), where □ denotes a vacancy. The authority lists renamed status and 1987 special procedure; this is not an IMA approval accession. This record denotes the Ce species, distinct from cordylite-(La), a rare-earth commodity or a mixed ore. Giester et al. (1998) investigated six specimens by chemical analysis and single-crystal X-ray diffraction and a seventh by X-ray methods alone, from Narssarssuk in Greenland, Mont Saint-Hilaire in Canada, Bayan Obo in China and the Kola Peninsula in Russia. The seventh crystal, original Flink material M.M. no. 392 (Narssarssuk 1*), suffered beam damage that prevented standard microprobe analysis; its qualitative EDX signal establishes Na presence without a quantitative Na concentration. The seven structures were refined in P63/mmc. Attempts in the lower-symmetry alternative P-62c did not give conclusive grounds to prefer it. The paper's idealized formula (Na1-xCax/2)BaCe2(CO3)4F, with 0 <= x <= 1, uses Ce as a proxy for the sum of rare-earth elements, not a measured pure-Ce endmember. X-ray scattering alone cannot resolve the Na/Ca proportion; the separate chemical analyses constrain it. CO2 in Table 5 is calculated by difference, selected Na determinations used direct-current argon-plasma spectrometry, and reliable water analysis was unavailable. These distinctions preclude treating all reported contents as direct microprobe measurements. Comparative and type material support the authors' identification of historical baiyuneboite-(Ce) as cordylite-(Ce) and revision of the older formula; the broader current IMA formula is retained separately from their 1998 model. Printed atomic coordinates and distances were inspected, but deposited anisotropic displacement Table 3 (AM-98-005) was not acquired. No controlled extraction, microbial mechanism, recovery yield, industrial deployment or transferred criticality designation is asserted.

Corkite

Corkite is the lead ferric sulfate-phosphate hydroxide mineral with ideal formula PbFe3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from arsenate-bearing beudantite, plumbojarosite, pyromorphite and elemental lead. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Ferrenti et al. (2023) synthesized corkite-bearing powders and characterized their structure and thermal behavior. The best products remained mixed with approximately 9.5 weight percent Pb5(PO4)3Cl; refined phase fractions are not synthesis yield or absolute purity. The authors favor centrosymmetric R-3m from combined diffraction and vibrational evidence, whereas the Handbook lists R3m for natural material. Both diffraction models fit similarly, and substitution, disorder and sample differences remain relevant. The accepted processes are laboratory abiotic synthesis and thermal alteration, without microbial activity, recovered-metal product or industrial demonstration. Criticality is not inherited from constituent elements.

Cuprosklodowskite is the copper uranyl silicate hydrate mineral Cu(UO2)2(SiO3OH)2(H2O)4·2H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, equivalent in bulk composition to Cu[(UO2)(SiO3OH)]2·6H2O. Status G denotes a grandfathered species; 1933 is the original-description year, not a numbered approval accession. Plášil's 2018 study provides original natural-crystal diffraction and hydrogen-position refinement despite the article's Review label. The diffraction crystal came from the National Museum in Prague collection; the article does not establish that it is the Musunoi specimen photographed separately in Figure 2d. Section 3.1 and Figure 4a describe copper's distorted sixfold coordination and the two longer bonds to uranyl oxygen, differing from magnesium's linkage to silicate oxygen in sklodowskite. The original supplementary CIF and Table 2 agree on the unit-cell parameters and R1 = 3.75% for 1033 reflections above I > 3 sigma(I). The CIF retains incomplete publication-template fields and different temperature entries (cell measurement 295(11) K; diffraction ambient 287 K), so a single exact experimental temperature is not imposed here. This record establishes mineral identity and specimen-specific structure; it does not assert a dissolution, microbial extraction, recovery, criticality or industrial-deployment claim.

Curite

Curite is the lead uranyl oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral with the IMA formula Pb3+x[(UO2)4O4+x(OH)3-x]2(H2O)2, distinct from elemental uranium, lead commodities and synthetic strontium analogues. The September 2026 IMA list gives grandfathered status G; 1921 is its original-description year, not an approval accession. A natural Shinkolobwe crystal was refined in orthorhombic Pnma in 2019. Hydroxyl hydrogen positions were refined from X-ray data, whereas water orientations required Torque calculations; these are not wholly independent experimental determinations of all hydrogen positions. Slight lead nonstoichiometry and a proposed local hydroxyl/oxide charge-balance mechanism remain distinguished from directly resolved substitution. Natural structural evidence and synthetic surface experiments concern separate specimens. No criticality designation, microbial mechanism or industrial recovery is inferred.

Dacostaite

IMA-approved hydrated potassium magnesium-aluminium fluoride-arsenate mineral (IMA 2024-015; symbol Dcs in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 54; status A, Approved 2024; full description published January 2025) with ideal end-member formula K(Mg2Al)[Mg(H2O)6]2(AsO4)2F6*2H2O (requiring As2O5 28.47 wt%, Al2O3 6.31 wt%, MgO 19.97 wt%, K2O 5.83 wt%, F 14.12 wt%, H2O 31.25 wt%, O=-F -5.95 wt%, sum 100.00 wt%; Biagioni et al., 2025, European Journal of Mineralogy 37:39-52). Represents the first mineral species in the K2O-MgO-Al2O3-As2O5-H2O-F system and is named in honour of Angelo Da Costa (1940-2022), Tuscan mineral collector active from the early 1970s who contributed to the exploration of mineralogical localities in northern Tuscany (Apuan Alps, Monte Pisano) and collaborated with the Museo di Storia Naturale of the University of Pisa. Discovered in a small exploitation void known as Stanza Santoni at the Cetine di Cotorniano Mine (43 deg 13 min N, 11 deg 09 min E), Chiusdino, Siena province, Tuscany, Italy (a former Sb ore deposit where stibnite ores are hosted in Upper Triassic Calcare cavernoso limestone replaced by black jasperoids and vuggy silica at the contact with overlying Liguride Nappe argillic formations), where it occurs in fewer than 10 known specimens associated with quartz, native sulfur, gypsum, F-bearing alunite, nannoniite (IMA 2024-010), and a microcrystalline pharmacosiderite-like phase replacing a cube-octahedral precursor, formed by late-stage oxidized (Al,F)-rich fluids; the holotype specimen is deposited in the Museo di Storia Naturale, University of Pisa, Via Roma 79, Calci (Pisa, Italy), under catalogue number 20073. Forms aggregates of thin pseudo-hexagonal micaceous, colourless-to-white flakes and bent laths up to 0.5 mm in size with a white streak, silky lustre, no UV fluorescence at 254 or 350 nm, brittle tenacity, flexible but non-elastic crystals, perfect {001} cleavage, and calculated density Dcalc = 2.162 g/cm3 (from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell parameters; Mohs hardness and direct density could not be measured owing to small crystal size and scarcity of material). Optically colourless and non-pleochroic in plane-polarized light, biaxial negative (-) with alpha = 1.4730(4), beta = 1.4801(4), gamma = 1.4805(4) (at 589 nm), 2Vmeas = 29(2) deg (spindle stage) and 2Vcalc = 27 deg, weak dispersion, undulatory extinction parallel or nearly parallel to the {001} cleavage, and a superior Gladstone-Dale compatibility index of -0.005. Micro-Raman spectroscopy (633 nm He-Ne laser at 8 mW, Thermo Scientific DXR dispersive Raman spectrometer at the National Museum in Prague; Figure 2, Section 4.1, pp. 40-42) shows a prominent nu1 symmetric AsO4 stretching band at 838 cm-1, AsO4 nu4 and nu2 bending and Mg(H2O)6/Al(F,OH,O)6 modes at 531 and 397 cm-1, lattice modes at 257, 176, and 130 cm-1, H-O-H bending at 1685 and 1633 cm-1, and broad O-H stretching bands at ~3180-3550 cm-1 (O...O distances 2.7-2.9 A, maximum at 2.73 A). Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (n = 10 spot analyses on unpolished carbon-coated crystal surfaces, Cameca SX100 at the National Museum in Prague, 15 kV, 5 nA, 10 um beam diameter; Si, S, Pb, Cl, Ni, and Co were below detection limits; Table 1) yielded (mean wt%, range, SD, and value normalized to 100.00 wt% with stoichiometric H2O) As2O5 35.42 wt% (34.37-35.98, SD 0.57; normalized 28.69 wt%), MgO 21.13 wt% (18.60-24.94, SD 2.13; normalized 17.12 wt%), F 13.15 wt% (9.13-16.59, SD 2.91; normalized 10.65 wt%), Al2O3 12.23 wt% (10.69-13.72, SD 1.01; normalized 9.91 wt%), K2O 4.13 wt% (2.85-5.43, SD 0.78; normalized 3.35 wt%), CuO 0.42 wt% (0.27-0.94, SD 0.19; normalized 0.34 wt%), CaO 0.36 wt% (0.27-0.46, SD 0.06; normalized 0.29 wt%), ZnO 0.34 wt% (0.21-0.47, SD 0.09; normalized 0.27 wt%), P2O5 0.17 wt% (0.02-0.27, SD 0.07; normalized 0.14 wt%), Na2O 0.15 wt% (0.05-0.33, SD 0.10; normalized 0.12 wt%), MnO 0.04 wt% (0.01-0.08, SD 0.02; normalized 0.03 wt%), FeO 0.04 wt% (0.00-0.08, SD 0.03; normalized 0.03 wt%), analytical sum 87.58 wt% (range 86.57-88.71, SD 0.78; normalized 70.94 wt%), O=-F -5.54 wt% (normalized -4.48 wt%), and H2Ocalc 41.40 wt% (normalized 33.54 wt%), giving an unnormalized total of 123.44 wt% (due to loss of 6-7 H2O groups in the microprobe vacuum and unpolished surface geometry) and normalized total of 100.00 wt%. Based on (As + P) = 2 apfu and electrostatic balance, the empirical formula is (K0.56Ca0.04Na0.03[]0.37)Sigma1.00(Al1.54Mg1.38Cu0.03Zn0.03)Sigma2.98[Mg(H2O)6]2[(As0.99P0.01)O4]2[F4.46(OH)1.46O0.08]Sigma6.00*2H2O (general crystal-chemical formula [K1-x(H2O)x](Mg2-xAl1+x)[Mg(H2O)6]2(AsO4)2F6-y(OH)y*2H2O with x ~ 0.5, y ~ 1.5). Crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group C2/m (#12), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 12.474(5) A, b = 7.198(3) A, c = 13.724(6) A, beta = 99.518(13) deg, V = 1215.3(8) A3, and Z = 2 (refined from 6874 measured and 1325 unique reflections collected at 293(2) K on a 0.070 x 0.040 x 0.020 mm crystal using MoKalpha radiation on a Bruker D8 Venture diffractometer to R1 = 0.0927 for 1022 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo), R1 = 0.1152 for all data, wR2 = 0.2574, GoF = 1.055, 102 parameters, Table 3, where the h index range is printed as "-15 <=h15" with a missing "<=" symbol; Gandolfi-like CuKalpha powder X-ray diffraction refined with UnitCell, Section 3.3 and Table 2, gave a = 12.4760(18) A, b = 7.1974(11) A, c = 13.7211(18) A, beta = 99.549(12) deg, V = 1215.0(2) A3). The crystal structure (Tables 4-7 and Figures 3-4) comprises crandallite/elliottite-like heteropolyhedral {001} layers of corner-sharing (Mg,Al)(F,OH,O)6 octahedra at M(1) (4e, <M(1)-phi> = 1.939 A) and M(2) (2b, <M(2)-phi> = 1.937 A) decorated by As(1)O4 tetrahedra (4i, <As(1)-O> = 1.676 A) and hosting split K(1) (2a) and K(2) (4i) cations in pseudo-hexagonal cavities, alternating along c with isolated interlayer Mg(3)(H2O)6 octahedra (4i, <Mg(3)-Ow> = 2.109 A, BVS = 1.94 v.u.) and split non-coordinated Ow(5a/5b/5c) H2O molecules linked by H bonds (note that Section 4.3.2 on pp. 43 and 45 cites BVS values of 5.14 v.u. for As(1) and 2.52 and 2.53 v.u. for M(1) and M(2), whereas Table 6 on p. 45 lists 5.11, 2.54, and 2.54 v.u., respectively; and Section 4.3.3 on p. 46 states that "O(2) accepts H bonds from two Ow(2) groups", whereas Tables 6 and 7 show that O(2) accepts two H bonds from Ow(3) at 2.670(13) A while Ow(2) donates H bonds to O(1) at 2.763(10) A). The six strongest observed powder X-ray diffraction lines (dobs in A (Iobs; hkl), Table 2) are 13.7 (s; 0 0 1), 5.48 (m; 1 1 1), 2.977 (m; 2 2 1), 5.98 (mw; -2 0 1), 3.581 (mw; 0 2 0, -3 1 1, 3 1 0), and 1.797 (mw; -6 2 1, 0 4 0). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Donnayite-(Y)

A sodium-strontium-calcium-yttrium carbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula NaSr3CaY(CO3)6(H2O)3. This mineral species is distinct from alicewilsonite-(YCe), a rare-earth element and a mixed ore. The authority lists renamed status and 1987 s.p.; that special-procedure year is not used here as a unique approval identifier. Lykova et al. (2023, Part 1) reexamined seven museum specimens catalogued as donnayite-(Y) cotypes from Mont Saint-Hilaire, Canada. Six were reassigned to alicewilsonite-(YCe); CMNMC 39396 was retained as donnayite-(Y) and designated its holotype under approved proposal 22-F. Historical data combined the two species and are not treated as a uniform donnayite dataset. Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses of the holotype used 20 kV, 10 nA and a 30 micrometre beam with corrections for beam instability. Table 2 reports mean Y2O3 of 10.18 wt% across 17 analyses; H2O and CO2 were calculated from stoichiometry, not directly measured. These specimen assays are not extraction yields. The holotype's single-crystal refinement gave R1 = 0.139 and no satisfactory structural model. The reported triclinic P1 structure with R1 = 0.055 instead used the separate specimen CMNMC 90405 at 293 K. Its model has split carbonate and water positions, unlocated hydrogen, and Dy scattering proxies for lanthanides; it does not directly measure ideal stoichiometry. Published Table 5 gives Rint = 0.092 while the official CIF gives 0.0342 for the equivalent-reflection agreement field; that difference remains unresolved. The official CIF, powder pattern and supplementary bond-valence table were inspected without independent diffraction refinement. The curated evidence establishes natural identity and characterization, not a controlled microbial, extraction or recovery experiment. No criticality designation is transferred from contained elements.

Dzhalindite

Dzhalindite is the indium hydroxide mineral species In(OH)3, listed as approved in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list with the special-procedure year 1967. It is distinct from elemental indium, indite (FeIn2S4), mixed ores and synthetic indium hydroxide products considered only by formula. Kiseleva and colleagues (2008) report a natural occurrence in one quartz-sulfide vein section from 50 metres below the surface at the Bugdaya deposit, eastern Transbaikalia, Russia. They describe 30-94 micrometre crystals in late quartz and zoned In-bearing grains examined by optical microscopy, backscattered-electron imaging and energy-dispersive elemental analysis. Their dzhalindite assignment rests on composition, optical properties and apparent crystal symmetry; X-ray diffraction was unsuccessful because the segregations were too small. Observed Fe zoning does not establish iron speciation or prove substitution within the mineral lattice. The suggested hypogene origin and precipitation from fluids that corroded sphalerite are interpretations, not demonstrated reaction pathways. Temperatures inferred from other phases or analogous veins are not direct measurements on these crystals. This particular occurrence does not establish a universal origin, a bulk resource grade, or an extraction yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is assigned.

Electrical steel

Specialty iron-silicon alloy steel commodity engineered for magnetic core applications, including grain-oriented electrical steel, non-grain-oriented electrical steel, and amorphous steel within the scope of the 2023 US Department of Energy Critical Materials Assessment and Final 2023 Critical Materials List (88 FR 51792-51798). The DOE Notice defines electrical steel as essential to clean energy transformers and electric-motor technologies and designates it as a critical material for energy under Section 7002(a) of the Energy Act of 2020. USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 tracks grain-oriented electrical steel as a distinct defense-stockpile material line item within the Iron and Steel chapter (printed p. 100, PDF p. 104) and documents ferrosilicon consumption by the steel industry in the Silicon chapter (printed p. 170, PDF p. 174). This record represents the manufactured alloy commodity rather than elemental iron (cmmmech:iron), elemental silicon (cmmmech:silicon), a natural mineral species, or undifferentiated carbon and structural steels. No ChEBI or IMA identifier applies to this multi-grade engineered steel family, and no microbial extraction, processing, or recovery mechanism is asserted.

Elpidite

Elpidite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2ZrSi6O15(H2O)3. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records grandfathered status and the year 1894; this is not a numbered approval accession. The species is distinct from elemental zirconium, zircon, catapleiite and mixed zirconium-bearing rocks. Cegiełka and colleagues (2022) assigned natural elpidite in a loose block collected from the Dyrnaes River, south Greenland, whose green colour and mineralogy they attributed to the Ilímaussaq Green Granite. Their electron-microprobe analyses, microscopy and zirconium map show elpidite-labelled material enclosing zircon and catapleiite. This is the authors' mineral assignment from a heterogeneous natural specimen, not a sample-specific diffraction confirmation or a pure elpidite feed. Main-paper Table 6 includes both elpidite and altered elpidite; its ideal formula does not imply uniformly stoichiometric analyzed grains. The proposed late-magmatic formation sequence and later hydrothermal sodium loss are interpretations of textures and compositions, not controlled reaction experiments. The cited supplementary analyses and detailed analytical appendix were not acquired, so this record retains bounded main-paper occurrence context without importing whole-dataset ranges or calculating alteration yields. Table 4 and Table 6 both list analysis IL-356 under different material headings; that unresolved assignment is not treated as independent phase proof. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

Eosphorite

Eosphorite is the Mn2+-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula Mn2+Al(PO4)(OH)2(H2O), distinct from Fe2+-dominant childrenite. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1878. Gatta et al. (2013) examined fragments of one natural crystal from the Chamachhu granitic pegmatite area in Pakistan. Their 22 electron-microprobe spots characterize this crystal rather than 22 independent specimens. The analysis gives Mn0.940 and Fe0.061 atoms per formula unit on a one-P basis; water was calculated using assumed anion stoichiometry. Neutron diffraction at 20 K supports an orthorhombic Cmca model and locates hydrogen sites. The refined mixed metal site contains Fe0.056(1), close to the chemical analysis, without evidence of additional Mn/Fe ordering in this low-Fe specimen. The model assigns O3 to hydroxyl and O4 to statistically shared hydroxyl/water configurations, with the two mirror-related H2 positions mutually exclusive and approximately half occupied. This corrects the hydroxyl/water assignment in Hoyos et al. (1993), whose different natural Taquaral specimen nevertheless supported the same general Cmca framework. The older paper's two-water formula in its introduction and Table 2 is not adopted over the one-water IMA formula and 2013 analysis. The 2013 chemical analysis includes fluorine, but attempted O/F occupancy refinement was not meaningful; its deposited model omits F and must not be read as complete measured composition. Table 5 and the discussion label an O4-H1-O4 angle where the accompanying short contact is described through H2, so no exact value for that disputed hydrogen-bond label is curated. These are specimen-specific structural observations, without a demonstrated extraction, formation or microbial recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from manganese, aluminium or phosphorus.

IMA-approved silver-lead-bismuth sulfosalt mineral (IMA 2012-082; symbol Erw; status A, Approved 2013; full description published April 2026) with ideal end-member formula Ag8Pb12Bi16S40 (requiring Bi 41.92 wt%, Pb 31.76 wt%, S 16.08 wt%, Ag 10.82 wt%, printed total 100.00 wt% in Table 2 column IF on p. 242 and Section 4 on p. 241, whereas the arithmetic sum of the four rounded weight percentages is 100.58 wt%), representing the natural orthorhombic N = 8 (8,8L) member of the lillianite homologous series with ideal andersenite/gustavite substitution percentage Subst. = 66.67% and x = 8 (Topa et al., 2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:237-247). Discovered at an unnamed prospect at 2390 m above sea level west of "Blei Beul" ("Beim Bleibau") in the Erzwies mining area, Gastein Valley, Hohe Tauern, Salzburg Province, Austria (47 deg 05 min 40 sec N, 13 deg 02 min 15 sec E; sampled by Herbert Putz in summer 2002), where it occurs in quartz nests hosted by Mesozoic dolomitic marble and Palaeozoic chlorite-mica schist within a Cu-poor, Ag-Bi-rich sulfosalt assemblage associated with galena, heyrovskyite, treasurite, bismuthinite, pyrite, aikinite, krupkaite, gustavite, vikingite, eskimoite, ourayite, gold (electrum), tetradymite, and quartz; the holotype polished block containing the crystal fragment used for structure determination is deposited at the Natural History Museum Vienna (NHMW), Austria, under catalogue number O 2407 (and the species has also been reported from Kutna Hora, Czech Republic, with 1.95-2.96 wt% Sb, and from Altenberg, Salzburg Province, Austria). Forms black needle-like or anhedral crystals up to ~1-3 mm in length with a black streak, metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, brittle tenacity, irregular fracture, no observable cleavage or parting, Vickers microhardness VHN50 = 195-224 kg/mm2 (mean 210 kg/mm2, corresponding to Mohs hardness 3-3.5), and calculated density reported as Dcalc = 7.075 g/cm3 in the Abstract (p. 237) vs 7.045 g/cm3 (empirical formula) and 7.074 g/cm3 (structural formula) in Section 3 (p. 240). In reflected light it is greyish-white with distinct pleochroism and distinct anisotropy showing weak to moderate bluish-grey to brownish-grey rotation tints; Commission on Ore Mineralogy (COM) reflectance values in air (Rmin, Rmax in %; Table 1) are 44.5, 47.6% (470 nm), 41.9, 45.0% (546 nm), 41.5, 44.5% (589 nm), and 40.4, 43.6% (650 nm). Field-emission electron microprobe analysis (JEOL JXA-8530F, 25 kV, 20 nA, 1.5 um beam; Table 2) of the grain used for single-crystal X-ray diffraction (Grain 4, n = 6 points) yielded Bi 42.90(63) wt%, Pb 29.50(77) wt%, S 16.08(11) wt%, Ag 11.10(27) wt%, Te 0.21(14) wt%, Cd 0.17(1) wt%, Se 0.08(5) wt%, Cu 0.04(3) wt%, and Sb 0.00(0) wt%, total 100.10(63) wt% (arithmetic sum 100.08 wt%), giving on the basis of 76 atoms per formula unit (36 Me + 40 S, Z = 1) the empirical formula Ag8.18Cu0.05Pb11.31Cd0.12Bi16.30Sb0.01S39.81Te0.13Se0.06, simplified as (Ag,Cu)8.23(Pb,Cd)11.43(Bi,Sb)16.31(S,Te,Se)40.03 with Nchem = 7.91(26), Subst. = 69.01(11)%, and x = 8.16(40) (while all four analysed grains span 8.01L55.6 to 7.91L69.0). Crystallizes in the orthorhombic system, space group Cmcm (#63), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 4.085(5) A, b = 13.462(15) A, c = 33.92(4) A, V = 1866(4) A3, and Z = 1 for Ag8Pb12Bi16S40 (or Z = 4 in Table 3 for the quarter-formula Ag2Pb3Bi4S10; refined to R1 = 0.0524, R(all) = 0.0632, wR(on Fo^2) = 0.1232, and GoF = 1.138 for 308 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) out of 352 unique reflections from 1423 measured on a 0.035 x 0.045 x 0.09 mm fragment using MoKalpha radiation, where Section 5 on p. 242 contains a copy-paste typo referring to "the available crystal from Madoc" from the companion lopatkaite paper and the Fig. 8 caption on p. 244 twice spells the mineral "erwiesite"). The symmetric 8,8L lillianite-type structure contains five independent cation sites (Table 4): bicapped trigonal-prismatic Pb2 (Pb1.00, CN = 8, BVS = 1.968 v.u.) on the mirror planes separating alternating 8-octahedra-wide (311)PbS-like slabs, and four octahedral slab sites (CN = 6), comprising marginal Pb1 (Pb0.63(4)Ag0.37(4), BVS = 1.672 v.u.), purely occupied Bi1 (Bi1.00, BVS = 2.915 v.u.), mixed Bi2 (Bi0.45(4)Pb0.25Ag0.30(4), BVS = 2.107 v.u.), and central Bi3 (Bi0.59(4)Ag0.41(4), BVS = 2.168 v.u.), giving the structural formula Ag8.64Pb11.04Bi16.32S40 (Z = 1). Ezcurrite

Ezcurrite is the grandfathered sodium-borate mineral Na2B5O7(OH)3·2H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The list's 1957 entry is the original-description year, not an IMA approval number. Hurlbut and Aristarain's 1967 restudy characterized natural crystals from Tincalayu, Argentina, embedded in borax; possible rivadavite inclusions were invoked to explain the departure of the wet analysis from ideal composition. Cannillo, Dal Negro and Ungaretti's 1973 study established a triclinic P-1 structure containing pentaborate units linked into chains along c, with two tetrahedral and three trigonal boron sites per unit. That study did not repeat the chemical analysis or unit-cell determination for its fragment. Only five of seven hydrogen positions were located; one hydrogen from each water molecule remained unresolved. The 1967 proposed hydroxyl/water partition was superseded by this structural model. The historical comparison with Suhr's synthetic borate does not make nasinite or associated kernite interchangeable with ezcurrite. This mineral species is distinct from elemental boron and the borates commodity; criticality, microbial activity and industrial recovery are not inferred.

Falcondoite

Hydrous nickel-magnesium phyllosilicate mineral of the sepiolite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Ni4Si6O15(OH)2(H2O)2·4H2O (the Ni-dominant analogue of sepiolite, written [Ni8(H2O)4(OH)4Si12O30]·(H2O)8 for the 8-octahedral half-cell), status A, and approval number IMA 1976-018. Springer (1976) described the holotype specimen (ROM M 34324, Royal Ontario Museum, Toronto) from a 2 cm-wide whitish-green garnierite vein at 3 m depth crosscutting decomposed serpentinized harzburgite in the Loma Peguera lateritic nickel deposit worked by Falconbridge Dominicana C. por A. near Bonao, Dominican Republic, where it is intergrown with sepiolite, Ni-bearing talc, and serpentine. Bulk wet-chemical/XRF analysis after drying at 60 degrees C (Table 2, p. 408: SiO2 45.93, NiO 26.7, MgO 8.46, FeO 1.99, Cr2O3 0.45, Al2O3 0.39, MnO <0.01, CoO <0.01, LOI 15.0 wt%, plus 7 wt% moisture lost below 60 degrees C) and four electron-microprobe point analyses of pure falcondoite fibers (Analyses A-D, Table 2, average: SiO2 49.2, NiO 23.6 [range 20.1-27.6], MgO 9.26 [6.89-12.5], FeO <0.03, Al2O3 and Cr2O3 <0.05, H2O/LOI 18.0 wt%) gave the average probe formula {(Ni0.58Mg0.42)8(H2O)4(OH)4[Si12O30]}·(H2O)8. Powder X-ray diffraction (Table 1, p. 407) indexed on an orthorhombic sepiolite-type unit cell with a = 13.5, b = 26.9 A (printed as 26.9 A on p. 408 and misprinted as 29.9 A in the p. 407 abstract; both the reported cell volume V = 1903 A3 = 13.5 x 26.9 x 5.24 A3 and d060 = 4.48 A in Table 1 confirm b = 26.9 A), c = 5.24 A, Z = 2 (for the 8-octahedral formula) or Z = 4 (for Ni4Si6O15(OH)2(H2O)2·4H2O), Dmeas = 1.9(1) g/cm3 (low due to microporous fibrous aggregation), and Dcalc = 2.54 g/cm3 (biaxial with mean refractive index <1.55, Mohs hardness 2-3). Differential thermal and thermogravimetric analysis up to 1000 degrees C demonstrated four-stage dehydration (15.1 wt% total mass loss) followed by exothermic crystallization of orthopyroxene above 850 degrees C. Distinct from sepiolite, willemseite, pimelite, nepouite, and elemental nickel or magnesium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Felsőbányaite

Felsőbányaite is the hydrated aluminium hydroxysulfate mineral with ideal formula Al4(SO4)(OH)10·4H2O. The September 2026 IMA list records it as grandfathered, with 1854 in the original-description year column. This owner denotes the mineral species, not elemental aluminium, a bulk mine-water precipitate, or the separately listed hydrobasaluminite. Farkas and Pertlik (1997) characterized natural type-locality felsőbányaite and a Sussex specimen called basaluminite by chemistry and single-crystal diffraction, interpreting the latter as a microcrystalline variety of the former. Their reported monoclinic P21 structure contains aluminium-oxygen layers; beam-induced dehydration reduced structural accuracy, and hydrogen positions were not determined. Later work questions whether poorly ordered materials called basaluminite in acid-mine-drainage studies are structurally equivalent to the crystalline mineral. The 2017 Carrero article's accessible abstract flags this uncertainty; its detailed measurements are not curated here. Nomenclatural synonymy alone therefore does not transfer every basaluminite experiment to this owner. Microbial precipitation, extraction, recovery and industrial deployment are unassessed for this record. No criticality designation is inherited from aluminium.

Described by Tian, Li, Sun, Liu, Mao, Dong, Liu, Jian, Yao, Wang, and Ye (2026) from a galena–quartz vein sample at 380 m elevation of the H5 polymetallic sulfide orebody in the Haopinggou Ag–Pb–Zn–Au deposit (34°10'54" N, 111°16'55" E), Xiayu orefield, ~60 km southwest of Luoning County, Henan Province, eastern Qinling, China (named in honor of Rui Feng, born in 1963, a renowned geologist specializing in mineral exploration; holotype polished section and the X-ray-studied single crystal deposited in the Geological Museum of China, Beijing, under catalogue no. GMCTM2024004, pp. 519–520). Occurs as irregular strip-like grains less than 20 x 80 um intergrown with galena, cervelleite, and chalcopyrite (Fig. 3), with other vein minerals quartz, ankerite, electrum, and tetrahedrite-group minerals (plus pyrite and sphalerite in Fig. 2 and acanthite in Section 5.3, p. 527), deposited at intermediate temperatures (163–213 °C) from 7.2–14.0 wt% NaCl eq. aqueous fluids (Section 2, p. 520, Figs. 1–3). Kissin and Owens (1989) characterized the type material from Geological Survey of Canada specimen 14747 (cotypes GSC 65048 polished section A and British Museum (Natural History) BM 1984, 844 grain mount) from a greisen-bordered vein on the 60-m level of the Cligga mine (Cligga Head), Perranzabuloe, Cornwall, United Kingdom, corresponding to the low-temperature polymorph previously referred to in the literature as 'isostannite'. Electron-microprobe analysis of the Cligga mine holotype (Table 1 analysis 4 and Table 4 analysis 1, pp. 675 and 678) yielded Cu 28.9, Fe 8.6, Zn 5.0, Sn 27.0, S 29.5, total 100.9 wt%, corresponding on an 8-atom basis to the empirical formula Cu1.99(Fe0.67Zn0.33)Sigma1.00Sn0.99S4.02, with Fe > Zn at the divalent B site of the kësterite structure. Precession single- crystal and powder X-ray diffraction (Table 6, p. 680) indexed in tetragonal space group I-4 (a = 5.433(36), c = 10.884(89) A, Z = 2), distinguishing ferrokësterite from its high-temperature polymorph stannite (space group I-42m) and from the Zn-dominant end-member kësterite (Cu2ZnSnS4, space group I-4). The 1989 characterization used powder and precession photography without a new single-crystal site-occupancy refinement on the Cligga mine holotype. Distinct from stannite, kësterite, petrukite, sakuraiite, and elemental tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Florencite-(Ce)

Florencite-(Ce) is the cerium-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral CeAl3(PO4)2(OH)6. It is distinct from other florencite species, the broader crandallite group, cerium as an element and mixed coal wastes containing REE-bearing particles. Li and colleagues (2022) synthesized a cerium phosphate preparation assigned to florencite by powder diffraction and morphology, then examined solid composition after alkaline treatment and subsequent acid leaching. These are abiotic laboratory experiments on a synthetic analogue. Changes in SEM-EDS composition support a qualified preferential-leaching interpretation; they do not quantify a mineral-specific extraction or isolated-product yield. The same article's bulk coal-waste recovery percentages and particle classifications are not transferred to this mineral. Microbial activity, criticality and industrial deployment are unrecorded.

Florencite-(La)

Florencite-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula LaAl3(PO4)2(OH)6, distinct from florencite-(Ce), other florencite species, elemental lanthanum and mixed rare-earth ores. The September 2026 IMA list records renamed status and the 1987 special procedure; this is not a numbered species accession or a critical-material designation. Lefebvre and Gasparrini (1980) characterized natural La-rich grains in a Shituru drill-core siltstone, using electron-microprobe chemistry, optical properties and powder diffraction. The Shituru analysis has La as the dominant measured rare earth; Pr was detected qualitatively but not quantified, and water was not measured. Reported rare-earth proportions therefore are not a complete independently measured end-member formula. The diffraction pattern from an extracted 60-micrometre crystal supported florencite identity, while a mixed hematite-florencite concentrate gave only one attributable reflection. The origin was interpreted from geology, with hydrothermal and later supergene alternatives; no controlled formation experiment was performed. Ghignone et al. (2024) separately examined a collection specimen F1 from Igarape Bahia, Brazil. Its unpolished, uncoated SEM-EDS measurements are explicitly semiquantitative, with an oxide total of 35.6 wt%, and cannot be treated as a complete bulk assay or proof of a pure La end-member. The measured Raman spectra of compositionally different florencites are similar; Raman matching alone cannot resolve the dominant rare-earth species. The computed ideal La structure and vibrational modes are models, not a new experimental single-crystal refinement of F1. No microbial mechanism, recovery yield, dated criticality claim or industrial deployment is established by these characterization studies.

IMA:1985-038
Fritzscheite

Fritzscheite is the manganese uranyl vanadate mineral Mn2+(UO2)2(VO4)2·4H2O. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list recognizes it with grandfathered status G; 1865 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval accession. This mineral-species owner is distinct from elemental manganese, uranium and vanadium, dissolved salts, other carnotite-group species and mixed uranium ore. Glasauer et al. (2022) assigned fritzscheite and metatyuyamunite to the starting natural uranium-vanadium sandstone using diffraction and composition. The paper reports fritzscheite as Mn(UO2)2(V2O8)·H2O, which differs in hydration from the current IMA formula; this record retains the authors' phase assignment without silently equating that reported hydration with the canonical species formula. Following incubation with living Shewanella putrefaciens CN32, fritzscheite was not detected by bulk X-ray diffraction in the final fine fraction, which contained K-carnotite and metatyuyamunite. Figure 1b and sections 3.1 and 3.3 support this detection comparison, not a quantitative disappearance or extraction yield. Mn and Ba concentrations in the fine fraction were relatively unchanged, so absence of its diffraction signature does not establish removal of those elements. Section 4.1 states that individual starting- mineral behavior could not be resolved. The conclusion assigns fritzscheite-to-K-carnotite conversion through interlayer-cation replacement, whereas section 3.2 names tyuyamunite as a precursor; this record does not select a unique pathway or claim that microbial activity was necessary for that phase replacement. The shared laboratory experiment used 1.6 g of mixed sandstone in 80 mL defined medium with 10 mM sodium lactate and 1 mM phosphate, nitrogen degassing and autoclaving before inoculation, followed by an anoxic glovebox incubation extending to ten months. Treatments were in triplicate. These three mineral records refer to the same experiment, not independent replications. Bacteria-free solution controls were included, but do not isolate each phase's fate. The mixed-ore spectra support partial V reduction while U remained predominantly U(VI); results from the separate soluble-salt arm must not be transferred to this mineral. Dissolved U was low, rather than established to be exactly zero. Section 3.2 gives a V plateau time of 120 days while Figure 2 labels the time axes in hours, so no exact kinetic endpoint is adopted. The species identity and bounded starting-phase context are curated without a mineral-specific mechanism assertion. No complete dissolution, isolated product recovery or industrial deployment is demonstrated, and no criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

Chao and Watkinson (1974) described the cotype specimens (National Museum of Natural Sciences, Ottawa, T73/2-1 and T73/2-2) from nepheline syenite pegmatites at Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada, as an orthorhombic dimorph of catapleiite associated with hilairite, analcime, nenadkevichite, and epididymite. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis combined with thermogravimetric H2O determination (Table 3, p. 318) yielded SiO2 42.51, ZrO2 30.21, Nb2O5 3.00, TiO2 0.42, Na2O 13.11, K2O 2.20, H2O 9.25, total 100.70 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 9 anhydrous O atoms to the empirical formula (Na1.72K0.19)Sigma1.91(Zr1.00Nb0.09Ti0.02)Sigma1.11Si2.88O9·2.10H2O. Chao (1985) solved the crystal structure in acentric orthorhombic space group P21nb (a = 11.740(3), b = 12.820(3), c = 6.691(1) A, V = 1007.03 A3, Z = 4, R = 3.92%, Rw = 3.60% for 1211 observed reflections with I > 3sigma(I) out of 1280 unique reflections), demonstrating sinuous [Si3O9]n6n- chains along [101] cross-linked by isolated [ZrO6] octahedra and two distorted [NaO4(H2O)2] and [NaO3(H2O)3] octahedra. Donnay and Chao (1986) corrected a typographical error in Table 2 of Chao (1985) for the O(5) y coordinate (0.0149 rather than 0.1940, giving Si(2)-O(5) = 1.594(5) A instead of 2.660 A) and established double-donor hydrogen bonding of both H2O molecules OW(10) and OW(11). Distinct from catapleiite, georgechaoite (NaKZrSi3O9·2H2O), hilairite, and elemental zirconium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Germanite

Germanite is the copper-iron-germanium sulfide mineral species Cu13Fe2Ge2S16, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered, with 1922 as the original-description year rather than an IMA approval number. The 1984 powder-XRD study of Tsumeb material uses the equivalent doubled formula Cu26Ge4Fe4S32 and supports a cubic structure, while explicitly retaining intergrown impurities and unresolved cation-site assignments. Its ideal formula does not establish the composition or purity of every specimen. The Handbook describes occurrence in dolostone-hosted hydrothermal copper-lead-zinc ore at Tsumeb and association with renierite and other sulfides. These are geological observations, not current production or recovery-performance claims. Germanite is distinct from germanium element, a mixed ore feed and renierite; no microbial mechanism or inherited criticality designation is assigned. The Handbook's printed F-43n space-group label conflicts with P-43n in the primary refinement, so it is not silently treated as confirming that primary space-group assignment.

CHEBI:30441
Gersdorffite

Gersdorffite is the nickel sulfarsenide mineral species with ideal formula NiAsS and cubic space group P2₁3. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list records it as renamed in 2022. CNMNC Newsletter 69 explicitly renamed gersdorffite-P2₁3 as gersdorffite, gersdorffite-Pa3 as paragersdorffite, and gersdorffite-Pca2₁ as orthogersdorffite; these other polymorphs are distinct species, not aliases of this record. Mauro and colleagues (2021, Section 3.1.1, Tables 1 and 3-5, Figures 2-4, and the original CIF) characterized natural zoned crystals from Contrada Zillì, Sicily, by electron-microprobe analysis and powder and single-crystal diffraction. The studied crystal has P2₁3 symmetry and a = 5.6968(7) Å. The specimen contains other minerals, and the gersdorffite grains show Fe/Co substitution and Sb/Bi-bearing zoning; this is not a pure bulk NiAsS feed. The proposed low-temperature, multistage geological origin is an interpretation of crystal chemistry and textures, not an experimentally demonstrated formation mechanism. Jaatinen's 2011 thesis supplies contextual mixed-concentrate leaching evidence under the older name: its GFC feed mineralogy, inherited from Wakeman et al. (2011), reports 30.6% gersdorffite but does not resolve the polymorph required by the current nomenclature. The GFC flask assays showed low culture activity and no consistent biological enhancement over their chemical controls. Dissolved metals from this mixed feed cannot establish dissolution of today's gersdorffite species or a recovered-product yield. A species-specific microbial mechanism and criticality designation are therefore unrecorded.

Ginelfite

IMA-approved complex silver-thallium-lead-antimony-arsenic boxwork sulfosalt mineral (IMA 2022-110; symbol Glf; status A, Approved 2023; full description published May 2025) with ideal end-member formula Ag2(Ag0.5Fe2+0.5)TlPb24.5(Sb,As)32.5S75.5 reported in the primary type description title, abstract, Section 4.1, and Table 7 (Biagioni et al., 2025, European Journal of Mineralogy 37:319-335; note that Table 8 on p. 332 prints the formula with S76 as Ag2(Ag0.5Fe0.5)TlPb24.5(Sb,As)32.5S76, and the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List, PDF p. 82, lists the pre-refinement formula Ag2(Ag0.5Fe2+0.5)TlPb23.5(Sb,As)33.5S76 prior to recognizing the half-occupancy of the S(71) site and final Pb/(Sb,As) site assignments). Named in honour of Carlo Gini (born 1954; technician from 1988 to 2019) and Francesco Guelfi (born 1947; technician from 1981 to 2011), former technicians at the X-ray laboratory of the Dipartimento di Scienze della Terra of the Universita di Pisa, by combining their surnames. Discovered in specimens collected by co-authors Georges Favreau, Jean-Claude Boulliard, and Vincent Bourgoin during a sampling campaign authorized by the Ecrins National Park at the Tl-rich hydrothermal deposit of Jas Roux, La Chapelle-en-Valgaudemar, Hautes-Alpes department, France (44 deg 44 min 45 sec N, 6 deg 19 min 18 sec E), from the centre of the cliff of the tectonic block indicated as "compartiment 2" by Mantienne (1974), where the Tl-Hg-Ag-Sb-As mineralization occurs within a 3.8 m thick baryte-rich zone hosted in Triassic metadolostone and marble (matching the earlier unnamed mineral UM2000-44-S:AgAsPbSb of Smith and Nickel, 2007, first reported by Mantienne, 1974, indicated as "madocite argento-thallifere" by Moelo, 1983, and examined by Johan and Mantienne, 2000). In type material, ginelfite occurs associated with Fe-poor sphalerite (pale brownish grains with trace Cd) and lopatkaite (5 spot analyses averaging Pb 55.82(29), As 3.80(8), Sb 20.98(8), S 19.93(6), total 100.52(30) wt%, corresponding on a 20 apfu basis to Pb4.84(3)Sb3.09(1)As0.91(2)S11.16(3), Ev(%) = -2.8(6)%) within a silicified matrix devoid of vugs, with baryte and quartz; holotype material is deposited in the collections of the Museo di Storia Naturale of the Universita di Pisa, Calci (PI), Italy (catalogue number 20023) and in the collections of the Department of Mineralogy and Petrology, National Museum in Prague, Czech Republic (catalogue number P1P 31/2022). Forms dark-grey acicular crystals up to 0.5 mm in length with a black streak, metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, brittle tenacity, conchoidal fracture, no observed cleavage, calculated density Dcalc = 5.765 g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell parameters, and historical Vickers microhardness VHN25 = 165 kg/mm2 (range 157-170 kg/mm2 for five indentations on five grains; Johan and Mantienne, 2000), corresponding to a Mohs hardness of 3 to 3.5. In reflected light in air, ginelfite is light grey with weak pleochroism and weak bireflectance, moderate anisotropism with weak brownish and blue tints, and no internal reflections; Commission on Ore Mineralogy (COM) reflectance values in air (Rmin, Rmax in %; MSP400 TIDAS spectrophotometer, 50x objective, WTiC Zeiss 370 standard; Table 1) are 35.4, 38.1% (470 nm), 34.6, 37.0% (546 nm), 33.7, 36.0% (589 nm), and 32.3, 34.6% (650 nm). Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (35 spot analyses, Cameca SX 100, 25 kV, 20 nA, 1 um beam diameter; Table 2) yielded Pb 45.44 wt% (range 44.81-45.83, e.s.d. 0.21), Sb 23.46 wt% (23.10-23.94, e.s.d. 0.19), S 21.07 wt% (20.62-21.32, e.s.d. 0.14), As 6.17 wt% (5.84-6.48, e.s.d. 0.17), Ag 2.34 wt% (2.20-2.42, e.s.d. 0.05), Tl 1.14 wt% (0.98-1.34, e.s.d. 0.09), Fe 0.22 wt% (0.20-0.25, e.s.d. 0.01), and Cu 0.07 wt% (0.00-0.09, e.s.d. 0.02), total 99.91 wt% (range 99.21-100.59, e.s.d. 0.32), corresponding on the basis of SigmaMe = 61 atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula Cu0.12(4)Ag2.51(5)Fe0.46(3)Tl0.65(5)Pb25.40(14)Sb22.32(18)As9.54(24)S76.12(74) (Sb + As = 31.86(12) apfu, Sb/(Sb + As) = 0.701(7), and relative error on valence equilibrium Ev(%) = -1.1(1.0)% with range -2.3 to +1.7% in Table 2 assuming Fe as Fe2+, or -0.8(1.0)% if Fe occurs as Fe3+). Crystallizes in the triclinic system, space group P-1 (#2), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 8.3635(6) A, b = 27.5481(19) A, c = 29.199(2) A, alpha = 95.335(3) deg, beta = 94.123(3) deg, gamma = 94.367(3) deg, V = 6657.7(8) A3, and Z = 2 (refined with twin ratio 62.2 : 37.8(2) around [100] to R1 = 0.0876, R(all) = 0.1131, wR2 = 0.1764, and GoF = 1.221 for 23,779 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) out of 30,492 unique reflections from 291,055 measured at 293(2) K using MoKalpha radiation, Table 4). The zinkenite-related boxwork sulfosalt structure (organized around two symmetry-independent Pb6S6 triangular rods) contains 61 independent cation sites (21 pure Pb sites Pb(1)-Pb(19), Pb(21), and Pb(22); 1 mixed ninefold tricapped trigonal prismatic Tl(20) site Tl0.65Pb0.35 with <Tl(20)-S> = 3.29 A and BVS = 1.30 v.u.; 12 mixed Pb/Sb sites M(1)-M(12) with M(9)-M(12) split into a/b sub-positions; 24 Sb/As sites comprising 8 pure Sb sites, 1 pure As site As(20) with <As(20)-S> = 2.27 A and BVS = 3.15 v.u., and 15 mixed Sb/As sites including split Sb(21a)/Sb(21b); 2 pure Ag sites Ag(1) and Ag(2) in 4+1 trigonal dipyramidal coordination with <Ag-S> = 2.78 and 2.79 A and BVS = 1.05 and 1.04 v.u.; and 1 mixed (Ag,Fe) site Ag(3) with refined occupancy Ag0.51(2)Fe0.49(2) in distorted 4+2 octahedral coordination, <Ag(3)-S> = 2.70 A, and BVS = 1.68 v.u.) and 76 independent S sites (including half-occupied S(71), occupancy 0.50; Tables 5-6), built by combining three boxwork modules: partition rod A (3 polyhedra wide x 4 atomic layers thick, Me12S16), fill-element rod B (4 atomic layers thick, Me14S18), and continuous (001) wall layer C (Me35S42, formed by two-atomic-layer-thick ribbons R1, R2, and R3), whose modular formula sum on p. 328 is (Ag0.51Fe0.49)Ag2(Tl0.65Pb0.35)Pb21(Sb7.59Pb4.41)Sigma12.00(Sb15.52As8.48)Sigma24.00S75.5 (Ev = -1.7%). The seven strongest observed Gandolfi powder X-ray diffraction lines highlighted in bold in Table 3 (dobs in A (Iobs; dcalc, Icalc, hkl), CuKalpha) are 3.413 (s; 3.417, 48, 0 8 0; 3.395, 84, 0 4 7; 3.393, 28, -2 -2 5; 3.393, 27, 2 -3 4), 2.965 (s; 2.960, 15, 2 -5 5; 2.957, 32, -2 4 6; 2.956, 34, 2 3 5), 2.805 (ms; 2.816, 13, -2 -5 6; 2.816, 17, 2 -6 5), 2.729 (ms; 2.733, 19, 0 10 0; 2.732, 17, -2 7 4; 2.732, 10, 2 -4 7; 2.731, 20, 2 6 3), 2.091 (vs; 2.091, 100, -4 1 1), 1.872 (ms; 1.873, 17, 2 -13 5; 1.873, 15, -2 -12 6), and 1.785 (ms; 1.780, 13, 4 3 6). Ginorite

Ginorite is the grandfathered calcium borate species listed as Ca2B14O20(OH)6(H2O)3·2H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its 1934 entry is a description year, not an approval identifier. The older Ca2[B14O20(OH)6]·5H2O formula has the same elemental stoichiometry. A natural Sasso Pisano crystal studied by Perchiazzi et al. has a monoclinic P21/a structure with borate sheets, calcium sites and hydrogen bonding; three water molecules per formula unit coordinate calcium and two do not. Hydrogen positions were refined with O-H distance restraints. The study's tabulated chemical analyses came from earlier publications, while its own preliminary SEM/EDAX screen found strontium below detection. This species is distinct from strontioginorite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Neither a criticality designation nor microbial extraction or commercial recovery is inferred from its boron content.

Anhydrous calcium-zirconium sorosilicate (pyrosilicate) mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula CaZrSi2O7, status A, and approval number IMA 1979-034. Ansell, Roberts, Plant, and Sturman (1980) described the holotype specimen (Geological Survey of Canada No. 19558) as chalky fine-grained intergrowths with apophyllite after eudialyte in pegmatitic lenses of the Kipawa River peralkaline alkalic complex, Villedieu Township, Temiscaming County, Quebec, Canada. Electron-microprobe analysis of the Kipawa holotype (p. 203) yielded CaO 18.4, ZrO2 40.3, SiO2 40.8, total 99.5 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 7 O atoms to the empirical formula Ca0.98Zr0.98Si2.03O7, with initial powder X-ray diffraction indexed on a monoclinic cell (a = 6.878(4), b = 8.674(4), c = 4.697(2) A, beta = 101.74(4) degrees, V = 274.34 A3, Z = 2). Roelofsen-Ahl and Peterson (1989) solved the single-crystal structure on a specimen from the Strange Lake peralkaline granite, Quebec-Labrador, Canada (NMC 66057; WDS composition CaO 18.8, FeO 0.3, PbO 0.2, ZrO2 40.3, SiO2 40.8, F 0.2, less O=F 0.1, total 100.5 wt%) in acentric monoclinic space group C2 (a = 6.852(2), b = 8.659(1), c = 4.686(2) A, beta = 101.69(2) degrees, V = 272.(1) A3, Z = 2, R = 3.1%, Rw = 3.9% for 513 observed reflections with I > 3sigma(I) out of 522 unique reflections), showing that ordering of [CaO6] and [ZrO6] octahedra within the octahedral sheets and bending of the pyrosilicate [Si2O7]6- bridge (Si-O1-Si = 147.4(5) degrees) lower the symmetry from the ideal C2/m thortveitite aristotype to C2. Distinct from armstrongite, vlasovite, eudialyte, and elemental zirconium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

CHEBI:29287
Goldmanite

Goldmanite is the calcium-vanadium garnet mineral with ideal formula Ca3V3+2(SiO4)3, status A and approval 1963-003 in the September 2026 IMA list. It is distinct from elemental vanadium, generic vanadium-bearing garnet and mixed uranium-vanadium ore. Moench and Meyrowitz described fine natural grains from a prospect pit in the Sandy mine area, Laguna district, New Mexico. The chemically analyzed separate was a substituted garnet, calculated as 59.8 mole percent goldmanite endmember with grossular, andradite, pyrope and spessartite components; this is a composition calculation, not a phase fraction or recovery yield. Its total vanadium was reported as V2O3, but the authors explicitly could not determine vanadium and iron valences chemically and inferred trivalence from crystal chemistry. Earlier unusually high vanadium assays may have included spinel contamination. The ideal species formula therefore does not describe every natural grain as a pure endmember. Abiotic laboratory syntheses are documented below. No criticality designation is inherited from vanadium, and these studies do not establish microbial extraction or industrial recovery.

Gorceixite

Gorceixite is the barium aluminium phosphate mineral with current IMA formula BaAl3(PO4)(PO3OH)(OH)6, distinct from calcium-dominant crandallite, strontium-dominant goyazite and cerium-dominant florencite-(Ce). The September 2026 IMA list records it as grandfathered, with original-description year 1906. Dzikowski, Groat and Jambor (2006) directly characterized a natural crystal from Crosscut Creek in the Rapid Creek area, Yukon, Canadian Museum of Nature specimen 51269. Electron-microprobe analysis and room-temperature single-crystal diffraction support a Ba-Al phosphate crystal with R-3m symmetry, a=7.0538(3) and c=17.2746(6) angstrom, refined using 253 unique reflections. This specimen-specific result does not overturn monoclinic Cm assignments for all other gorceixite specimens; the authors explicitly retain compositional and locality differences and an unresolved reason for symmetry variation. Chemistry suggests nearly full Ba occupation, whereas the crystallographic Ba occupancy refines to 0.882(6); proposed absorption/scattering explanations are unresolved. Hydrogen-related constraints and an inferred O/OH distribution support charge balance but do not locate every hydrogen atom directly. The study provides natural-mineral identity evidence, not an experimentally demonstrated formation, leaching, microbial extraction or industrial recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from its constituent elements.

Gowerite is the Ca(H2O)[B5O8(OH)][B(OH)3]·2H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with approved status A and special-procedure notation 1962 s.p.; the notation is not a unique approval identifier. The older CaO·3B2O3·5H2O and Ca[B5O8(OH)][B(OH)3]·3H2O formulas have the same elemental stoichiometry. Graphite anode material for lithium-ion batteries

Graphite raw-material products manufactured and supplied as active material for lithium-ion battery negative electrodes. This end-use commodity family is a subset of the broader graphite commodity family, not a second disjoint graphite identity; no single origin or numerical qualification threshold is assigned to all members. SGL Carbon describes synthetic graphite anode materials with properties tailored to customer applications and distinguishes them from carbon-silicon composites and conductive additives. The record excludes complete electrodes, electric-arc-furnace electrodes and spent battery waste. SAMR names the product standard GB/T 24533-2019 for graphite negative-electrode materials, but its full technical tables were not inspected. Manufacturer use and testing descriptions establish product context, not a universal battery-grade purity rule or a microbial recovery result. No criticality designation is generalized from the broader graphite record.

Graulichite-(La)

IMA-approved lanthanum iron arsenate hydroxide mineral of the dussertite group in the alunite supergroup (IMA 2020-093; status A, Approved 2021; full description published June 2022) with ideal end-member formula LaFe3+3(AsO4)2(OH)6 (requiring As2O5 33.49 wt%, Fe2O3 34.90 wt%, La2O3 23.74 wt%, H2O 7.88 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Biagioni et al., 2022, European Journal of Mineralogy 34:365-374). Represents the La-dominant analogue of graulichite-(Ce) and the Fe3+-dominant analogue of arsenoflorencite-(La) in accordance with Levinson REE nomenclature. Discovered on a specimen originally collected in the late 1960s by Jacques Emile Dietrich in the active underground workings of the Patte d'Oie mine, Bou Skour Cu-hydrothermal mining district, Djebel Saghro mountain range, ~50 km southeast of Ouarzazate, Anti-Atlas, Morocco, where it formed by oxidation of primary sulfide-bearing quartz veins (chalcopyrite, bornite, chalcocite, galena, and tetrahedrite-group minerals) and occurs on malachite grown on iron oxides in association with malachite, agardite-(La), conichalcite, and an undetermined synchysite-like REE carbonate; the holotype specimen is deposited in the Museo di Storia Naturale, University of Pisa, Calci (Pisa), Italy, under catalogue number 19924. Forms yellow rhombohedral crystals up to 0.1 mm in size (internally porous and composed of very thin fragile laminae) with a light-yellow streak, resinous lustre, transparent diaphaneity, very weak pleochroism from light yellow to yellow, non-fluorescence, brittle tenacity, irregular fracture, no observed cleavage or parting, estimated Mohs hardness ~3.5, Gladstone-Dale mean refractive index n = 1.889 (Domain #1) and 1.928 (Domain #2), and calculated density Dcalc = 3.907 g/cm3 (for Domain #1) and 3.962 g/cm3 (for Domain #2). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser, 50x objective, 6.25 mW; Figure 3) displays bands at 846 cm-1 (strongest band, nu1 symmetric stretching of (AsO4) groups), 995 and 1092 cm-1 (nu1 and nu3 stretching modes of (SO4) and (PO4) groups), 714 cm-1 (O-H deformation modes), 466 cm-1 (strongest bending band, nu4 mode of (AsO4) groups with a low-wavenumber nu2 (SO4) shoulder), 565 and 618 cm-1 (nu4 modes of (SO4) and nu2 modes of (PO4) groups), 330 cm-1 and lower wavenumbers (M-O and lattice vibrations), a broad weak O-H stretching band between 2900 and 3800 cm-1, an unattributed sharp feature at 2906 cm-1, and a band at 1441 cm-1 interpreted as (SO4) overtone modes. Wavelength- dispersive electron microprobe analysis (JEOL JXA 8200, 20 kV, 10 nA, 1 um beam on an unpolished flat crystal surface due to fragility; Table 1) identified two chemically homogeneous domains (n = 4 spot analyses each) with low raw analytical totals due to crystal porosity: Domain #1 yielded Fe2O3 22.52(22) wt% (normalized 28.75 wt%), As2O5 18.55(28) wt% (norm. 23.68 wt%), La2O3 7.16(18) wt% (norm. 9.14 wt%), Al2O3 5.63(11) wt% (norm. 7.19 wt%), Ce2O3 4.28(13) wt% (norm. 5.46 wt%), SO3 3.90(16) wt% (norm. 4.98 wt%), P2O5 3.65(36) wt% (norm. 4.66 wt%), CuO 2.06(12) wt% (norm. 2.63 wt%), PbO 1.36(20) wt% (norm. 1.74 wt%), SrO 0.97(9) wt% (norm. 1.24 wt%), CaO 0.79(2) wt% (norm. 1.01 wt%), K2O 0.25(2) wt% (norm. 0.32 wt%), and H2Ocalc 7.22 wt% (norm. 9.22 wt%), total 78.34 wt% (norm. printed as 100.00 wt%, arithmetic sum 100.02 wt%), giving on the basis of 6 cations and 14 O atoms per formula unit the empirical formula (La0.34Ce0.20Ca0.11Sr0.07Pb0.05K0.04)Sigma0.81(Fe3+2.16Al0.84Cu0.20)Sigma3.20(As1.23P0.39S0.37)Sigma1.99O14H6.13; Domain #2 yielded Fe2O3 28.60(128) wt% (norm. 34.19 wt%), As2O5 14.48(73) wt% (norm. 17.31 wt%), La2O3 8.59(35) wt% (norm. 10.27 wt%), P2O5 4.89(55) wt% (norm. 5.85 wt%), Ce2O3 4.87(31) wt% (norm. 5.82 wt%), SO3 4.40(56) wt% (norm. 5.26 wt%), Al2O3 3.41(36) wt% (norm. 4.08 wt%), CuO 2.15(8) wt% (norm. 2.57 wt%), PbO 1.62(34) wt% (norm. 1.94 wt%), SrO 1.46(30) wt% (norm. 1.75 wt%), CaO 0.69(8) wt% (norm. 0.82 wt%), K2O 0.40(8) wt% (norm. 0.48 wt%), and H2Ocalc 8.10 wt% (norm. 9.68 wt%), total 83.66 wt% (norm. printed as 100.00 wt%, arithmetic sum 100.02 wt%), giving (La0.38Ce0.22Sr0.10Ca0.09Pb0.05K0.06)Sigma0.90(Fe3+2.60Al0.49Cu0.20)Sigma3.29(As0.91P0.50S0.40)Sigma1.81O14H6.53. Crystallizes in the trigonal system, space group R-3m (#166), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 7.252(13) A, c = 16.77(3) A, V = 764(3) A3, c : a = 2.3125, and Z = 3 (refined isotropically with fixed Uiso and 7 parameters to R1 = 0.0956 for 36 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) and R(all data) = 0.1222, wR(on Fo^2) = 0.2162, Goof = 1.237 for 47 unique reflections up to 2theta = 31.75 deg from 118 measured on a 0.040 x 0.035 x 0.030 mm lamina using MoKalpha radiation, Table 3; Gandolfi CuKalpha powder data refined from 13 reflections to a = 7.2469(9) A, c = 16.767(2) A, V = 762.59(17) A3). The alunite-type hexagonal tungsten bronze (HTB) layered structure (Tables 4-6) comprises 12-fold-coordinated A sites (<A-O> = 2.78 A, s.o.f. La0.95, BVS = 2.22 v.u.), octahedral B sites (<B-O> = 1.98 A, s.o.f. Fe0.94, BVS = 3.20 v.u.), and tetrahedral X sites (<X-O> = 1.58 A, s.o.f. As0.70, BVS = 5.49 v.u., where an apparent bond-length inversion X-O(1) = 1.65(9) A vs X-O(2) = 1.56(5) A x 3 is noted by the authors as an artifact of low data resolution). The eight strongest observed Gandolfi X-ray powder diffraction lines (dobs in A (Iobs; dcalc, Icalc, hkl), CuKalpha, Table 2) are 5.86 (m; 5.88, 60, 1 0 1), 3.045 (s; 3.042, 100, 1 1 3), 2.511 (mw; 2.513, 17, 0 2 4), 2.239 (m; 2.238, 24, 1 0 7), 1.960 (mw; 1.960, 24, 0 3 3), 1.813 (mw; 1.813, 23, 2 2 0), 1.689 (mw; 1.686, 5, 2 1 7), and 1.478 (m; 1.479, 10, 0 2 10). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.
