Grimmite

Grimmite (IMA 2020-060) is an IMA-accepted cubic nickel-cobalt sulfide mineral of the spinel supergroup, thiospinel group, linnaeite subgroup (filling the 0.50 <= x <= 1.50 compositional interval of the Co(3-x)NixS4 solid-solution series between linnaeite Co2+Co3+2S4 and siegenite CoNi2S4), with September 2026 IMA Master List ideal formula NiCo2S4 (status A, PDF p. 86; ideal composition Ni 19.26, Co 38.67, S 42.07, total 100.00 wt%) and single-crystal grain empirical formula Ni1.01(Co1.99Fe0.06Pb0.01Bi0.01)Sigma2.07S3.92 on the basis of 7 apfu (Škácha et al. 2021, pp. 175, 177–178). WDS electron-microprobe analysis of the single-crystal structure grain (n = 13 points at 15 kV, 20 nA, 1 um beam; Table 2, p. 177) gave Ni 19.27 (range 18.62–20.59), Co 38.23 (36.39–39.36), Fe 1.16 (0.95–1.53), Bi 0.62 (0–1.30), Pb 0.46 (0.24–0.92), As 0.09 (0–0.56), Cu 0.08 (0–0.21), Mn 0.03 (0–0.14), S 41.05 (40.28–41.87), total 100.99 wt%; across all 125 point analyses from the cotype polished sections (83 Fe-poor points with Fe <= 0.14 apfu and 42 Fe-enriched points, Table 3, p. 178), CoFe-1 substitution reaches up to 0.88 apfu Fe (15.57 wt% Fe in spot 15). Described by Škácha, Sejkora, Plášil, Dolníček, and Ulmanová (2021) from the mine dump of shaft no. 9, Jerusalem deposit, Příbram uranium and base-metal district, central Bohemia, Czech Republic (49°40'12.806" N, 14°1'48.102" E; two cotype polished sections deposited at the National Museum, Prague, catalogue number P1P 49/2020, and the Mining Museum Příbram, catalogue number 3/2020), where it occurs in siderite–sphalerite gangue cementing brecciated Upper Proterozoic greenish-black shale (pp. 175–176). Strongly zoned aggregates of skutterudite-subgroup minerals (skutterudite, nickelskutterudite, and ferroskutterudite) rimmed by nickeline and gersdorffite (with occasional glaucodot and arsenopyrite) were hydrothermally leached during precipitation of younger siderite II, and the leached cavities were filled by quartz containing pyrite, sphalerite II, grimmite, galena, Bi-rich ullmannite, bismuthinite, parkerite, and xenomorphic jaipurite (CoS) inclusions within grimmite (pp. 176–177, Fig. 2). Named in honor of Johann Grimm (1805–1874), second director of the Příbram Mining College; material of this composition was previously referred to in the mineralogical literature under the unapproved name "nickellinnaeite" (pp. 176, 180–182). Forms idiomorphic to hypidiomorphic isometric grains up to 200 x 70 um or veinlet aggregates up to 500 x 30 um, grey with a pinkish tint, metallic lustre, opaque, no cleavage observed, uneven fracture, estimated Mohs hardness 4.5–5.5 by analogy with linnaeite-subgroup thiospinels, Dcalc = 4.96 g/cm3 (for the empirical formula) and 4.89 g/cm3 (for ideal NiCo2S4; 4.843 g/cm3 for the refined structural formula in Table 5, p. 179); in reflected light in air it is creamy grey with a pinkish tint and isotropic, with COM reflectance values (R%, Table 1, p. 177) of 42.5 (470 nm), 45.9 (546 nm), 47.7 (589 nm), and 50.2 (650 nm). Cubic, space group Fd-3m (Z = 8), a = 9.3933(9) Å, V = 828.81(14) Å3; single-crystal X-ray diffraction on a 0.028 x 0.009 x 0.007 mm FIB-SEM extracted fragment (MoKalpha, lambda = 0.71073 Å, 79 unique / 76 observed reflections with I > 3sigma(I) refined to Robs = 0.0539, wRobs = 0.1746, Rall = 0.0554, wRall = 0.1753, GOF(obs) = 1.46 in Table 5, p. 179; printed as R = 0.0489 on 735 observed reflections in the abstract on p. 175) places Ni at the tetrahedral Wyckoff site 8b (T–S1 = 2.1866(10) Å x 4) and Co at the octahedral Wyckoff site 16c (M–S1 = 2.2635(10) Å x 6; Table 6, p. 179), with seven strongest calculated CuKalpha powder X-ray diffraction lines [d in Å (Irel) (hkl)] at 3.3210 (74.7)(220), 2.7116 (7.2)(222), 2.3483 (80.7)(400), 1.9174 (26.7)(422), 1.6605 (100.0)(440), 1.4852 (10.6)(620), and 1.3558 (15.1)(444) (Table 4, p. 179). Distinct from linnaeite (Co2+Co3+2S4), siegenite (CoNi2S4), polydymite (Ni2+Ni3+2S4), violarite (Fe2+Ni3+2S4), carrollite (CuCo2S4), and elemental nickel or cobalt; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Gysinite-(Nd)

A natural lead-neodymium carbonate mineral of the ancylite group, distinct from its La- and Ce- dominant counterparts and from synthetic Pb-free Nd carbonates. The September 2026 IMA list gives PbNd(CO3)2(OH)(H2O), status renamed and 1987 special procedure; that date records nomenclature action, not a species-specific approval accession. Sarp and Bertrand's 1985 original description used the name gysinite and a Geneva museum specimen, catalogue 410/85, labelled schuilingite from Shinkolobwe. Deliens and Stalder's 1995 type catalogue instead assigns the material to Kasompi copper mine because its mineral association is characteristic of Kasompi; it lists Geneva 410/85 and 435/60. The original label and later reassignment are retained as provenance evidence, not a newly verified collection locality. The original study's diffraction supports orthorhombic Pmcn; film-derived cell estimates and subsequently refined cell parameters are separate measurements. Its 21 microprobe analyses found Nd-dominant Pb-La-Nd chemistry with slight variation and no particular zoning. Carbon was measured, but water was obtained by difference. The reported combined thermogravimetric CO2-plus-water loss of about 23 wt.% differs from the 26.2 wt.% sum of the Table 2 mean components; the paper calls this agreement, but the record does not reconcile the difference or treat the empirical hydration as exact. Its 4.82 g/cm3 density is calculated, not measured. Effervescence in cold dilute HCl is a qualitative observation without a quantified dissolution or recovery experiment. The proposed geological REE source was an interpretation, not a controlled transformation. The separately cited 1985 atomic refinement and its original reflection data were not acquired here; no site occupancies or hydrogen positions are adopted from secondary summaries. No criticality designation, microbial mechanism or industrial recovery is asserted.

Hafnon

Hafnon is the hafnium silicate mineral species with ideal formula HfSiO4, approved as IMA 1974-018. It is distinct from zircon, elemental hafnium and synthetic hafnium-silicate products. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes the species as tetragonal but explicitly identifies its cell parameters, calculated density and powder pattern as synthetic data; those values are not measurements of a natural Brazilian specimen. Pereira, Ávila and Neumann (2004), in their study of cassiterite from eight concentrate samples in the São João del Rei Pegmatite Province, report zirconian hafnon as an inclusion in cassiterite from a pan concentrate collected in a stream crossing body E of the Volta Grande mine, Minas Gerais, Brazil. Table 2 assigns that occurrence to this sample, rather than to every surveyed locality. The study uses backscattered-electron imaging and semiquantitative SEM-EDS, and its hafnon discussion explicitly cites the overlapping 2002/2003 work. This is a qualified source-reported natural occurrence, not a new independent replication of the older microanalyses or a pure-phase diffraction refinement. Its geological formation interpretation is not a controlled transformation experiment. No occurrence-wide grade, extraction, microbial mechanism, industrial deployment or inherited hafnium criticality designation is assigned.

Haradaite

Haradaite is a strontium-vanadyl silicate mineral with ideal formula SrV4+Si2O7, status A and approval 1963-011 in the September 2026 IMA list. The approval identifier is distinct from the 1967 structural paper and the later 1982 natural description. Natural material from the Noda-Tamagawa and Yamato mines, Japan, contains substitutions; the analyzed Yamato type material was calcian and barian, not the pure Sr endmember. The 1967 structure analysis preferred orthorhombic Amam over Ama2, with silicate chains joined by vanadium, while explicitly discussing limited reflections and possible intensity errors; that historical model is not a claim that every specimen and later refinement has been reassessed. The 1982 paper likewise prefers Amam and separates the two localities. Haradaite is distinct from elemental vanadium, generic vanadium ore and other vanadium silicates. Abiotic reagent synthesis supports a qualified formation mechanism. Geological association with other minerals does not demonstrate microbial formation, extraction or recovery, and criticality is not inherited from its constituents.

Heavy rare-earth commodities, EU assessment convention

This commodity subgroup uses the EU 2020 critical-raw-material assessment's ten-member heavy-rare-earth convention: europium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, lutetium and yttrium. Scandium is assessed separately and promethium is excluded in that source. The assessment covers oxide mixtures and low-purity single oxides in its initial-processing stage, and high-purity metals or interalloys in advanced refining. These are related commodity forms, not one mineral or alloy. The EU 2024 Annex II designation names heavy rare earth elements without enumerating members; its mapping here uses the explicitly stated EU 2020 assessment convention. Light/heavy boundaries in other conventions are not asserted equivalent. This group overlaps individual element records and the broader rare-earth commodity family; no group-wide microbial mechanism or strategic designation is inferred from individual members.

Heimite

IMA-approved hydrous basic lead-copper arsenate mineral (IMA 2022-019; status A, Approved 2022; full description published January 2024; symbol Him used in Section 7.2, p. 163, of the primary paper; no separate symbol column is printed in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 91) with ideal end-member formula PbCu2(AsO4)(OH)3(H2O)2 in the September 2026 IMA Master List (PDF p. 91) and PbCu2(AsO4)(OH)3*2H2O (or PbCu2(AsO4)(OH)3*2(H2O) in Section 4, p. 155, and Table 2, p. 157, requiring CuO 28.40 wt%, PbO 39.84 wt%, As2O5 20.51 wt%, H2O 11.25 wt%, total 100.00 wt%) in Malcherek, Mihailova, Schlueter, Roth, and Meisser (2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:153-164). Named in honour of Professor Albert Heim (1849-1937), Swiss geologist at ETH Zurich and author of Geologie der Schweiz (1919-1922), whose recognition of the Glarus overthrust established the Alpine nappe- thrust model in the UNESCO World Heritage Glarus thrust region hosting the type locality (Section 1, pp. 153-154). Discovered during systematic EDXS screening of dump material collected in 2003 by Philippe Roth at the Grosses Chalttal Cu-(U) deposit, Muertschenalp district, Canton Glarus, Switzerland (latitude 47 deg 04 min 09.9 sec N, longitude 9 deg 11 min 26.5 sec E; hosted in the Permian Verrucano fanglomeratic sernifite breccia of the Helvetic nappes, where primary tennantite-(Cu), pyrite, bornite, chalcopyrite, galena, uraninite, and brannerite with secondary spionkopite-yarrowite underwent Middle Pleistocene interglacial supergene oxidation; associated on the holotype with spherical bayldonite aggregates and chrysocolla, and on cotype specimens in decreasing frequency with chrysocolla, malachite, azurite, duftite, mimetite, brochantite, euchroite, bayldonite, cerussite, wulfenite, cyanotrichite, strashimirite, and parnauite, including epitactic overgrowths of prismatic duftite on tabular heimite with (001)_Him || (001)_Dft; also reported from four other Swiss Alpine Pb-Cu occurrences: Hochmaettli in Glarus, Tieftobel near Schmitten in Grisons, and Collioux Superieur and Termino near Saint-Luc in Val d'Anniviers, Valais; Section 2, pp. 154-155, and Section 7, pp. 161-163); the holotype specimen is deposited at the Museum der Natur Hamburg - Mineralogie, Leibniz- Institut zur Analyse des Biodiversitaetswandels (LIB), Hamburg, Germany (catalogue number Ro3701), and the cotype (MGL 094490) and paragenetic study specimens (MGL 087051 to 087070) are conserved at the Departement de geologie, Museum cantonal des sciences naturelles (Natureum), University of Lausanne, Switzerland (Section 1, pp. 153-154). Occurs as radial sprays of transparent, light-pistachio-green to pale-blue lath-like prismatic crystals up to 450 um long and 40 um wide elongated along [100], dominated by {001} and delimited by {010}, {110}, and {100} (some crystals turn blue under the SEM electron beam or in situ without measurable EDXS compositional change, attributed to partial charge-neutral dehydration of axial H2O ligands converting [4+2] CuO6 octahedra locally to [4+1] square pyramids; Section 3, p. 155, and Section 7.2, p. 163). Crystals have a pale-green streak, vitreous-to-silky lustre, no observable fluorescence, perfect cleavage on {001}, ready solubility in hydrochloric acid, biaxial optical character with measured 2V = 87 deg, Gladstone-Dale calculated average refractive index n_av = 1.816, faint pleochroism from faint green || [100] to bright green || [010], and calculated density Dcalc = 4.708 g/cm3 based on the single-crystal unit cell and empirical formula with seven H atoms, or 4.769 g/cm3 based on the ideal formula (Abstract, p. 153; Section 3, p. 155; and Table 2, p. 157). Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses (Cameca SX100 at Technische Universitaet Clausthal; 15 kV, 30 nA, 5 um beam diameter; standards chalcopyrite for CuO, galena for PbO, calcite for CaO, and arsenopyrite for As2O5; n = 11 sample spots; Section 4, p. 155, and Table 1, p. 155) yielded mean CuO 28.64 wt% (range 27.26-30.68, SD 1.05), PbO 39.89 wt% (range 38.08-41.75, SD 0.93), CaO 0.25 wt% (range 0.03-0.85, SD 0.26), As2O5 21.73 wt% (range 20.39-23.04, SD 0.72), with H2O_calc = 9.49 wt% by difference to 100.00 wt%, yielding on the basis of 9 O apfu the empirical formula Pb1.04Ca0.03Cu2.10As1.10H6.14O9 (printed as Pb1.04Ca0.03Cu2.1As1.1H6.14O9 in Section 4, p. 155), whereas fixing 7 H apfu (3.5 H2O per 9 O, i.e. 5.5 non-H2O O apfu) in agreement with the crystal-structure determination gives H2O_calc = 11.64 wt%, total = 102.15 wt%, and the empirical formula Pb0.97Ca0.02Cu1.95As1.02H7O9 (Section 4, p. 155). Single-crystal FTIR transmission spectroscopy on a ~0.01 mm (001) plate (Bruker VERTEX 70 / HYPERION 2000, 630-7000 cm-1; Section 6 and Figure 5, pp. 160-161) recorded sharp absorption bands at 3606 and 3489 cm-1 (hydroxyl O-H stretching of O7-H7...Ox1 and O4-H4...O5 / O6-H6...O4), a broad band at 2800-3400 cm-1 (hydrogen-bonded H2O O-H stretching of Ox1 and Ox2 around 3093-3140 cm-1), and bands at 1010, 912, and 750 cm-1 (AsO4 tetrahedral vibrations). Crystallizes in the monoclinic system, pseudo-orthorhombic space group P21/n (#14, subgroup of Pnma #62 via symmetry breaking of adjacent hydrogen- bonded H2O ligands Ox1 and Ox2 across the pseudo-mirror plane), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters (Nonius KappaCCD four-circle diffractometer, MoKalpha radiation, lambda = 0.7107 A, on a 0.27 x 0.035 x 0.012 mm light-blue two-domain crystal; Abstract, p. 153; Section 5, pp. 155-157; and Table 2, p. 157) a = 5.9132(5) A, b = 7.8478(6) A, c = 16.8158(15) A, beta = 90.007(6) deg, V = 780.33(8) A3 in the Abstract (p. 153) or V = 780.33(11) A3 in Table 2 (p. 157), and Z = 4 (Le Bail refinement of the Gandolfi-type powder X-ray diffractogram in P21/n with beta = 90 deg gave a = 5.967(5) A, b = 7.896(6) A, c = 16.779(16) A, V = 790.5(9) A3; Section 5, pp. 160-161). The crystal structure was solved by charge flipping (Superflip) and refined on F2 (Jana2006) in P21/n to Robs = 0.0275 for 1869 observed reflections with I > 3sigma(I) and Rall = 0.0359 for all 2269 unique reflections out of 26,146 measured reflections (Rint = 0.0566, GooF = 1.11 for 140 parameters; comparative orthorhombic Pnma refinement with a = 7.8478(6) A, b = 5.9132(5) A, c = 16.8158(15) A gave Robs = 0.0248 for 1076 observed reflections but an unphysical 1.15 A intermolecular H-H contact across the mirror plane that relaxes to 1.83 A in P21/n; Section 5, pp. 156-157, and Table 2, p. 157). The unique structure type is built from chains of edge-sharing, Jahn-Teller-distorted [4+2] Cu1O6 and Cu2O6 octahedra (tetragonality factor T = <Cu-O>_eq / <Cu-O>_ax = 0.8, <Cu1-O> = 2.1372 A, <Cu2-O> = 2.1348 A) running along [100], cross-linked by AsO4 tetrahedra (<As1-O> = 1.6905 A) and lone-pair-active six-coordinated trigonal-antiprismatic Pb2+ cations (<Pb1-O> = 2.5920 A) into corrugated layers stacked along [001] and linked across the interlayer space by OH- and H2O-mediated hydrogen bonds, structurally related to duftite (PbCu(AsO4)(OH)) by formal removal of one Cu(OH)2*2H2O unit per formula unit (Tables 3-7, pp. 157-159, and Section 7.2, pp. 162-163). The five strongest lines in the calculated powder X-ray diffraction pattern [dcalc in A (Icalc; dmeas, Imeas) hkl; Abstract, p. 153, and Table 8, p. 160] are 8.425 (100; 8.419, 27) (002), 3.713 (60; 3.729, 30) (014), 3.276 (54; merged dmeas = 3.185, Imeas = 100) (120), 3.221 (42; merged with 120 at dmeas = 3.185, Imeas = 100) (023), and 2.645 (61; 2.642, 53) (016). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Heterosite

Heterosite is the ferric phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe3+(PO4), listed as grandfathered by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with original-description year 1826. Natural specimens can contain substantial trivalent manganese. It is distinct from lithium-bearing triphylite and Mn3+-dominant purpurite. Eventoff et al. (1972) refined a natural Fletcher Quarry, New Hampshire crystal of approximate composition (Fe0.65Mn0.35)PO4 with an effectively vacant lithium site. The 2023 triphylite-group nomenclature retains heterosite while discrediting ferrisicklerite and sicklerite; the historical oxidation experiment already curated under cmmmech:triphylite is not counted here as a new experiment. The separate Reich et al. (2024) study concerns a synthetic heterosite-structure FePO4 sorbent made from commercial carbon-coated LiFePO4, not mined natural heterosite. Its laboratory lithium uptake from pretreated natural geothermal brine and a separate synthetic brine does not establish purified lithium recovery, natural-ore extraction, microbial activity or industrial deployment. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Hureaulite

Hureaulite is the manganese(II) hydrogen phosphate hydrate mineral with current IMA formula Mn2+5(PO3OH)2(PO4)2(H2O)4. The September 2026 list records renamed status, 2007 s.p.; this is not a new-species approval number. Natural material can contain iron and other substitutions. Garcia Guajardo et al. (2024) prepared a synthetic manganese phosphate assigned to monoclinic C2/c hureaulite by powder diffraction and vibrational spectroscopy, then tested composite electrodes made from that powder. The synthetic reagent-derived material is distinguished from mined natural hureaulite, from lithiophilite and from a merely hureaulite-like phase. Its laboratory charge-storage behavior is not microbial transformation, extraction of manganese from ore, recovery of an isolated metal product or industrial deployment. Charge-partition and proton-transfer explanations are model-based interpretations, and the exact redox reaction remains unresolved. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Igelströmite

Igelströmite (IMA 2021-035) is an IMA-accepted anhydrous iron(III)–antimony(III)–lead(II) oxide mineral of the minium group (schafarzikite subgroup, general formula MX2O4) with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula Fe3+(SbPb)O4 (PDF p. 100, status A; written Fe3+(Sb3+Pb2+)O4 in the article title/Abstract and Fe(SbPb)Sigma=2O4 in Section 4, p. 314; IMA symbol Ig; ideal composition PbO 49.73 wt%, Sb2O3 32.48 wt%, Fe2O3 17.79 wt%, total 100 wt%). Described by Holtstam, Langhof, Friis, Karlsson, and Erambert (2024) from the Hindenburg working (150 m level) of the Långban Långban-type Fe–Mn skarn deposit (59.85° N, 14.26° E), Filipstad district, Värmland Province, Sweden (named after Swedish mineralogist Lars Johan Igelström, 1822–1897; holotype specimen deposited in the Department of Geosciences, Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm, under catalogue no. GEO-NRM 19255056, with single-crystal mount KNR 44278 at the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo, pp. 311–312). Occurs as tiny lenticular crystals forming compact rounded aggregates up to 1 mm across on open fractures (some filled with grey to white calcite) in a fine-grained, bluish-grey hematite ore with minor aegirine, a serpentine-group mineral, and fluorcalcioroméite; in the fractures it grows on globular masses of a greyish-black serpentine-group mineral associated with nadorite, thin tabular hematite, colourless baryte, senarmontite, white acicular mimetite, and Pb-bearing rhodochrosite (Section 2, p. 312, Fig. 1, p. 313). Macroscopically dark reddish-brown to black with submetallic lustre, translucent in thin edges, brownish streak, estimated Mohs hardness ~3.5, brittle with uneven fracture, indistinct {110} cleavage, non-fluorescent under UV, and Dcalc = 6.33(1) g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit cell (Section 3, p. 313, and Table 4, p. 315). In reflected light it is bluish-greyish-white, weakly bireflectant, nonpleochroic, with weak anisotropy (greyish to brownish rotation tints) and sparse deep-red internal reflections; reflectance values in air (R2, R1, Section 3, p. 313, where the spectral window is printed as "400–70 nm range" for 400–700 nm, and Table 2, p. 314) at the four COM wavelengths are 16.1, 15.2% (470 nm), 15.1, 14.4% (546 nm), 14.9, 14.2% (589 nm), and 14.8, 14.1% (650 nm). Micro-Raman measurements (532 nm laser) produced no usable spectrum due to laser-induced breakdown of the sample surface (Section 6.1, p. 315), whereas 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy with a 57Co rhodium-matrix point source (Section 6.2, pp. 316–317, Fig. 4) yielded a single paramagnetic quadrupole doublet with centre shift CS = 0.42(2) mm/s, quadrupole splitting QS = 0.89(3) mm/s, and asymmetry parameter a12 = 0.60(2), confirming predominance of octahedrally coordinated high-spin Fe3+ (with any Fe2+ < 15% of total Fe). Mean of 12 WDS electron-microprobe point analyses (CAMECA SX100, 15 kV, 10 nA, 1–2 um beam; Section 4, pp. 313–314, Table 3, p. 315) yielded Sb2O3 42.89 wt% (2sigma 5.41), PbO 34.42 (2sigma 4.53), Fe2O3 11.05 (2sigma 1.73) and FeO 1.14 (2sigma 1.92) (recast from total Fe for charge balance on 3 cations and 4 O), MnO 4.78 (2sigma 1.57), As2O3 3.88 (2sigma 1.41), MgO not detected, printed Total = 98.17 wt% (arithmetic sum of rounded means = 98.16 wt%), corresponding on 3 cations and 4 O to the empirical formula (Fe3+0.59Mn2+0.29As3+0.06Fe2+0.06)Sigma=1.00(Sb3+1.24Pb2+0.65As3+0.11)Sigma=2.00O4. Tetragonal, space group P42/mbc (no. 135), Z = 4 (Section 5, pp. 314–319, Tables 4–7, 10–11, Fig. 5): single-crystal MoKalpha XRD refinement on a 0.007 x 0.028 x 0.041 mm fragment (Rigaku Synergy-S with HyPix-6000HE detector; MoKalpha wavelength printed as "lambda = 0.71703 Å" for 0.71073 Å in Section 5.1 on p. 314; 411 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) out of 500 unique, 6571 collected, Rint = 3.93%, R1 = 3.73%, R1(all) = 4.60%, wR2 = 6.66%, GoF = 1.315, Table 4, p. 315) gives a = 8.4856(2) Å, c = 6.0450(3) Å, V = 435.27(3) Å3, with [001] chains of edge-sharing M(Fe)O6 octahedra (4d site, Fe–O1 = 2.097(6) Å x 2, Fe–O2 = 2.064(5) Å x 4, <Fe–O> = 2.075 Å, BVS = 2.60 v.u., refined SOF = 0.978(17) Fe, site composition Fe3+0.59Mn2+0.29Fe2+0.06As0.06 with 25.22 SXRD vs 26.13 EPMA e-, Tables 5–7, 10, pp. 316, 318; note Table 5 header on p. 316 prints "Site | x | y | x" with a duplicate "x" for "z") cross-linked via corner-sharing chains of trigonal-pyramidal X(Sb,Pb)O3 polyhedra (8h site, refined SOF 0.76(3) Sb + 0.24(3) Pb, Sb–O1 = 2.070(3) Å x 2, Sb–O2 = 2.051(7) Å, <Sb–O> = 2.063 Å, BVS = 2.40 v.u.; Table 6 lists site composition Sb0.625Pb0.325As0.055 summing to 1.005 per site = 2.01 pfu, 58.44 SXRD vs 60.34 EPMA e-) surrounding stereoactive 5s2/6s2 lone-pair tunnels; Gandolfi CuKalpha powder XRD (23 observed reflections, Section 5.2, p. 314, Table 11, p. 319) refines to a = 8.484(3) Å, c = 6.038(3) Å, V = 434.6(3) Å3, with seven strongest observed lines [dmeas in Å (Imeas; hkl)] at 3.21 (100; 2 1 1), 2.46 (22; 2 0 2), 2.69 (20; 1 1 2, 3 1 0), 1.946 (19; 4 1 1), 1.667 (16; 3 3 2), 4.25 (14; 2 0 0), and 1.778 (14; 2 1 3) (followed by 3.01 (13; 0 0 2, 2 2 0)). Distinct from co-described manganoschafarzikite (Mn2+Sb3+2O4, IMA 2022-129), schafarzikite (Fe2+Sb3+2O4), and minium (Pb2+2Pb4+O4); no criticality designation for igelströmite itself, no microbial or biological mechanism, and no industrial recovery yield are asserted.

It is distinct from inderite, hydroboracite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Gatta et al.'s natural crystals from Quarry 98, Inder Deposit, Kazakhstan, have a monoclinic C2/c structure: borate rings connect Ca and Mg polyhedra into sheets, with hydrogen bonds linking the sheets. Their openly deposited Revision_1 manuscript reports EPMA-WDS on three crystals, including quartz micro-inclusions and modest beam damage; near-ideal Ca and Mg composition is a specimen-level observation, not a universal purity or ore-grade claim. Inderborite-II below is an experimental high-pressure label, not an asserted independently approved natural species. No criticality or microbial activity is inherited from boron or associated minerals.

Inderite

Inderite is the Mg[B3O3(OH)5](H2O)4·H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with status A and year notation 1962 s.p. for a special procedure, not a fabricated sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from its dimorph kurnakovite, from inderborite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Gatta et al. studied natural Kramer Deposit, California, material by EPMA-WDS, laser-ablation mass spectrometry and neutron diffraction. The P21/c structure comprises borate-ring/Mg-polyhedron clusters connected by hydrogen bonds, with four Mg-bound water molecules and one interstitial water per formula unit. The chemical characterization is specimen specific, including modest electron-beam damage and an assumed B/H stoichiometry in the EPMA formula; it is not a resource-grade survey. Commodity criticality and microbial activity are not inherited.

Indite

Indite is the iron-indium sulfide mineral species with ideal formula FeIn2S4. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list marks it approved and gives the year as 1967 s.p.; this special-procedure notation is not a numbered approval accession. Genkin and Murav'eva (1963) described natural grains in cassiterite-quartz ore from the Dzhalinda deposit, Little Khingan, in the Russian Far East. Reflected-light microscopy, quantitative microspectrographic analysis and powder X-ray diffraction support the identification. The diffraction comparison with previously synthesized FeIn2S4 supports a cubic spinel-type assignment; it is not a new single-crystal structure refinement of the natural material. The measured natural grains had variable, approximately determined iron-indium-sulfur proportions rather than uniformly ideal end-member stoichiometry. Nearly all observed indite grains were replaced to varying degrees by veinlets of the distinct indium hydroxide mineral dzhalindite. Natural and synthetic diffraction intensities also differ for the 311 reflection, which the authors retain in their structural comparison. The ideal species formula therefore does not establish purity of the analyzed grains or of the surrounding ore. The proposed later hydrothermal introduction of indite during quartz-associated replacement of cassiterite is a geological interpretation of textures and associations, not an experimentally demonstrated formation pathway. Cited laboratory synthesis conditions and separate heating experiments on dzhalindite are not natural indite formation conditions. This record denotes the mineral species, separately from elemental indium, synthetic FeIn2S4 materials and the mixed cassiterite ore. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned by this identity and natural-specimen evidence.

Ion-adsorption rare-earth leach residue

A processed, mixed mineral residue remaining after ammonium-sulfate extraction of ion-exchangeable rare earths from weathered ion-adsorption ore. Zhang and colleagues (2024) prepared the studied material in the laboratory from Guangdong, China ore; this is not evidence of sampling an industrial tailings deposit. It is distinct from the natural ion-adsorption rare-earth clay feed, individual mineral species and isolated rare-earth products. The preparation included repeated salt leaching, rinsing, 60-mesh sieving, drying and crushing. The authors' ion-unexchangeable designation is operational, referring to the rare earths remaining after that pretreatment. It does not mean resistance to every subsequent extractant. The experimental feed contains mainly kaolinite, quartz, orthoclase and muscovite, with minor Fe-bearing and rare-earth-bearing phases. Its composition is not a universal tailings specification, and no criticality designation is inherited from its constituent elements.

Johanngeorgenstadtite (IMA 2019-122) is an IMA-accepted anhydrous nickel(II) arsenate mineral with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula Ni2+4.5(AsO4)3 (PDF p. 105, status A; ideal composition NiO 49.37 wt%, As2O5 50.63 wt%, total 100 wt%), representing the monoclinic unprotonated alluaudite-type dimorph of tetragonal garnet-like niasite (IMA 2019-105, Ni2+4.5(AsO4)3, I-42d), whereas synthetic tetragonal Ni4.35As3O11.7(OH)0.3 (Barbier, 1999) is isostructural with niasite and johanngeorgenstadtite is its monoclinic alluaudite-type polymorph (pp. 375, 378). Described by Kampf, Nash, Plášil, Smith, and Feinglos (2020) on a single museum specimen (American Museum of Natural History holotype catalogue no. 17956, consisting of three major fragments and numerous smaller ones including 10 pieces mounted on two acrylic discs, also the holotype of niasite; Section 2, p. 374) from Johanngeorgenstadt, Erzgebirge, Saxony, Germany, where it formed as a secondary oxidation product from the breakdown of primary nickeline (niccolite) under dry, oxidizing conditions (possibly influenced by 17th-century underground fire-setting) in association with niasite, aerugite, bunsenite, quartz, rooseveltite, and xanthiosite (pp. 373–375, Fig. 4). Occurs as sugary aggregates of pink-orange irregular, rounded grains or short prisms about 70 um in diameter with no discernible crystal forms or twinning, pale-pink streak, transparent with resinous to subadamantine lustre, non-fluorescent under long- or short-wave UV, estimated Mohs hardness ~5, brittle tenacity with curved and stepped fracture, multiple cleavage planes probably corresponding to {010}, {110}, and {1-10} by analogy with other alluaudite-group minerals, rapid loss of colour and slow dissolution in dilute HCl at room temperature, and calculated density Dcalc = 4.801 g/cm3 for the empirical formula and 4.808 g/cm3 for the ideal formula on the single-crystal unit cell (Section 3.2, p. 376; Table 3 on p. 380 reports Dx = 4.880 g/cm3 for the refined cell contents Ni4.61(AsO4)3). Kaliborite

Kaliborite is the grandfathered potassium-magnesium borate species KHMg2B12O16(OH)10(H2O)4 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its 1889 entry is an original-description year, not an approval identifier. Burns and Hawthorne studied a natural Kazakhstan crystal from Canadian Museum of Nature specimen 53372 and refined a monoclinic C2/c structure with borate chains parallel to b. Their 1994 study located hydrogen by difference-Fourier analysis with O-H distance restraints. The apparently symmetric hydrogen bond was interpreted as dynamically disordered from structural and bond-valence arguments; this was not a direct measurement of hydrogen motion. The paper did not provide a new bulk chemical analysis of that crystal. A separate museum material supplied the thermal experiments below. This mineral is distinct from elemental boron and the borates commodity; neither criticality, microbial activity nor industrial recovery is inferred.

Karlseifertite

IMA-approved lead-gallium-germanium arsenate hydroxide mineral of the dussertite group in the alunite supergroup (IMA 2024-007; Warr symbol Karl in the primary description and Ksf in the IMA Master List; status A, Approved 2024; full description published September 2024) with ideal end-member formula Pb(Ga2Ge)(AsO4)2(OH)6 (requiring As2O5 28.76 wt%, PbO 27.93 wt%, Ga2O3 23.46 wt%, GeO2 13.09 wt%, H2O 6.76 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Kampf et al., 2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:873-878). Represents the first member of the alunite supergroup containing essential Ge and the first member of the dussertite group defined by valency-imposed double site occupancy (Ga3+2Ge4+) at the octahedral G site; named in honour of German mining engineer Karl Markus Seifert (1911-2000), mining engineer for Tsumeb Corporation Ltd. (1963-1967), using the full name karlseifertite to avoid homonymy with seifertite (SiO2). Discovered on specimens collected by Karl Seifert from the second oxidation zone of the Tsumeb mine, Tsumeb, Namibia (19 deg 15 min S, 17 deg 42 min E), where it occurs as a secondary oxidation-zone mineral on fracture surfaces in germanite-chalcocite ore; one holotype specimen (catalogue number 76334) and one cotype specimen (catalogue number 76335) are deposited in the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Los Angeles, California, USA. Occurs in rosettes of thin, transparent, yellow hexagonal plates bounded by {001} and {100} up to ~0.2 mm in diameter and <0.01 mm thick with a pale-yellow streak, subadamantine lustre, estimated Mohs hardness ~4, brittle tenacity, irregular fracture, perfect {001} cleavage, non-fluorescence under long- or short-wave ultraviolet light, room-temperature insolubility in dilute HCl, and calculated density Dcalc = 4.993 g/cm3 for the empirical formula (or 5.037 g/cm3 for the SREF formula Pb0.99Ga3.10As1.92O14H6 in Table 3) on the single-crystal unit cell. Optically uniaxial (+) in white light with omega = 1.890(5), spindle-stage Berek-compensator birefringence epsilon - omega = 0.004 giving calculated epsilon = 1.894, slight pleochroism with O light yellow > E pale yellow, and Gladstone-Dale compatibility index 1 - (Kp/Kc) = -0.001 (superior). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser; Figure 2) shows a very broad O-H stretching band from ~3400 to ~2800 cm-1, nu3 and nu1 AsO4 stretching bands at 942, 855, and 767 cm-1, nu4 and nu2 AsO4 bending bands at 577 and 498 cm-1, and lower-wavenumber lattice modes at 305, 247, 205, and 140 cm-1. Field-emission electron microprobe analysis (8 points, JEOL JXA-iHP200F, 15 kV, 5 nA, 10 um beam; Table 1) yielded PbO 26.80(33) wt% (range 26.33-27.46), As2O5 21.05(44) wt% (20.35-21.47), Ga2O3 18.05(24) wt% (17.62-18.42), GeO2 8.60(22) wt% (8.36-9.06), Fe2O3 5.53(55) wt% (4.88-6.42), WO3 4.82(25) wt% (4.49-5.08), SO3 3.00(22) wt% (2.70-3.31), Al2O3 0.75(3) wt% (0.72-0.78), and structure- calculated H2O 6.45 wt% (based on O = 14 and As + S + W = 2), total 95.05 wt% (low total due to poor polish and <10 um plate thickness), corresponding on the basis of 14 O atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula Pb2+0.99(Ga3+1.60Ge4+0.68Fe3+0.57Al3+0.12)Sigma2.97[(As5+0.76S6+0.15W6+0.09)Sigma1.00O4]2(OH0.99)6 and simplified formula Pb(Ga,Ge,Fe3+,Al)[(As,S,W)O4]2(OH)6 as printed on p. 874 (where the subscript 3 on the octahedral G-site group (Ga,Ge,Fe3+,Al)3 corresponding to the alunite-supergroup general formula DG3(TX4)2X'6 is omitted in the paper's text). IMA-approved silver-copper-zinc antimony sulfosalt mineral (IMA 2020-075; symbol Kattr-Zn; status A, Approved 2020) with ideal end-member formula [Ag6]4+(Cu4Zn2)Sb4S12[] (written Ag6(Cu4Zn2)Sb4S12[] in the September 2026 IMA Master List; requiring Ag 33.99 wt%, Sb 25.58 wt%, S 20.21 wt%, Cu 13.35 wt%, Zn 6.87 wt%, total 100 wt%), representing the Zn-dominant keno-member of the freibergite series in the tetrahedrite group and the Zn analogue of kenoargentotetrahedrite-(Fe) (Qu et al., 2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:397-409). Discovered at the Yindongpo gold deposit in the Weishancheng Au-Ag-Pb-Zn ore belt, Tongbai County, Nanyang City, Henan Province, China (32 deg 33 min 02 sec N, 113 deg 25 min 25 sec E), where it occurs in hydrothermal veins hosted by silicified and carbonaceous quartz-sericite schist of the upper Neoproterozoic Waitoushan Formation, associated with kenoargentotetrahedrite-(Fe), tetrahedrite-(Zn), sphalerite, galena, pyrite, acanthite, chalcopyrite, and quartz; the holotype specimen is deposited at the Geological Museum of China, Beijing, under catalogue number M16112. Forms black, opaque anhedral grains and equant crystals up to 40 um in size with a black streak, metallic lustre, brittle tenacity, conchoidal fracture, indistinct cleavage, Vickers microhardness VHN50 = 288.7-324.1 kg/mm2 (mean 309.7 kg/mm2, corresponding to Mohs hardness ~3.5-4), and calculated density Dcalc = 5.209 g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell parameters. In reflected light it is greenish-grey and optically isotropic with brown-red internal reflections. Micro-Raman spectroscopy (785 nm laser; Section 6, Fig. 6) shows a major band at 353 cm-1 (symmetric nu1 X(3)-S(1) stretching of SbS3 pyramids) with a shoulder at 346 cm-1 (antisymmetric nu3 Sb-S stretching), bending modes at 314 cm-1 (symmetric nu2 SbS3 bending) and 282 cm-1 (antisymmetric nu4 SbS3 bending), and lattice vibrations at 214, 201, and 160 cm-1. IMA:2020-075
Kernite

Kernite is the Na2B4O6(OH)2·3H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1927 rather than a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from elemental boron, the broad borates commodity and the separately hydrated borax and tincalconite species. Gatta et al. characterized a natural Kramer Deposit, California, museum specimen by chemical analyses, single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293 K and neutron diffraction at 20 K, supporting monoclinic P21/c kernite. Their Table 3 reports the specimen-specific empirical formula Na1.99B3.99O6(OH)2·3.01H2O and 50.90 +/- 0.20 wt% B2O3. Water at 26.40 +/- 0.20 wt% was estimated by treating the mass loss on heating to 800 degrees C as water, rather than being a separately measured recovery product. Table 2 reports Li2O below 0.01 wt%, and Table 1 reports rare-earth oxide signals below its element-specific detection limits; these censored observations neither mean zero nor establish the composition of all kernite deposits. The neutron refinement and maximum-entropy analysis favor static positional disorder for two water-hydrogen populations in this specimen, refining the older X-ray model rather than defining another species. Proton tunneling was not completely excluded. The two temperature refinements retained the same general structure, an endpoint comparison rather than a continuously measured stability interval. This identity and crystal-chemistry record does not adopt the paper's general criticality language, proposed industrial applications or inferred natural formation conditions as demonstrated extraction, microbial activity or deployment.

 mineral — None — —
Kësterite

Kësterite is the mineral species Cu2ZnSnS4, recorded as grandfathered (G) with original-description year 1956 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. That year is not an IMA approval identifier. This natural mineral identity is distinct from elemental tin or zinc, mixed ores, synthetic CZTS photovoltaic materials, stannite and ferrokësterite. Historical papers often spell the name kesterite and describe Fe-bearing members. Černý and colleagues (2001) measured four natural Peerless pegmatite nodules, assigning two Zn-dominant specimens to ferroan kesterite from electron-microprobe composition and characterizing powder-diffraction unit cells. They explicitly named specimens by composition and did not refine cation ordering or establish each specimen's space group. Their specimens are compositionally variable natural materials, not pure endmembers. The microbial study below tested separately synthesized material identified by the historical authors as kesterite; it did not test natural kësterite, solar-cell films or industrial feed. No criticality designation is inherited from tin, zinc or copper.

Keutschite

IMA-approved copper-silver-arsenic sulfosalt mineral of the stannite group (IMA 2014-038; status A, Approved 2014; full description published January 2026; no mineral symbol is printed in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 112, or in the primary type description) with ideal end-member formula Cu2AgAsS4 (requiring Cu 29.01 wt%, Ag 24.62 wt%, As 17.10 wt%, S 29.28 wt%, sum 100.01 wt%, printed as "29.01 Cu, 24,62 Ag, 17.10 As, and 29.28 S, for a total of 100.00" with a comma decimal separator in "24,62 Ag" in Section 3, p. 3; Topa, Takagi Fredrickson, Stanley, and Dinca, 2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:1-7). Represents the Ag-As analogue of stannite (Cu2FeSnS4) and is named in honour of Frank Keutsch (born 1971) for his significant contributions to the mineralogy of the Uchucchacua deposit, who first brought attention to this mineral during his study of the alabandite zone and was instrumental in the discovery and description of manganoquadratite, menchettiite, agmantinite, spryite, hyrslite, ramosite, and oyonite (and first identified argyrodite, billingsleyite, canfieldite, diaphorite, ferdowsiite, metastibnite, pirquitasite, smithite, stannite, stephanite, and trechmannite at this site; Abstract, p. 1, and Section 1, p. 2). Discovered in a sample extracted from the alabandite zone (Socorro section of the mine, characterised by high concentrations of Ag and Mn) of the Ag-Pb-Zn polymetallic deposit at Uchucchacua, Oyon District, Catajambo, Lima Department, Peru (type locality for seven Mn-bearing sulfides/sulfosalts -- benavidesite, uchucchacuaite, manganoquadratite, menchettiite, oyonite, agmantinite, and ramosite -- and seven Ag minerals including spryite); the sample utilised for description consists predominantly of alabandite and Mn-bearing calcite with associated crystals of manganoquadratite, proustite, and billingsleyite, as well as massive diaphorite and seligmannite-bournonite, with the alabandite zone also hosting chemically or structurally related agmantinite, pirquitasite, stannite, and kesterite, and keutschite having since been described at the Clara mine in Germany (Kolitsch et al., 2019) and the Sacaramb ore deposit in Romania (Dinca et al., 2025) (Abstract, p. 1; Section 2, p. 2; and Section 5, p. 5). The holotype material is deposited in the reference collection of the Naturhistorisches Museum Wien, Vienna, Austria (specimen no. N 9736), part of the specimen used for the study is deposited in the collection of the Mineralogical & Geological Museum Harvard (no. 2017.13.10), and another part (Figure 1, p. 3) is deposited in the Frank Keutsch collection (Section 1, p. 2). Occurs as rare metallic, highly lustrous, blocky, free-standing crystals measuring up to 3 mm (Figure 1 caption on p. 3 notes a twinned crystal 2.5 mm in size on proustite and manganoan calcite; Table 3 on p. 4 lists crystal colour Grey and crystal habit Irregular) that exhibit a grey colour with a slight green-brassy tint on manganoquadratite and proustite crystals (Abstract, p. 1, and Section 2, p. 2); crystals are opaque with a grey-black (Abstract, p. 1) / black (Section 2, p. 2) streak, non-fluorescent, brittle tenacity, neither fracture nor cleavage observed, Mohs hardness 4-5, Vickers micro-indentation hardness VHN25 = 352-380 with a mean of 368 kg mm-2, and calculated density Dcalc = 4.663 g cm-3 in Section 2 (p. 2, from the empirical formula and single-crystal X-ray data) or 4.66 g cm-3 in Table 3 (p. 4; density could not be measured directly owing to limited size and material available). In plane-polarised incident light, keutschite is grey-white in colour, with very weak bireflectance and very weak pleochroism in greenish-grey to grey tints, and under crossed polars is weakly anisotropic with rotation tints in shades of greenish grey to grey and no internal reflections (Abstract, p. 1, and Section 2, p. 2); reflectance values (Rmin, Rmax in %) measured in air using a Zeiss Axiotron microscope, a Crystal Structures (Lanham) superstage, a J&M Tidas diode array spectrometer, a Zeiss WTiC standard, and Cavendish Instruments Onyx software from 400 to 700 nm at 0.823 nm intervals (Abstract, p. 1, Section 2, pp. 2-3, and Table 1, p. 3) at the four COM standard wavelengths are 25.2, 26.1 (470 nm), 29.6, 29.4 (546 nm), 29.4, 29.2 (589 nm), and 28.5, 28.6 (650 nm) (reported from 400 to 700 nm in 20 nm steps in Table 1, p. 3). Wavelength-dispersive field-emission electron-microprobe analyses (JEOL "Hyperprobe" JXA 8530F FE-EPMA at the Central Research Laboratories of the Natural History Museum, Vienna; 25 kV, 20 nA, 2 um beam diameter, 10 s peak / 5 s background; standards synthetic Ag metal for AgLalpha, natural chalcopyrite for CuKalpha, synthetic hauerite for MnKalpha, synthetic InAs for AsLalpha, natural stibnite for SbLalpha, natural galena for PbMalpha, and natural sphalerite for SKalpha; n = 5 analyses on one grain; Section 3, p. 3, and Table 2, p. 4) yielded mean Ag 23.46 wt% (range 23.14-23.94, SD 0.34), Cu 29.53 wt% (range 29.32-29.74, SD 0.18), Mn 0.031 wt% (range 0.02-0.04, SD 0.01), As 16.09 wt% (range 15.29-16.71, SD 0.67), Sb 1.20 wt% (range 0.48-2.14, SD 0.84), Pb 0.11 wt% (range 0.04-0.14, SD 0.07), S 29.06 wt% (range 28.80-29.11, SD 0.15), and mean of spot totals 99.46 wt% (range 99.12-99.97, SD 0.50; sum of rounded element means = 99.481 wt%). Both the Abstract (p. 1) and Section 3 (p. 3) print the empirical formula as Cu2.05Ag0.96(As0.95Sb0.04)Sigma0.99S4.00 ("based on eight atoms"), whereas Table 2 (p. 4) gives three empirical formula normalizations: Cu2.00Ag0.97(As0.95Sb0.04)Sigma1.99S4.03 (SigmaMe = 3.97) on the basis of 8 apfu (4Me + 4S), Cu1.99Ag0.96(As0.95Sb0.04)Sigma1.99S4.00 (SigmaMe = 3.95) on the basis of 4 S apfu, and Cu2.02Ag0.97(As0.96Sb0.04)Sigma2.00S4.05 (SigmaMe = 4) on the basis of 4 Me apfu (where Table 2 prints Sigma1.99 instead of Sigma0.99 for 0.95 + 0.04 = 0.99 and Sigma2.00 instead of Sigma1.00 for 0.96 + 0.04 = 1.00). Crystallizes in the tetragonal system, space group I-42m (#121), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters (Oxford Diffraction Xcalibur E diffractometer, graphite-monochromatised MoKalpha radiation, lambda = 0.71073 A in Table 3, p. 4, misprinted as "lambda = 0.7173 A" in Section 4, p. 3, at T = 293(2) K on an irregular 0.118 x 0.088 x 0.050 mm crystal fragment) a = 5.5834(15) A, c = 10.021(3) A, V = 312.40(14) A3, and Z = 2 (note that the Abstract on p. 1 prints the axial ratio as "a:b:c = 1:1:0.897", which equals c/(2a) = 0.8974 rather than c/a = 1.7948). The crystal structure was solved by charge flipping (SUPERFLIP) and refined on F2 (JANA2006) to R = 1.99% and Rw = 4.61% for 286 observed reflections with I > 3sigma(I) (R = 2.17%, Rw = 4.78% for all 308 unique reflections out of 1490 measured reflections, Rint [I > 3sigma(I), all] = 2.62%, 2.63%, S = 1.05 for 15 parameters; Table 3, p. 4). In the stannite-derivative structure (Table 4 and Section 5, p. 5), tetrahedrally S-coordinated cations occupy Wyckoff positions Cu at 4d (0, 0.5, 0.75; Ueq = 0.024 A2), Ag at 2b (0, 0, 0.5; Ueq = 0.032 A2), and As at 2a (0, 0, 0; Ueq = 0.009 A2) with S at 8i (0.77733(13), 0.77733(13), 0.86852(10); Ueq = 0.014 A2), forming alternating (001) cation layers of Cu atoms and ordered (Ag + As) atoms. The five strongest powder X-ray diffraction lines measured on a Rigaku Rapid II 2D image-plate diffractometer with MoKalpha radiation [dmeas in A (Im, Irel, dcalc in A) (hkl); Table 5, p. 5] are 3.09 (vs, 100, 3.1011) (112), 2.79 (ms, 11.4, 2.7917) (200), 1.966 (s, 20.4, 1.974) (220), 1.864 (s, 34.2, 1.8646) (204), and 1.659 (s, 27.2, 1.6653) (312) (note that the Abstract on p. 1 prints the five strongest lines as "[d in A (intensity) hkl]: 3.101 (100) 110; 2.792 (11) 200; 1.974 (20) 220; 1.665 (34) 204; and 2.846 (27) 312", misprinting 110 for 112, 1.665 for 1.865 on 204, and 2.846 for 1.665 on 312). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Holland (32 deg 10 min S, 119 deg 44 min E), southern Yilgarn Block, Western Australia, Australia, where it is intimately intergrown with black cesstibtantite, manganotantalite, antimonian microlite, rankamaite-like fibers, and montmorillonite, having formed by supergene weathering of a primary tantalum mineral (likely tantalite or Rankamaite). Kornelite

Kornelite is a monoclinic ferric sulfate mineral, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as Fe(III)2(SO4)3(H2O)6·1.75H2O. Its additional channel water is variable; historical seven-water formulae are not exact hydration measurements for every specimen. The evidence below separates abiotic synthesis of a characterized crystalline product from provisional diffraction assignments in mixed bacterial-culture solids. Neither experiment establishes a recovered iron product from ore or waste, industrial deployment or a criticality designation.

Kozoite-(La)

Kozoite-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant orthorhombic rare-earth hydroxyl carbonate mineral with ideal formula La(CO3)(OH), approved as IMA 2002-054. It is distinct from elemental lanthanum, other kozoite species, hydroxylbastnäsite-(La) and commercial rare-earth feeds. The original Mitsukoshi, Japan material consists of minute crystals in spherical aggregates with concentric La-dominant and Nd-dominant zones. Four La-domain microprobe analyses have average La0.83 and Nd0.40 on a two-cation basis, with appreciable Ca0.43; this is not a chemically pure La end member. Carbon and hydrogen could not be measured in that intergrown material: the reported carbonate, hydroxyl and water contents were calculated from an ancylite-type formula, while infrared bands support carbonate and OH. The analytical total including calculated volatiles is 101.19 wt%. Powder diffraction gives Pmcn and a = 4.986(4), b = 8.513(6), c = 7.227(10) Å; no single-crystal analysis was possible. Nearly matching diffraction patterns of the La and Nd species require chemical discrimination. The mechanism below concerns separately synthesized La carbonate, not dissolution of the natural zoned specimen. These sources do not establish microbial causality, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Kozoite-(Nd)

Kozoite-(Nd) is the neodymium-dominant orthorhombic rare-earth hydroxyl carbonate mineral with ideal formula Nd(CO3)(OH), approved as IMA 1998-063. It is distinct from elemental neodymium, kozoite-(La), hydroxylbastnäsite-(Nd) and commercial rare-earth feeds. The original Niikoba, Hizen-cho, Japan material consists of crystals smaller than 10 µm in an alkali olivine basalt cavity. Six-grain microprobe analyses show a mixed rare-earth composition, including Nd0.85 and La0.61 on a two-cation basis, rather than a pure Nd end member. Fluorine was not detected; no detection limit is supplied. Carbon and hydrogen were measured separately by triplicate elemental analysis using approximately 5 mg portions. Synchrotron powder diffraction and Rietveld refinement give Pmcn, a = 4.9829(1), b = 8.5188(2), c = 7.2570(2) Å and Z = 4. Hydrogen positions were not located, and the original study could not exclude a nearly orthorhombic monoclinic structure without suitable single crystals. The thermal experiment below concerns this natural mixed-REE material, not an isolated synthetic Nd end member. These sources do not establish microbial formation, industrial recovery or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Kukharenkoite-(Ce)

A barium-cerium fluorocarbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula Ba2Ce(CO3)3F and approval identifier 1995-040. This record denotes the Ce-dominant mineral species, not kukharenkoite-(La), a carbonatite ore or its constituent elements. Zaitsev et al. (1996) described natural specimens from the Khibina and Vuorijarvi massifs in Russia and the Mont Saint-Hilaire and Saint-Amable massifs in Quebec. Their KH1 specimen has mean Ce2O3 of 15.30 wt% and La2O3 of 6.61 wt% across twelve microprobe analyses (Table 2); this is a mixed-rare-earth natural composition, not the ideal pure-Ce formula or a recovery measurement. CO2 was calculated from stoichiometry because insufficient material was available for direct determination. Small apparent La dominance in KH5 was explicitly considered inconclusive because of interference-correction uncertainty; it is not assigned to the La species here. Krivovichev et al. (1998) refined a natural KH1 crystal from manganoan ankerite carbonatite at 293(2) K in monoclinic P21/m, with R = 0.044 using 2296 observed reflections. The idealized Ba2Ce(CO3)3F structural model and fluorine-centered coordination describe that mixed-REE natural crystal; they do not constitute a mineral-formation or extraction experiment. The 1996 description reports solubility in hydrochloric acid with effervescence without specifying acid concentration, duration, temperature, solid loading or yield. No quantified leaching or isolated-product recovery is inferred. Its suggested equivalence to historical zhonghuacerite-(Ce) was tentative because original material was unavailable. Deposited observed and calculated structure factors cited by the 1998 paper were not acquired. No microbial mechanism, industrial deployment or dated criticality designation is asserted.

 mineral — None —
IMA:1995-040
Kuliokite-(Y)

A natural yttrium-bearing aluminium fluorosilicate mineral, with current IMA formula Y4Al(SiO4)2(OH)2F5 and approval 1984-064. The accepted primary characterization is a 2025 re-investigation of Ploskaya Mountain, Kola Peninsula, Russia, material from the type locality, not an assertion that the analysed crystals are the original holotype. Wavelength-dispersive microprobe analyses of three crystals, each averaging 4–7 spots, show variable Yb and other heavy rare-earth contents; water was calculated from structural data rather than measured directly. A single-crystal refinement at 293(2) K supports monoclinic Im symmetry, replacing the triclinic interpretation discussed in the paper. The model used mixed Y/Yb scattering curves with total occupancy constrained to one for each Y site; those occupancies are not separate direct assays of every lanthanide at each site. Its seven-coordinate Y2 site was interpreted as favouring heavier REEs relative to eight-coordinate Y1. This is a crystal-chemical interpretation of natural material, not a demonstrated separation or recovery process. Only one hydrogen position was located; the F3 hydroxyl/fluoride ratio was fixed during refinement. The studied sample's idealized (OH)2.5F4.5 composition differs from the current IMA end-member formula. Suggested fluorokuliokite and hydroxykuliokite species remain hypothetical in this study and are not aliases or new records. The 1986 original descriptions and the 1993 natural-alteration study are contextual citations within the 2025 paper, not independently acquired evidence here. No criticality-list designation, microbial mechanism, laboratory synthesis, extraction yield or industrial deployment is asserted.

IMA:1984-064
Kurnakovite

Kurnakovite is the Mg[B3O3(OH)5](H2O)4·H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1940. The year is not an approval identifier. Its triclinic P-1 structure distinguishes it from its monoclinic dimorph inderite. It is also distinct from elemental boron, the borates commodity and a mixed borate-bearing experimental precipitate. Gatta et al. characterized natural Kramer Deposit, California, material by wet chemistry and neutron diffraction at 293 and 20 K. The structural model contains Mg-bound water and an interstitial water molecule, with chains connected by hydrogen bonds. Its specimen-specific chemistry is not a resource-grade survey: the reported water content assumes furnace mass loss is entirely water, and minor measured silicon may reflect impurities rather than structural substitution. Criticality and microbial activity are not inherited from boron content.

Kutnohorite

Kutnohorite is the CaMn2+(CO3)2 mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in its September 2026 master list (PDF page 119). Its status is grandfathered; 1903 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval number. The Handbook of Mineralogy places it in the dolomite group and describes ordered calcium and manganese in approximately equal proportions, commonly with magnesium and ferrous-iron substitution. Its generalized formula Ca(Mn2+,Mg,Fe2+)(CO3)2 and natural-specimen analyses describe compositional variation around the IMA endmember, not an invariant manganese grade. The Handbook reports occurrence in deposits associated with manganese-bearing sediments and identifies analyzed material from Kutna Hora in the Czech Republic and Franklin, New Jersey. The spelling kutnahorite appears in a historical reference title; the accepted species name used here is kutnohorite. This mineral is distinct from the dolomite group as a whole, bulk manganese ore, elemental manganese and manganese oxalates. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

L-chondrite meteorite

Naturally occurring L-group ordinary chondritic meteorite material considered as a potential experimental feed, not a mineral species, secondary waste or established commercial ore. The curated experiment used fragments identified by its authors as Northwest Africa 869, an L3-6 regolith breccia, containing heterogeneous silicate, sulfide and metal phases. These Earth-collected fragments were transported to the International Space Station; the study did not mine an asteroid in situ. Results apply to the tested specimens and conditions, not every L-chondrite. Constituent metals do not confer a criticality designation on this resource.

Laforêtite

Laforêtite is the silver-indium sulfide mineral species AgInS2, listed as approved by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 under 1995-006. Meisser and colleagues' original description concerns tiny natural inclusions in a single galena specimen collected from the Montgros mine dumps in Haute-Loire, France. Reflected-light observations, eight electron-microprobe analyses on two grains, and in-situ X-ray diffraction support the mineral assignment. The diffraction measurement used a roughly 20 by 30 micrometre inclusion; galena reflections were removed, and preferred orientation limits comparison of intensities with the separate synthetic reference. The natural material was assigned to the tetragonal low-temperature AgInS2 form. The authors' laboratory synthesis produced a multiphase comparator, not a pure natural specimen or microbial product; synthetic hardness measurements and preparation temperatures are not natural-specimen measurements. This species is distinct from elemental indium, bulk mine waste, and manufactured AgInS2 polymorphs considered solely by chemical formula. The sampled inclusions establish neither a bulk resource grade nor an extraction yield. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery claim, or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

The year is not an approval identifier. It is distinct from nesquehonite, other magnesium carbonates, magnesium metal and mixed mineral resources. Lanthanite-(Ce)

Lanthanite-(Ce) is the cerium-dominant lanthanite mineral, approved as IMA 1983-055, with ideal formula Ce2(CO3)3(H2O)6·2H2O, equivalently Ce2(CO3)3·8H2O. It is distinct from elemental cerium, cerianite, the lanthanite group and rare-earth ores or commodities. Bevins et al. (1985) characterized natural plates from oxidized copper ore at Britannia Mine, North Wales. Their measured mixed-REE composition gave the empirical cation terms Ce0.78La0.55Nd0.55Sm0.09Gd0.05Y0.04 on the reported 17-oxygen basis, with 7.96H2O; it is not a pure Ce end-member or an ore-grade measurement. Water was determined thermogravimetrically, carbon dioxide by CHN analysis and rare-earth composition by electron microprobe; sample deterioration limited analytical totals. Diffraction indicated orthorhombic Pbnb, a nonstandard setting of Pccn. Atencio et al. (1989) also found their historically labelled Bastnäs lanthanite specimen to be Ce-dominant. The mechanism below concerns separately synthesized Ce carbonate phases and does not establish microbial weathering of these natural specimens, industrial recovery or a dated criticality designation.

IMA:1983-055
Lanthanite-(La)

Lanthanite-(La) is the lanthanum-dominant lanthanite mineral, with ideal formula La2(CO3)3(H2O)6·2H2O, equivalently La2(CO3)3·8H2O. The September 2026 IMA list treats it as a renamed species, with year 1987 s.p.; this nomenclatural action is not a unique mineral approval number. It is distinct from elemental lanthanum, the lanthanite group, other carbonate hydrates and commercial rare-earth feeds. Historical locality labels require caution: the IMA row retains Sweden, whereas Atencio et al. (1989) found their Bastnäs specimen B10531 to be Ce-dominant. Their reassessment of published Curitiba analyses includes La-dominant and Nd-dominant specimens, so neither all Bastnäs material nor all Curitiba material can be assigned to this species solely from its locality. The experiment below concerns a separately synthesized La carbonate analogue of lanthanite, not dissolution of a natural mixed-REE specimen. No jurisdiction-specific criticality designation, microbial process or industrial deployment is established by these sources.

Lanthanite-(Nd)

Lanthanite-(Nd) is the neodymium-dominant lanthanite mineral, approved as IMA 1979-074, with ideal formula Nd2(CO3)3(H2O)6·2H2O, equivalently Nd2(CO3)3·8H2O. It is distinct from elemental neodymium, the lanthanite group and other rare-earth carbonate species. Morrison et al. (2013) characterized a natural specimen from Mitsukoshi, Saga Prefecture, Japan. Electron-microprobe results averaged over 23 analysis points gave a mixed rare-earth composition with Nd0.95La0.61Pr0.17Sm0.12Gd0.08Y0.04Eu0.03 per two rare-earth cations in the reported empirical formula; water was assigned by difference. This is specimen chemistry, not a pure neodymium end-member, ore grade or recovered-metal yield. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 296 K resolved an orthorhombic Pccn structure containing sheets of rare-earth coordination polyhedra and carbonate groups. All rare-earth elements were modeled as Nd because of their similar X-ray scattering, so this refinement does not determine their individual site distributions. Water hydrogen positions could not be assigned reliably and were excluded from refinement; the proposed hydrogen-bond connections rely on oxygen geometry and bond-valence interpretation. The original CIF and reflection downloads remain unverified despite access to the complete article and its rendered supplementary crystallographic information. This record establishes identity and characterization without asserting microbial formation, extraction performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Larderellite

Larderellite is the ammonium borate mineral (NH4)B5O7(OH)2·H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its grandfathered status G and year 1854 describe its nomenclatural history, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from other ammonium borates, a generic experimental ammonium salt, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Fastelli and colleagues characterized natural material from Larderello, Italy, by powder diffraction, reflectance spectroscopy and thermal analysis. Figure 1b's starting-sample diffraction fit reports 94.3% larderellite, 0.4% bassanite and 5.3% polyhalite. These are fitted phase fractions in a mixed specimen, not an independent chemical-purity assay. The study does not establish biological origin or microbial activity merely because the mineral contains ammonium, and no criticality designation is inherited from boron.

Laueite

Laueite is a grandfathered triclinic manganese-ferric phosphate mineral with IMA ideal formula Mn(II)Fe(III)2(PO4)2(OH)2(H2O)6·2H2O and historical year 1954 in the September 2026 list. It is distinct from stewartite and pseudolaueite, which have different framework arrangements, and from strunzite, which has a different water content. Moore (1965) determined the P-1 structure of a natural Palermo No. 1 Quarry, New Hampshire crystal; hydrogen positions were not located. Baur (1969) proposed Mn(III) substitution from earlier bond lengths, while acknowledging other substituents; this was an interpretation, not a direct oxidation-state assay or current species formula. Grey et al. (2025) demonstrated an epitaxial orientation of laueite on stewartite in a natural Hagendorf-Sud composite crystal by single-crystal diffraction and indexed faces. Its rhomb contained both minerals. The EDS-derived laueite metal composition Mn0.66Mg0.17Fe2.17, scaled to three metal atoms, differs from the simplified refined Mn/Mg site occupancy 0.93(2)/0.07; neither is the ideal species formula. The ferric assignment and adjusted hydroxyl/water proportions were inferred from bond-valence and charge-balance considerations. Deposited checks flag displacement parameters, missing hydrogen sites and formula/Z reporting differences, limiting detailed atomistic interpretation. Suggested solution changes and heterosite-assisted nucleation remain paragenetic hypotheses. No controlled transformation, microbial mechanism, recovery performance or inherited criticality designation is curated.

Laurentthomasite

Laurentthomasite (IMA 2018-157, approved April 2019) is an IMA-accepted anhydrous magnesium-potassium-beryllium-aluminium milarite-group (osumilite-type) double-ring cyclosilicate mineral (Strunz 9.CM.05) with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula Mg2K(Be2Al)Si12O30 (PDF p. 122, status A; printed with a missing trailing zero as Mg2K(Be2Al)Si12O3 in Table 1 on p. 357 of Ferraris et al. 2020), representing the anhydrous Mg-dominant A-site analogue of milarite Ca2K(Be2Al)Si12O30 and related to oftedalite ScCaKBe3Si12O30 and friedrichbeckeite Mg2NaKBe3Si12O30. Described by Ferraris, Pignatelli, Cámara, Parodi, Pont, Schreyer, and Wei (2020) from pockets in a coarse-grained quartz-syenite pegmatite (~550 Myr Pan-African granitoid hosted in the 2550–2500 Myr Antananarivo block reworked at ~750–500 Myr) in the Ihorombe region, Fianarantsoa Province, ~80 km northeast of Betroka (23°16'03" S, 46°05'49" E), southern Madagascar (discovered in late 2017 by Laurent Thomas; holotype MNHN_MIN_218.1_a and cotypes MNHN_MIN_218.1_b and MNHN_MIN_218.1_c deposited at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle, Paris, France, pp. 355–357). Occurs as euhedral tabular hexagonal crystals up to 15 mm wide and 5 mm thick flattened on {0001} and bounded by {10-10} prism and {0001} pinacoid forms (only one crystal in matrix has been found so far, whilst isolated specimens are more common; no garnet is present), associated with orthoclase, massive quartz, rare pale green apatite crystals, phenakite, beryl, albite, magnetite, and SEM-EDS-identified thortveitite (Sc2Si2O7), cheralite (CaTh(PO4)2), and microscopic unknown Nb–Ta–W phases, while hosting dark micrometric inclusions of elongated crystals of an Fe2+-rich phase (pp. 356–358). Physical and optical characterization (pp. 355–359, Figs. 1–4) shows transparent crystals with vitreous lustre, light blue streak, non-fluorescence, Mohs hardness ~6, brittle tenacity with irregular to conchoidal fracture, poor {0001} cleavage, Dmeas = 2.67(8) g/cm3 (hydrostatic balance), Dcalc = 2.66(4) g/cm3, colourless appearance in 23 um thin section, uniaxial (+) optics at 589 nm with omega = 1.540(2) and epsilon = 1.545(3), Gladstone–Dale compatibility index 1 - (KP/KC) = 0.028 (excellent), and strong cobalt-blue (along [0001]) to green-yellow (along [1000] / perpendicular to [0001]) dichroism attributed by 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy (miniaturized backscattering MIMOS II spectrometer, Section 4, p. 358, Section 5.1, p. 358, Fig. 3, and Table 4, p. 360) to intervalence charge transfer between octahedral Fe2+ at the A site (Fe(II) octaLaur: CS = 1.21 mm/s, QS = 2.31 mm/s, RA = 92.0%) and tetrahedral Fe3+ at the T(2) site (Fe(III) tetraLaur: CS = 0.25 mm/s, QS = 0.71 mm/s, RA = 5.8%, plus Fe(II) octaIncl from the Fe2+-rich inclusions at CS = 0.85 mm/s, QS = 1.9 mm/s, RA = 2.2%; normalized to 100% of the iron in laurentthomasite itself, Fe2+ constitutes 94%), while Raman spectroscopy (modified Princeton Instruments spectrometer with nanosecond pulsed DPSS laser at 532 nm, 1.5 ns pulse, 10–2000 Hz, up to 1 mJ; Section 4, p. 358, and Section 5.1, pp. 358–359, Fig. 4) shows the most intense peak around 480 cm-1 and splitting of the band around 280 cm-1 into two components with maxima at 263 and 288 cm-1. Combined 40-point WDS electron-microprobe analysis (CAMECA SX100, 15 kV, 10 nA, 5 um beam), ICP-OES/ICP-MS (on about 0.1 g of powdered sample for Be, Y, and trace elements), and Mössbauer Fe partitioning (Section 4, p. 358, and Section 5.1, p. 359, Tables 2–3) yielded SiO2 73.10 wt% (range 71.29–74.90, SD 0.41), BeO 6.02 (ICP-MS, <5% uncertainty), K2O 4.30 (3.92–4.67, SD 0.03), MgO 4.01 (3.80–4.09, SD 0.07), Sc2O3 3.78 (3.70–3.86, SD 0.05), Al2O3 3.11 (3.03–3.20, SD 0.05), FeO 2.69 (printed range 2.50–2.67, where the printed mean 2.69 wt% slightly exceeds the printed upper range bound 2.67 wt%, SD 0.07), MnO 1.91 (1.77–2.04, SD 0.07), Y2O3 0.22 (ICP-MS, <5% uncertainty), Fe2O3 0.19 (calculated from FeO and Mössbauer ratio), BaO 0.16 (0.09–0.23, SD 0.04), Na2O 0.15 (0.10–0.18, SD 0.02), CaO 0.07 (0.06–0.08, SD 0.01), ZnO 0.04 (0.01–0.07, SD 0.03), TiO2 0.02 (printed range 0.02–0.019, SD 0.01), total 99.77 wt% (plus Table 3 ICP-MS trace elements in ug/g including Y 1754, Rb 1405, Yb 922, Lu 321, Zn 176, Er 91.2, Cs 82.9, Tm 43.4, Ga 37.3, As 36.6, Dy 29.4, Sr 21.2, Ni 15.3, Ho 12.8, Zr 7.81, In 7.72, Hf 6.59, Gd 5.56, Cr 5.5, Nd 3.88, Ce 3.62, Co 3.49, V 3.4, Sm 3.07, Cu 3.0, Nb 2.99, Sn 2.36, Tb 2.32, Ge 2.15, Ta 2.02, La 1.50, Th 0.87, Pb 0.85, Pr 0.749, U 0.70, Sb 0.57, Eu 0.239, Bi 0.07, Cd 0.07), giving on 30 anions pfu the empirical formula (Mg0.86Sc0.54Fe2+0.35Mn0.26)Sigma2.01(K0.89Na0.05Y0.02Ca0.01Ba0.01)Sigma0.98[(Be2.35Al0.50Mg0.11Fe3+0.03)Sigma2.99(Si11.90Al0.10)O30] and simplified formula (Mg,Sc)2(K,Na)[(Be,Al,Mg)3(Si,Al)12O30] (ideal Mg2K(Be2Al)Si12O30 requires SiO2 75.92, MgO 8.49, Al2O3 5.37, BeO 5.27, K2O 4.96, total 100 wt%). Hexagonal, space group P6/mcc (no. 192), Z = 2 (Section 4, p. 358, and Sections 5.2–5.3, pp. 359–363, Tables 5–9, Fig. 5): Rietveld powder XRD refinement (Bragg–Brentano X'Pert Pro MPD, CuKalpha1, HighScore suite, p. 359) gives a = 9.95343(6) Å, c = 14.15583(8) Å, V = 1214.54(1) Å3 (ten strongest observed PXRD lines with I >= 2 in Table 5, p. 361: 3.171 (10)(211), 4.064 (8)(112), 2.881 (8)(114), 4.965 (6)(110), 2.732 (4)(204), 3.533 (3)(004), 7.055 (2)(002), 4.302 (2)(200), 3.675 (2)(202), and 1.825 (2)(315) Å, whereas the Abstract on p. 355 prints 2.732 – (8) – 204 in place of 2.881 – (8) – 114 before 2.732 – (4) – 204 and omits 1.825 (2)(315)); single-crystal CuKalpha XRD refinement (Agilent SuperNova, Dual, AtlasS2, 430 reflections with Io > 2sigma(I) out of 431 independent, R1 = 1.89%, wR2 = 4.76%, GoF = 1.224) is reported in Table 6 (p. 362) as a = 9.95800(10) Å, c = 14.14920(10) Å, V = 1215.085(19) Å3 for crystal size 0.40 x 0.29 x 0.17 mm, whereas Section 5.2 prose (p. 359) prints a = 9.95800(7) Å, c = 14.114916(11) Å (a digit-duplication typo for 14.14916(11) Å, as confirmed by the reported volume), V = 1215.081(15) Å3 and Section 4 (p. 358) gives crystal size 39.6 x 28.7 x 16.9 um, with refined site populations (Table 7, p. 362) K+1.005(8) at C (2a, 19.1(2) vs EMP 19 e.p.s.), Mg0.430(9)Sc0.285(4)Fe2+0.285(4) at A (4c, 18.56(8) vs EMP 18.51 e.p.s.), Be0.745(7)Al0.255(7) at T(2) (6f, 6.30(6) vs EMP 5.88 e.p.s., <T(2)–O> = 1.674 Å, TAV = 196.13 deg2), and Si at T(1) (24m, 14 e.p.s., <T(1)–O> = 1.608(2) Å, TQE = 7.39 deg2). P1P 11/2022, pp. 641–643). Lemoynite

Hydrated sodium-calcium-zirconium phyllo/tectosilicate mineral of the lemoynite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Na2CaZr2Si10O26(H2O)5-6, status A, and approval number IMA 1968-013. Perrault, Semenov, Bikova, and Capitonova (1969) originally described lemoynite from pegmatites of the Mont Saint-Hilaire alkaline intrusion, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada, reporting a classical wet-chemical analysis (Table 2, p. 591: SiO2 47.32, ZrO2 23.23, TiO2 0.43, Nb2O5 2.18, RE2O3 1.18, Fe2O3 1.62, MnO 0.10, CaO 5.06, SrO 0.05, Na2O 4.75, H2O 13.33, total 99.25 wt%) and monoclinic symmetry (a = 10.48, b = 16.20, c = 9.07 A, beta = 105 degrees 20 minutes). Le Page and Perrault (1976) re-analyzed Mont Saint-Hilaire lemoynite by XRF and atomic absorption (Table 1, p. 133: SiO2 55.40, Al2O3 0.22, ZrO2 20.30, Nb2O5 0.87, TiO2 0.49, CaO 4.40, MnO 0.04, Fe2O3 0.57, TR2O3 <1, ZnO 0.19, CuO 0.08, SrO 0.07, MgO 0.16, K2O 3.70, Na2O 3.02, Rb2O 0.03, H2O 9.50, total 99.04 wt%, showing that the 1969 analysis had underestimated SiO2 and missed K2O) and solved the crystal structure in monoclinic space group C2/c with doubled c axis (a = 10.384(3), b = 15.947(7), c = 18.601(6) A, beta = 104.59(3) degrees, Z = 4, R = 7.9% for 4200 intensities; C2/m pseudocell with c' = c/2 = 9.300 A), revealing a rigid open [ZrSi5O13]2- framework of 7-A-thick hexagonal-ring silicate sheets linked by 6-coordinated [ZrO6] octahedra and pervaded by wide tunnels containing disordered Na+, K+, Ca2+, and H2O molecules. Distinct from natrolemoynite, armstrongite, elpidite, and elemental zirconium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Liandratite

Hexavalent uranium niobate-tantalate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved end-member formula U6+Nb2O8 (natural solid-solution formula U6+(Nb,Ta)2O8 with Nb:Ta ~ 5:1), status A, and approval number IMA 1975-039. Mucke and Strunz (1978) described the type material from the giant-grained beryl-columbite-petscheckite zone B of the Antsakoa I granitic pegmatite near Berere, ~40 km northeast of Tsaratanana, Madagascar, where liandratite forms 1-2 mm yellow to yellow-brown glassy, conchoidally fracturing metamict crusts epitaxially coating oxidized petscheckite (U4+Fe2+(Nb,Ta)2O8) crystals embedded in quartz. Cameca MS-46 electron-microprobe and microchemical analysis (Table 2, p. 944) yielded ~50 wt% UO2 (present in the hexavalent U6+ oxidation state, corresponding to 48.73 wt% UO3 in the theoretical Nb:Ta = 5:1 formula), ~50 wt% combined Nb2O5 + Ta2O5 with atomic ratio Nb:Ta ~ 5:1 (theoretical Nb2O5 36.22, Ta2O5 15.05 wt%), ~0.5 wt% H2O, and trace Fe, Mn, Th, and Pb. Unheated natural liandratite is completely X-ray amorphous (metamict) with isotropic refractive index n = 1.83, reflectance ~8.6% in air, Mohs hardness ~3.5, and measured density ~6.8 g/cm3. Heating metamict liandratite at red heat (~650 degrees C) and for 24 hours at 1000 degrees C recrystallized it as a single trigonal/hexagonal phase in space group P-31m (D3d^1) with a = 6.36, c = 4.01 A, c/a = 0.6305, Z = 1, Dmeas = 7.0 g/cm3, and Dcalc = 7.11 g/cm3 (for Nb:Ta = 5:1; Dcalc = 6.80 g/cm3 for pure UNb2O8 and 9.01 g/cm3 for UTa2O8), isostructural with synthetic hexagonal UTa2O8. Distinct from petscheckite (U4+Fe2+(Nb,Ta)2O8), oxyuranobetafite, samarskite-(Y), and elemental uranium, niobium, or tantalum; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Light rare-earth commodities, EU assessment convention

This commodity subgroup uses the EU 2020 critical-raw-material assessment's five-member light-rare-earth convention: lanthanum, cerium, praseodymium, neodymium and samarium. Promethium is excluded and scandium is assessed separately in that source. The assessment covers oxide mixtures and low-purity single oxides in its initial-processing stage, and high-purity metals or interalloys in advanced refining. These are related commodity forms, not one mineral or alloy. The EU 2024 Annex II designation names light rare earth elements without enumerating members; its mapping here uses the explicitly stated EU 2020 assessment convention. Light/heavy boundaries in other conventions are not asserted equivalent. This group overlaps individual element records and the broader rare-earth commodity family; no group-wide microbial mechanism or strategic designation is inferred from individual members.
