Liguowuite

Liguowuite (IMA 2020-097) is an IMA-accepted monoclinic tungsten trioxide mineral of the perovskite supergroup, non-stoichiometric perovskite group, and the first natural member of the A-site vacant single-oxide ([]BO3) perovskite subgroup (Nickel–Strunz 04.EA.10, Dana 04.05.01.02), with September 2026 IMA Master List ideal formula WO3 (status A, PDF p. 125) and empirical formula W1.00O3 on the basis of O = 3 (Xue et al. 2022, pp. 95, 98, 102–103). WDS electron-microprobe analysis (15 spots on 4 grains at 15 kV, 10 nA, 5 um beam; Table 1, p. 98) gave WO3 99.23 (range 98.19–99.93, SD 0.56), CaO 0.06 (n.d.–0.11, SD 0.03), Na2O 0.04 (n.d.–0.10, SD 0.03), TeO2 0.03 (n.d.–0.14, SD 0.05), K2O 0.01 (n.d.–0.05, SD 0.02), Al2O3 n.d. (n.d.–0.01, SD 0.00), total 99.37 wt% (ideal WO3 = 100 wt%). Described by Xue, Sun, He, Chen, and Yang (2022) from the vicinity of Nanyang village, Huaping County, Lijiang Prefecture, Yunnan Province, southern Panzhihua–Xichang (Pan–Xi) region, Southwest China (26°46'8.21" N, 101°27'13.86" E in the abstract on p. 95; printed as 26°46'18.21" N, 101°27'13.86" E in Section 2.1 on p. 96; type specimens deposited at the Museum of China University of Geosciences, Beijing, catalogue number 21K005, and the Geological Museum of China, Beijing, catalogue number M16121), where it occurs in a Neoproterozoic (Sinian) semi-weathered biotite-quartz monzonite (biotite adamellite) stock near the contact zone with Permian basites and 300 m north of a fault-hosted pyrite-quartz vein gold deposit in Permian gabbro (pp. 95–97). Closely associated with tewite (IMA:2014-053) and wumuite (IMA:2017-067a), as well as scheelite, tellurite, monazite-(Ce), allanite-(Ce), bastnasite-(Ce), xenotime-(Y), hornblende, pargasite, ferro-hornblende, annite, hydrobiotite, phlogopite, orthoclase, microcline, albite, quartz, kaolinite, ilmenite, goethite, hematite, magnetite, pyrite, zircon, zoisite, titanite, epidote, diopside, tourmaline, almandine, fluorapatite, and moissanite (p. 96). Named in honor of Prof. Li Guowu (b. 1964) of China University of Geosciences (Beijing). Forms greenish-yellow, transparent to translucent prismatic to short-columnar grains (0.05–0.1 mm in diameter) displaying triclinic pseudomorphism ({100}, {010}, {001}, and {120} forms) composed of 100–200 nm monoclinic nanoparticles with cracks and nanovoids resulting from a high-to-low-temperature phase transition (pp. 96–97, 104–106, Figs. 1–2); greasy lustre, white streak, brittle tenacity, uneven fracture, no cleavage, Mohs hardness ~3–4, no UV fluorescence, Dcalc = 7.22 g/cm3, and calculated Gladstone–Dale refractive index n = 2.24 (p. 97). FTIR micro-reflection (Fig. 3, p. 99: [WO6] stretching bands at 870 and 792 cm-1; W–O bending bands at 548, 511, 490, 464, 439, and 418 cm-1) and 532 nm micro-Raman spectra (Fig. 4, p. 99: nu(O–W–O) stretching at 806 and 716 cm-1; delta(O–W–O) bending at 327 and 272 cm-1; lattice mode at 134 cm-1) confirm the absence of O–H or H2O groups. Monoclinic, space group P21/n (no. 14, Z = 8); Rietveld powder X-ray diffraction refinement (CuKalpha, lambda = 1.5418 Å, 106 reflections in 2theta = 15–80° refined from the ICSD 16080 starting model to Rwp = 0.0604, Rp = 0.0454, chi2 = 1.707; pp. 99–101, Tables 2–5, Figs. 5–6) gives a = 7.32582(18) Å, b = 7.54767(18) Å, c = 7.71128(18) Å, beta = 90.678(3)°, V = 426.348(19) Å3, with five strongest powder X-ray diffraction lines [d in Å (I%) (hkl)] at 3.6590 (100)(-200), 3.8552 (88)(002), 3.7685 (88)(020), 2.6258 (60)(202), and 2.6928 (43)(022) (Table 2, p. 100), and corner-sharing distorted and tilted [W1O6] (W1–O = 1.7404(16)–2.1948(16) Å, mean 1.938 Å, BVS 6.033 v.u.) and [W2O6] (W2–O = 1.7322(17)–2.1763(16) Å, mean 1.931 Å, BVS 6.195 v.u.) octahedra (Glazer tilt system a-b+c-) with vacant A sites. Distinct from hydrous tungsten oxides (meymacite WO3·2H2O, hydrotungstite WO2(OH)2·H2O), anthropogenic burned-dump orthorhombic WO3 ("krasnogorite", invalid mineral name; p. 96), and elemental tungsten; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Lithiophilite

Lithiophilite is the lithium manganese(II) phosphate mineral LiMn2+(PO4), listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered with original-description year 1878, not an approval identifier. It is distinct from Fe2+-dominant triphylite, synthetic battery materials of unspecified phase and oxidized lithium-deficient group members. Losey2004 measured natural Mn-rich crystals from the Bennett Quarry, Maine, and Fillow Quarry, Branchville, Connecticut, using microprobe and single-crystal diffraction in orthorhombic space group 62 (Pbnm setting; Handbook Pmnb is another setting). Natural samples contain substitutional Fe and are not pure endmembers. Lithium in that study was constrained or assumed rather than independently measured. The separate Schmid-Beurmann2013 oxidation assay used a laboratory-synthesized, diffraction-assigned LiMnPO4 powder and found no detected phase or lattice change under one specified treatment. That conditional null does not establish universal resistance to lithium dissolution. Neither source demonstrates microbial transformation, isolated lithium recovery or inherited criticality.

Lithium carbonate commodity

Lithium carbonate (Li2CO3) supplied as a manufactured chemical commodity. This product family is distinct from elemental lithium, lithium-bearing brines and ores, and other lithium salts. Albemarle describes separate technical, battery and pharmaceutical product grades; grade names do not make every lithium carbonate lot interchangeable. Its dated product 401125 technical sheet specifies at least 99.0% Li2CO3 and lists cathode manufacture among its applications, illustrating why a battery-related use alone does not establish a universal battery-grade threshold. That supplier-specific assay is not the definition of this whole family. SAMR separately registers YS/T 582-2023 for battery-grade lithium carbonate, but its complete technical tables were not inspected. No criticality designation, microbial production or qualified recovered-product yield is asserted here.

 commodity — None — —
Lithium hydroxide monohydrate commodity

Manufactured lithium hydroxide monohydrate products, with nominal composition LiOH.H2O. The hydration state distinguishes this commodity from anhydrous LiOH; it is not elemental lithium or the general battery-grade lithium umbrella. Albemarle product 401106 is a crystalline monohydrate with a supplier specification of at least 55.0% LiOH by acidimetric titration, expressed as LiOH rather than as monohydrate purity. Its stated applications include lubricating greases and alkaline storage batteries. SAMR separately names a battery-grade monohydrate standard, GB/T 26008-2020; the complete qualification tables were not inspected. The supplier assay and the existence of that narrower standard do not qualify every monohydrate product for lithium-ion cathode manufacture. No criticality designation or microbial production mechanism is asserted.

Lithium-mica ore

Natural lithium-bearing ore containing lithium micas together with other mineral phases. The 2020 curated experiment used crushed ore from Beauvoir, France, supplied by the University of Birmingham and called lepidolite by Sedlakova-Kadukova et al. Its initial XRD pattern was assigned to polylithionite, muscovite and kaolinite in supplementary Figure S2A. These are source-qualified assignments in a heterogeneous feed, not a certified pure polylithionite specimen or quantitative phase proportions. Lepidolite is series terminology, not an unambiguous mineral-species identifier. This extracted geological feed remains a primary resource, distinct from an individual mica species, elemental lithium, a processing waste or a purified lithium product. A separate 2025 experiment used a supplier-provided mixed feed called lepidolite, with mica, albite and quartz assignments and additional celadonite labels in its initial diffraction figure; no mine provenance or quantitative species composition was supplied. The two feeds are separate experiments within this resource category. No criticality designation or industrial deployment is inferred from its lithium content.

Lopatkaite

IMA-approved lead-antimony-arsenic sulfosalt mineral (IMA 2012-083; symbol Lpk; status A, Approved 2013; full description published April 2026) with ideal end-member formula Pb5Sb3AsS11 (Z = 8; written Pb10As2Sb6S22 with Z = 4 in the type description, requiring Pb 56.64 wt%, Sb 19.97 wt%, S 19.29 wt%, As 4.10 wt%, total 100.00 wt%), representing the ordered As-rich homeotype/isotype of monoclinic boulangerite (MDO1 polytype) in the boulangerite homologous series (Topa et al., 2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:217-229). Discovered at the Taylor Pit, Lot 13, Concession XIV, Huntingdon Township, Madoc area, Hastings County, Ontario, Canada (collected by Russian-Canadian mineral collector Vladimir Lopatka, b. 1957, in 1995), where it occurs in nested sulfosalt aggregates >500 um across hosted by Grenvillian Precambrian cipollino (calcite-dolomite) marbles, associated with boulangerite (which overgrows and partially replaces lopatkaite), veenite, sterryite, calcite, sphalerite, jamesonite, arsenopyrite, and pyrite; the holotype polished section is deposited at the Natural History Museum Vienna (NHMW), Austria, under catalogue number O 3954 (transferred from the Mineralogical Museum of the University of Salzburg, former catalogue number 15008). Forms greyish-black subhedral to anhedral grains up to 300 um and aggregates >500 um with a dark-grey streak, metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, brittle tenacity, irregular fracture, no cleavage or parting, Vickers microhardness VHN50 = 189-208 kg/mm2 (mean 200 kg/mm2, corresponding to Mohs hardness 3-3.5), and calculated density Dcalc = 6.168 g/cm3 for the empirical formula and 6.096 g/cm3 for the ideal formula on the single-crystal unit cell. In reflected light it is greyish-white with distinct bireflectance, distinct pleochroism, and distinct anisotropy showing greyish to brownish-grey rotation tints; Commission on Ore Mineralogy (COM) reflectance values in air (Rmin, Rmax in %; Table 1) are 37.0, 39.3% (470 nm), 34.1, 36.9% (546 nm), 33.1, 36.2% (589 nm), and 31.3, 34.1% (650 nm). Field-emission electron microprobe analysis (JEOL JXA-8530F, 25 kV, 20 nA, 1.5 um beam; Table 2) of the grain used for single-crystal X-ray diffraction (Group 5, n = 4 points) yielded Pb 57.81(4) wt%, Sb 20.03(9) wt%, S 19.08(6) wt%, and As 3.53(8) wt%, total 100.46(22) wt% (arithmetic sum 100.45 wt%), corresponding on the basis of 40 atoms per formula unit (Me18S22, Z = 4) to the empirical formula Pb10.28(3)As1.74(4)Sb6.06(3)S21.92(3) (As/Sb = 0.287, Pb/(Sb+As) = 1.32), while the most As-enriched domain (Group 6, n = 5 points) yielded Pb 57.36(6) wt%, Sb 18.77(13) wt%, S 19.20(1) wt%, and As 4.43(7) wt%, total 99.77(2) wt% (arithmetic sum 99.76 wt%), giving Pb10.17(1)As2.17(3)Sb5.66(4)S21.99(1) (As/Sb = 0.383, Pb/(Sb+As) = 1.30). Crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group P21/c (#14), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 8.0806(6) A, b = 23.3597(18) A, c = 21.4880(16) A, beta = 100.7090(10) deg, V = 3985.4(5) A3, and Z = 4 for Pb10As2Sb6S22 (or Z = 8 for Pb5Sb3AsS11; refined to R1 = 0.0412, R(all) = 0.0498, wR(on Fo^2) = 0.0842, and GoF = 1.032 for 3569 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) out of 4241 unique reflections from 25,691 measured at 300(2) K on a 0.05 x 0.08 x 0.12 mm fragment using MoKalpha radiation, Table 4). The structure consists of rod-layers of lozenge-shaped [100] SnS-archetype rods composed of three double ribbons (R1, R2, R3) with 18 independent cation sites and 22 S sites (Table 5), giving the refined structural formula Pb10.336As1.567Sb6.088S22 (Z = 4, cation sum 17.991 apfu), defined by dominant As occupancy at two peripheral ribbon sites, (As,Sb)3 (As0.673(16)Sb0.327(16), BVS = 3.263 v.u.) and (As,Sb)8 (As0.581(15)Sb0.419(15), BVS = 3.399 v.u.), together with minor As at (Sb,As)4 (Sb0.723(15)As0.277(15), BVS = 3.342 v.u.) and (Sb,As)7 (Sb0.955(15)As0.045(15), BVS = 3.307 v.u.), and mixed Pb/Sb occupancy at (Pb,Sb)4 (Pb0.922(8)Sb0.078(8), where Table 5 on p. 223 prints the bond valence sum without a decimal point as "2128" for 2.128 v.u.), (Sb,Pb)5 (Sb0.892(9)Pb0.108(9), BVS = 2.912 v.u.), and (Sb,Pb)6 (Sb0.694(9)Pb0.306(9), BVS = 2.660 v.u.). The seven strongest calculated powder X-ray diffraction lines (dcalc in A (Irel; hkl), CuKalpha, Table 3) are 3.712 (100; 0 3 5), 2.020 (47; -4 0 2), 2.780 (43; 2 6 0), 2.804 (41; -2 6 1), 3.728 (39; 2 1 1), 2.779 (38; -2 6 2), and 3.653 (35; 0 6 2). IMA:2012-083
Lorenzenite

Lorenzenite is the sodium titanium silicate mineral with ideal formula Na2Ti2O3(Si2O6), equivalent to Na2Ti2Si2O9. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list gives grandfathered status G and original description year 1901, not an IMA approval number. Ramsayite is a historical name for the same species, not a separate material owner. Sundberg, Lehtinen and Kivekas (1987) refined a natural crystal from Helsinki museum specimen 4937, labelled from Lovozero on the Kola Peninsula. Their Pbcn model contains pyroxene-type silicate chains, distorted TiO6 octahedra and seven-coordinate sodium. The single-crystal refinement used 778 selected reflections from 1167 measured independent reflections and reported R=0.026. The chemistry cited for that specimen was from earlier work, not a new bulk assay in 1987. Historical cell-setting and oxygen-coordinate discrepancies are discussed in the original study. This identity record does not assert a dissolution, synthesis or microbial mechanism, a recovery yield, industrial use or criticality inherited from titanium.

Lucasite-(Ce)

Lucasite-(Ce) (IMA 1986-020) is an IMA-accepted cerium-titanium oxide-hydroxide mineral with IMA September 2026 Master List formula CeTi2O5(OH) and crystal-chemical formula CeTi2(O,OH)6 (empirical formula Ce0.51La0.27Nd0.11Pr0.11Ti2(O,OH)6). Described by Nickel, Grey, and Madsen (1987) from heavy-mineral concentrates of the Argyle AK1 diamondiferous olivine lamproite tuff, East Kimberley region, Western Australia, Australia. Table 1 (p. 1007) reports the mean of eight electron-microprobe analyses: Ce2O3 24.99, La2O3 13.12, Nd2O3 5.90, Pr2O3 5.50, CaO 0.62, TiO2 47.93, MgO 0.03, SiO2 0.25, Al2O3 0.04, total 98.38 wt% (with F not analyzed and the low 98.38 wt% total together with bond-valence sums interpreted as indicating hydroxyl/water substitution). Monoclinic (space group I2/a, equivalent to standard C2/c; refined to R = 0.054 for 977 independent reflections), with a = 5.178(1) Å, b = 8.756(4) Å, c = 9.768(5) Å, beta = 93.52(4)°, Z = 4, Dcalc = 5.00 g/cm3, Vickers microhardness VHN10 = 761–900 kg/mm2 (mean 824 kg/mm2), {001} cleavage, and refractive indices n > 2.0 (Gladstone-Dale calculated mean n = 2.321).

IMA:1986-020
Ludlamite

Ludlamite is the ferrous phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+3(PO4)2(H2O)4, recorded as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA list. It is a distinct mineral species from the three-water phosphoferrite and eight-water vivianite. Moore (1971) investigated natural ludlamite crystals from the Palermo number 1 mine in an abiotic heating comparison. The lower-temperature arms retained the starting powder pattern, whereas the 240 degrees C arm gave a ferric product with diffuse diffraction unrelated to the initial mineral. This observation does not identify a pure crystalline product or establish a general transformation temperature for all ludlamite specimens. The ludlamite and phosphoferrite observations curated in this corpus are different mineral arms of the same study, not independent replications. No microbial process, isolated-product recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is asserted.

Ludwigite boron-iron ore

Ludwigite ore denotes a heterogeneous boron-bearing iron ore or its beneficiated boron-iron concentrate, represented here by the mixed geological feed used by Liang et al. (2024). It is not the mineral species ludwigite, elemental boron or iron, a borates commodity specification, or the secondary residue left after processing. The experimental substrate for water leaching was a soda-ash-roasted derivative of that concentrate; its altered composition must not be assigned to the original ore. The paper's Table 2 reports 5.12 wt% B2O3 and 58.23 wt% total iron in this reduced feed, and Figure 9 identifies metallic iron, sodium magnesium silicate, sodium silicate and magnesium-ferrous oxide. Its bulk-feed result cannot establish which individual original boron mineral supplied the dissolved boron. The exact mine/sample identifier and original batch mineral proportions are not established in the inspected 2024 article, which refers to earlier work for the ore characterization. No constituent's criticality designation is transferred to this resource.

Anhydrous sodium-cerium fluorocarbonate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Na3Ce2(CO3)4F, status A, and approval number IMA 1996-033. Grice and Chao (1997) described the cotype specimen (CMNMI 81535, formerly provisional phase UK80) from a pegmatite vein at the Poudrette quarry, Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada, where it occurs with microcline, sodalite, catapleiite, fluorite, aegirine, siderite, astrophyllite, and Petersenite-(Ce). Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (mean of 5 analyses on 1 grain, p. 1257) with CO2 calculated by stoichiometry yielded Na2O 14.94, CaO 0.10, SrO 0.12, La2O3 16.36, Ce2O3 29.48, Pr2O3 1.95, Nd2O3 5.88, F 3.58, CO2 28.40 (calc), less O=F 1.51, total 99.30 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 4 C atoms (13 anions) to the empirical formula (Na2.99Ca0.01Sr0.01)Sigma3.01(Ce1.11La0.62Nd0.22Pr0.07)Sigma2.02(CO3)4F1.17. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction refined in hexagonal space group P63/mmc (single-crystal cell a = 5.0612(8), c = 22.820(9) A, V = 506.2(2) A3; Debye-Scherrer powder XRD cell a = 5.068(1), c = 22.87(5) A, V = 509(1) A3, Z = 2, R = 3.4%, wR = 4.0% for 335 observed reflections with F > 5sigma(F) out of 399 unique reflections) confirmed that lukechangite-(Ce) is isostructural with synthetic Na3La2(CO3)4F, featuring layered sheets of [CeO9], [Na1O6F2], [Na2O6], and [CO3] polyhedra stacked along c. The mineral is soluble with effervescence in 1:1 HCl. Distinct from cordylite-(Ce), baiyuneboite-(Ce) (cordylite-(Ce) synonym/polytype), huanghoite-(Ce), and elemental cerium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

IMA-approved silver-copper-lead-bismuth selenide sulfosalt-like mineral (IMA 2018-154; symbol Lux in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 129; status A, Approved 2019; full description published August 2020) with ideal end-member formula AgCuPbBi4Se8 (reported on p. 450 as requiring Ag 5.58 wt%, Cu 3.44 wt%, Pb 11.22 wt%, Bi 45.28 wt%, and Se 34.22 wt% for a total of 100.00 wt%, where Ag 5.58 wt% is a digit-transposition misprint for the true stoichiometric value 5.84 wt% so the printed ideal values sum to 99.74 wt%; Philippo et al., 2020, European Journal of Mineralogy 32:449-455). Represents the ordered Ag-Cu analogue of watkinsonite, Cu2PbBi4Se8 (with Ag ordered at the octahedral Ag1 site and Cu ordered at the tetrahedral Cu2 site, and closely related to litochlebite, Ag2PbBi4Se8, with which it shows very limited solid solution), and is named after the city and Grand Duchy of Luxembourg as the first new mineral species discovered in Luxembourg. Discovered during winter 2012 tunnel excavation works by the Societe Electrique de l'Our at Bivels in the Oesling (Ardennes) region of northern Luxembourg (49 deg 57 min 8 sec N, 6 deg 10 min 41 sec E), where it occurs in hydrothermal veins cutting Lower Devonian reddish schists Affected by Variscan metamorphism, deposited as tiny acicular fibres on translucent rhombohedral dolomite crystals (up to 2 mm) associated with siderite; cotype specimens are deposited in the mineralogical collection of the Natural History Museum of Luxembourg (Musee National d'Histoire Naturelle, catalogue number FD040; portion used for EPMA) and the Laboratory of Mineralogy, University of Liege, Belgium (catalogue number 21302; portion used for SCXRD). Forms grey metallic millerite-like fibres up to 200 um in length and 5 um in diameter (Figure 1) with a black streak, metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, brittle tenacity, no observed cleavage, Mohs hardness 3 (estimated by comparison with litochlebite), and calculated density reported as 8.00 g/cm3 in the Abstract (p. 449), Section 3 (p. 450), and Table 6 (p. 454) from the chemical analysis and unit-cell parameters vs Dcalc = 7.397 g/cm3 in Table 3 (p. 452; optical properties not determined due to the 5 um fibre diameter). Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (average of 5 point analyses, JEOL JXA-8200, 15 kV, 5 nA, 1 um beam; Table 1) yielded Bi 43.73 wt% (range 42.66-44.26), Se 31.04 wt% (30.37-32.04), Pb 11.95 wt% (10.50-12.79), Ag 6.60 wt% (5.68-9.04), Cu 2.66 wt% (2.23-2.81), Fe 0.02 wt% (0.00-0.05), S 0.01 wt% (0.00-0.02), and As 0.00 wt%, total 96.01 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 15 atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula Ag1.00(Cu0.82Ag0.20Fe0.01)Sigma1.03Pb1.13Bi4.11(Se7.72S0.01)Sigma7.73. Macraeite

IMA-approved monoclinic paulkerrite-group hydrated potassium manganese iron-titanium oxyhydroxyphosphate mineral (IMA 2023-065; status A, Approved 2023; full description published March 2024; no mineral symbol assigned in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 130, or in the type description) with ideal end-member formula [(H2O)K]Mn2(Fe2Ti)(PO4)4[O(OH)](H2O)10*4H2O (written [K(H2O)]Mn2(Fe2Ti)(PO4)4[O(OH)](H2O)10*4H2O in the IMA Master List and misprinted as [(H2O)K]Mn2(Fe2Ti)(PO4)4[(O(OH)]2(H2O)10*4H2O in Table 7 on p. 277; requiring K2O 4.75 wt%, MnO 14.31 wt%, Fe2O3 16.11 wt%, TiO2 8.06 wt%, P2O5 28.63 wt%, and H2O 28.14 wt%, total 100 wt%; Grey et al., 2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:267-278). Represents the Fe3+-dominant analogue of rewitzerite (K(H2O)Mn2(Al2Ti)(PO4)4[O(OH)](H2O)10*4H2O, IMA 2022-144) and the OH-dominant analogue of fluormacraeite (IMA 2024-054), and is named in honour of Colin MacRae (b. 1961), head of the Microbeam Laboratory at CSIRO Mineral Resources, Clayton, Victoria, Australia, for his development of liquid-nitrogen cold-stage electron microprobe techniques and water-inclusive matrix-correction software used to characterize 40 approved new mineral species since 2010. Discovered in phosphate nodules of weathered triplite, heterosite, and lithiophilite collected in 1984 on the dumps of the Chao do Castanheiro mining concession at the Cubos-Mesquitela-Mangualde pegmatite (40 deg 35 min 13.7 sec N, 7 deg 45 min 04.3 sec W), near Mesquitela and Mangualde, Viseu district, Portugal, associated with deep reddish-purple strengite, tan deeply etched triplite, reddish-brown bermanite, inky-blue phosphosiderite, and occasional switzerite; the holotype specimen is housed in the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, USA, under catalogue number 76293, and a cotype specimen is housed in the Bavarian State Collection for Mineralogy (SNSB), Munich, Germany, under registration number MSM 38050. Forms colourless to light-greenish-yellow equant, pseudo-rhombic dodecahedral crystals (sub-100 to ~150 um individually and in complex intergrowths up to 0.5 mm) displaying forms {010}, {001}, {111}, and {11-1}, with calculated density Dcalc = 2.39 g/cm3 (from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell volume), biaxial positive (+) optics with alpha = 1.605(3), beta = 1.611(3), gamma = 1.646(3) (white light), 2Vmeas = 45(3) deg (EXCALIBR) and 2Vcalc = 25.8 deg, strong r < v dispersion, optical orientation X = b, Y = c, Z = a, and an excellent Gladstone-Dale compatibility index of 0.020. Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm diode laser at 4 mW, Horiba XploRA PLUS spectrometer with 200 um slit, 1800 grooves/mm grating, and 100x objective; Figure 5, Section 5, p. 270) shows a broad O-H stretching band centred at 3460 cm-1 with shoulders reported at 3580, 3460 (printed twice in Section 5), and 3250 cm-1, water H-O-H bending at 1645 cm-1, symmetric PO4 stretching at 955 cm-1 (shoulders at 1005 and 980 cm-1), antisymmetric PO4 stretching at 1125 and 1077 cm-1, intense Ti-O/M2-O stretching bands at 830 and 780 cm-1 from linear M2-M3-M2 octahedral trimers, and PO4 bending bands at 595, 465, and 450 cm-1. Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (n = 17 analyses on 17 crystals, JEOL JXA-8500F Hyperprobe, 15 kV, 2.2 nA, 10 um defocused beam; Table 1) yielded P2O5 29.55 wt% (range 26.20-32.01, SD 2.20), MnO 14.63 wt% (13.33-15.91, SD 0.86), Fe2O3 11.80 wt% (10.24-13.66, SD 0.86), TiO2 9.85 wt% (8.65-11.10, SD 0.83), K2O 4.14 wt% (3.70-4.89, SD 0.37), Al2O3 1.65 wt% (0.23-3.68, SD 0.96), F 1.04 wt% (0.39-2.03, SD 0.47), MgO 0.35 wt% (0.21-0.55, SD 0.12), H2Ocalc 28.90 wt%, and -O=F -0.44 wt%, for a mean total of 101.47 wt% (individual totals 96.4-108.8 wt% due to vacuum dehydration and parallel crystal cracking). Manganese sulfate monohydrate commodity

Manufactured manganese sulfate monohydrate products, nominally MnSO4.H2O. The monohydrate commodity is distinct from manganese metal, other sulfate hydration states, dissolved manganese in a leachate, and a mineral specimen. Pan Chem supplies monohydrate powder for feed and fertilizer applications, and Ihumate publishes the monohydrate formula and an agricultural product specification. These sources establish a manufactured product family rather than one battery qualification. Walsun separately describes high-purity manganese sulfate for lithium-ion cathode precursors, while SAMR registers HG/T 4823-2023 for manganese sulfate for batteries; the complete standard tables were not inspected. Neither that end use nor this one salt exhausts the broader battery-grade manganese family. No universal purity cutoff, criticality designation or microbial production of qualified crystals is asserted.

Manganite is the manganese(III) oxide hydroxide mineral MnO(OH), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The year 1826 is its historical date, not an IMA approval accession. It is distinct from elemental manganese, manganese ore, the MnO2 minerals pyrolusite and ramsdellite, and other MnOOH polymorphs. Manganoschafarzikite

IMA-approved manganese(II) antimony(III) oxide mineral (IMA 2022-129; symbol Msfz; status A, Approved 2023) with ideal end-member formula Mn2+Sb3+2O4 (requiring MnO 19.57 wt%, Sb2O3 80.43 wt%, total 100 wt%), representing the Mn2+ analogue of schafarzikite (Fe2+Sb3+2O4) in the newly established minium group (MX2O4; Holtstam et al., 2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:311-322). Discovered at the Hindenburg working (~150 m level) of the Langban Fe-Mn skarn deposit (59.85 deg N, 14.26 deg E), Filipstad district, Varmland Province, Sweden, where it occurs in late-stage ("period D") open fractures cutting banded fine-grained hematite-andradite skarn, associated with calcite, native lead, hydrocerussite, nadorite, Pb-bearing rhodochrosite, mimetite, and a serpentine-group mineral; the holotype specimen is deposited at the Department of Geosciences, Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm (catalogue no. GEO-NRM 19339699), and a crystal fragment is deposited at the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo (catalogue no. KNR 44410). Forms dark reddish-brown to black platy, subhedral crystals in subparallel aggregates up to 5 mm across (locally showing an iridescent "peacock" tarnish) with a yellowish-brown to dark-brown streak, submetallic lustre, translucent diaphaneity in thin fragments, distinct {110} cleavage, brittle tenacity, uneven to conchoidal fracture, estimated Mohs hardness 3-4, non-fluorescence under ultraviolet light, and calculated density Dcalc = 5.37(2) g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell volume. In reflected light it is greyish-white, weakly bireflectant, nonpleochroic, and weakly anisotropic with abundant dark-brown to red internal reflections; Commission on Ore Mineralogy (COM) reflectance values in air (R2, R1 in %; Table 2; note Section 3 on p. 313 prints the spectral window as "400-70 nm range" for 400-700 nm) are 15.4, 14.1% (470 nm), 14.7, 13.6% (546 nm), 14.4, 13.4% (589 nm), and 14.1, 13.2% (650 nm). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser; Section 6.1, Fig. 3) shows bands at 669 cm-1 (strongest, symmetric Sb-O stretching of SbO3 pyramids), 543 cm-1 (very weak, Mn-O stretch), 522 cm-1 (weak, antisymmetric Sb-O stretch), 460 cm-1 (strong, Mn-O stretch or Sb-O-Sb bending), 402 cm-1 on p. 315 vs 405 cm-1 on p. 316 and Fig. 3 (weak, Sb-O-Sb bending), 348 cm-1 (very weak), 290 cm-1 (strong, Sb-O-Sb bending), and 220 cm-1 (medium, Sb-O-Sb bending). Electron microprobe analysis (7 point analyses, CAMECA SX100, 15 kV, 10 nA, 2-10 um beam; Table 3) yielded Sb2O3 80.15 wt% (2sigma = 0.38), MnO 12.72 wt% (2sigma = 0.42), FeO 4.98 wt% (2sigma = 0.23), As2O3 0.96 wt% (2sigma = 0.10), PbO 0.92 wt% (2sigma = 0.24), and MgO 0.89 wt% (2sigma = 0.10), with Bi and Zn not detected and total 100.62 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 4 O atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula (Mn2+0.64Fe2+0.25Mg0.08)Sigma=0.97(Sb3+1.97As3+0.03Pb0.01)Sigma=2.01O4. Crystallizes in the tetragonal system, space group P42/mbc (#135), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 8.65159(8) A, c = 5.97175(9) A, V = 446.986(11) A3, and Z = 4 (refined to R1 = 1.51%, R1(all) = 1.57%, wR2 = 3.74%, and GoF = 1.233 for 462 reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) out of 475 unique reflections from 31,859 measured on a 0.040 x 0.060 x 0.110 mm crystal using MoKalpha radiation, where Section 5.1 on p. 314 prints the wavelength as "lambda = 0.71703 A" for 0.71073 A). The structure consists of infinite [001] rutile-like chains of edge-sharing MnO6 octahedra at the 4d site (refined site occupancy Mn0.969(4), Mn-O1 = 2.196(2) A x 2, Mn-O2 = 2.1218(16) A x 4, BVS = 2.28 v.u.; mean bond distance printed as 2.147 A in Table 10 vs 2.146 A in Section 7.1 prose, exact mean 2.1465 A) cross-linked via corner-sharing with chains of SbO3 trigonal pyramids at the 8h site (Sb1.00, Sb-O1 = 1.9987(11) A x 2, Sb-O2 = 1.932(2) A, mean 1.976 A, BVS = 2.72 v.u.) whose stereoactive 5s2 lone-pair electrons project into empty [001] channels. Gandolfi powder X-ray diffraction (CuKalpha, 23 reflections; Section 5.2, Table 11) gives refined cell parameters a = 8.6273(5) A and c = 5.9683(5) A (with unit-cell volume printed as V = 442.23(5) A3 on p. 315 via a digit typo for a^2 * c = 444.22(5) A3), and the strongest observed reflections (dmeas in A (Imeas; hkl)) are 3.24 (100; 2 1 1), 1.976 (28; 4 1 1), 2.72 (26; 3 1 0), 4.30 (22; 2 0 0), 2.45 (20; 2 0 2), 1.680 (18; 3 3 2), 1.767 (17; 2 1 3), 1.441 (15; 4 1 3), and 2.98 (14; 0 0 2). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Margaritasite

Hydrated cesium-uranyl divanadate mineral of the carnotite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Cs2(UO2)2(VO4)2·H2O (structural formula Cs2(UO2)2V2O8·H2O), status A, and approval number IMA 1980-093. Wenrich, Modreski, Zielinski, and Seeley (1982) described the type specimen (deposited at the U.S. National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.) from the Margaritas uranium-molybdenum deposit (site 19 and drill hole #33), Sierra Pena Blanca Uranium District, Chihuahua, Mexico, where it occurs as 1-3 um yellow tabular plates filling matrix pores and lining leached phenocryst molds in altered Oligocene rhyodacitic tuff breccia of the lower Escuadra Formation alongside quartz, feldspar, kaolinite, pyrite, and barite. ARL-SEMQ electron-microprobe analysis of 14 grains (Table 4, p. 1282) yielded an anhydrous mean of UO3 55.4, Cs2O 17.6, V2O5 17.0, K2O 1.63, Ca 0.33, Ba 0.19, Si 0.14, Sr 0.07, Al 0.02, sum 91.63 wt% (recalculated with 2.5 wt% H2O to 100%: UO3 58.9, Cs2O 18.7, V2O5 18.1, K2O 1.73 wt%), while AAS, ICAP-AES, and CHN wet-chemical analysis of three ultrasonic-concentrated splits (containing ~11 wt% admixed quartz, Table 4) yielded UO3 49.6, Cs2O 17.0, V2O5 15.9, H2O 2.5, K2O 1.20 wt% (recalculated quartz-free to 100%: UO3 57.5, Cs2O 19.7, V2O5 18.4, H2O 2.9, K2O 1.39 wt%), corresponding to the empirical formula (Cs1.38(H3O)0.35K0.29)Sigma2.02(UO2)1.99(V2O8)1.00·1.07H2O. X-ray powder diffraction (Tables 2-3, pp. 1279-1280) refined in monoclinic space group P21/a (Z = 2) gave a = 10.514(3), b = 8.425(3), c = 7.252(5) A (7.25 A in abstract), beta = 106.01 degrees, V = 617.48(44) A3, and Dcalc = 5.41 g/cm3 (5.40 g/cm3 in Table 3; biaxial negative, nalpha ~ 1.797 calc, nbeta = 1.925-1.930, ngamma = 1.945-1.950, 2V = 42(5) degrees). Hydrothermal CsCl ion-exchange experiments at 200 degrees C converted natural carnotite into margaritasite. IMA:1980-093
Mcallisterite

Mcallisterite is the Mg2[B6O7(OH)6]2·9H2O mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, approved as 1963-012. The original 1965 description used the spelling Macallisterite and the equivalent oxide formula 2MgO·6B2O3·15H2O. Natural material from the Mott prospect, Furnace Creek Wash, California was intimately mixed with ginorite, sassolite and other impurities. Its powder pattern matched separately synthesized mcallisterite, with residual impurity peaks; the authors did not obtain an impurity-free natural powder pattern. Larger synthetic crystals supplied the single-crystal and accurate physical-property measurements. Natural chemical compositions were calculated after subtracting assumed impurity contributions, rather than measured on pure mineral. This boron-bearing species is distinct from elemental boron and the borates commodity. Criticality, microbial activity and industrial recovery are not inferred.

IMA:1963-012
Mckelveyite-(Y)

Hydrated sodium-calcium-barium-yttrium carbonate mineral of the mckelveyite (donnayite) group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC redefined formula NaCaBa3Y(CO3)6(H2O)3, status Rd, and approval number IMA 1964-025. Milton et al. (1965) originally described mckelveyite from four subsurface core and trona-mine localities in the Eocene Wilkins Peak Member of the Green River Formation, Sweetwater County, Wyoming, USA, proposing the uranium-bearing trigonal P-3 formula Na1.9Ba4.0Ca1.1Sr0.2RE1.5U0.3(CO3)9·5H2O after recalculating wet-chemical analyses of massive and crystal-aggregate fractions for 18.0-20.7 wt% acid-insoluble impurities (organic matter, authigenic biotite, acmite, and quartz). Subsequent studies cited by Demartin et al. (2008) showed that type mckelveyite-(Y) is triclinic P1 (mckelveyite-(Y)-1A) with formula NaBa3(Ca,U)Y(CO3)6·3H2O. Demartin et al. (2008) solved the first complete crystal structure on a uranium-free monoclinic Cc polytype, mckelveyite-(Y)-2M (a = 15.8213(7), b = 9.1364(4), c = 13.7522(6) A, beta = 112.44(1) degrees, Z = 4, R = 0.0283 for 4454 reflections with I > 2sigma(I)), from hydrothermal carbonate veins at the Cava Fabi talc quarry, Val Malenco, Sondrio, Lombardy, Italy, where CO2 and H2O were derived from structure solution rather than direct gas analysis. Following IMA-CNMNC guidance, the monoclinic Alpine material is a polytype (mckelveyite-(Y)-2M) of the species rather than a separate mineral species. Distinct from mckelveyite-(Nd), donnayite-(Y), ewaldite, and elemental yttrium or rare earths; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Melanterite

Melanterite is the monoclinic ferrous sulfate heptahydrate mineral, FeSO4·7H2O, grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA list. It is distinct from dissolved ferrous sulfate, other sulfate hydrates and ferric oxides. The accepted primary study assigns minor melanterite in a mixed solid from a nitrate/Fe(II) microcosm containing Comamonas strain HJ-2. The strain's species identification is unresolved.

Metalliferous black shale

Metal-bearing, organic-matter-containing sedimentary shale considered as a geological resource. This heterogeneous rock is distinct from its constituent elements, individual mineral species, a standardized traded concentrate and processing-generated waste. The cited Pakistani, Polish and incompletely localized experimental feeds are not interchangeable. Metallurgical coal commodity family

Coal products used in steelmaking, scoped here to the broader commodity family recognized by the EIA glossary and the IEA Coal 2020 report. EIA includes coking coal and pulverized coal consumed in steelmaking; IEA includes coking, semi-soft blending coal and pulverised coal injection (PCI) coal. This family explicitly overlaps cmmmech:coking-coal as a narrower coke-making subset; it is not a second disjoint coking-coal identity. IEA excludes anthracite from its metallurgical category even when used in metallurgy. In contrast, USGS Fact Sheet 2026-3061 uses metallurgical coal and coking coal interchangeably within its coke-production scope. These source-dependent boundaries are retained rather than asserted to be a universal coal classification. The record denotes an end-use commodity, not elemental carbon, a mineral species, manufactured coke or every coal burned industrially. No numerical grade threshold, criticality designation or microbial mechanism is generalized across this family.

Metaschoepite is a uranyl oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral, distinct from schoepite, elemental uranium and the products historically called dehydrated schoepite. The September 2026 IMA list gives (UO2)8O2(OH)12·10H2O and grandfathered status G; 1960 is the original description year, not an approval accession. IMA:1981-055
Metatorbernite

Metatorbernite is the copper uranyl phosphate mineral Cu(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)4·4H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1916 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal eight-water composition is distinct from twelve-water torbernite, arsenate metazeunerite, calcium meta-autunite, uranyl ions and elemental uranium or copper. Locock and Burns grew synthetic metatorbernite in copper-bearing silica gel at room temperature over three weeks and refined an epoxy-coated, merohedrally twinned crystal in P4/n. Its 88.3(6)% fitted copper-site occupancy and constrained hydrogen model are specimen-specific; proposed oxonium charge compensation was not directly established. The 2023 natural Cornwall crystal instead gave the preferred P4/nmm model with a smaller c repeat. These are source-specific structural models, not grounds to replace all specimens with one symmetry or transfer occupancy between them. Thermal behavior below is abiotic laboratory evidence; neither criticality nor microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is inferred.

Metatyuyamunite

Metatyuyamunite is the calcium uranyl vanadate mineral Ca(UO2)2(VO4)2·3H2O. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list recognizes it with grandfathered status G; 1954 is the original-description year, not an IMA approval accession. This mineral-species owner is distinct from tyuyamunite, carnotite, the broader carnotite group, elemental uranium or vanadium and the mixed sandstone used experimentally. Glasauer et al. (2022) identified metatyuyamunite, written meta- tyuyamunite in the paper, together with fritzscheite in the starting natural uranium-vanadium sandstone. After incubation with living Shewanella putrefaciens CN32, metatyuyamunite was still identified by X-ray diffraction in the final fine fraction together with K-carnotite. Figure 1b and sections 3.1 and 3.3 support presence in both assemblages; they do not quantify its surviving mass or prove that the same crystals persisted. Section 4.1 explicitly states that the two starting minerals could not be observed separately during incubation. Thus the mixed-ore vanadium reduction cannot be assigned specifically to metatyuyamunite, and residual detection does not demonstrate complete resistance to transformation. Section 3.2 names tyuyamunite as a carnotite precursor while the conclusion instead names fritzscheite; neither statement establishes a resolved phase-specific pathway. The shared laboratory experiment used 1.6 g of mixed sandstone in 80 mL defined medium with 10 mM sodium lactate and 1 mM phosphate, nitrogen degassing and autoclaving before inoculation, followed by an anoxic glovebox incubation extending to ten months. Treatments were in triplicate. These three mineral records refer to the same experiment, not independent replications. Bacteria-free solution controls were included, but do not isolate each phase's fate. The mixed-ore spectra support partial V reduction while U remained predominantly U(VI); results from the separate soluble-salt arm must not be transferred to this mineral. Dissolved U was low, rather than established to be exactly zero. Section 3.2 gives a V plateau time of 120 days while Figure 2 labels the time axes in hours, so no exact kinetic endpoint is adopted. The species identity and bounded mixed-assemblage occurrence are curated without a mineral-specific mechanism assertion. There is no supported pure-metatyuyamunite rate, recovered-product yield or industrial- deployment claim here. No criticality designation is inherited from its constituent elements.

Metazeunerite

Metazeunerite is the copper uranyl arsenate mineral Cu(UO2)2(AsO4)2(H2O)4·4H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1937 is a historical description year, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal eight-water composition is distinct from twelve-water zeunerite, phosphate metatorbernite, calcium meta-autunite and elemental uranium, arsenic or copper. Locock and Burns synthesized its analogue hydrothermally at 220(1) degrees C for 24 h after controlled heating, then refined an epoxy-coated, twinned crystal in P4/n at room temperature. The hydrogen model was constrained; metatorbernite copper deficiency is not a metazeunerite result. A later natural German specimen gave a preferred P4/nmm model with a smaller c repeat, while synthetic low-temperature powder data were indexed orthorhombically. These specimen- and condition-specific models are preserved rather than merged. The thermal evidence is laboratory and abiotic; no criticality, microbial mechanism, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is inherited from composition.

These values are not silently normalized or corrected. No criticality designation or microbial activity is inferred from boron content.

Moabite

Moabite (IMA 2020-092) is an IMA-accepted anhydrous nickel-iron(III) oxyphosphate mineral with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula NiFe3+(PO4)O (PDF p. 145, status A), representing the first naturally occurring mineral with the alpha-Fe2PO5 (alpha-Fe2OPO4 / A2+B3+OPO4) structure type and the natural analogue of synthetic NiFe3+(PO4)O. Described by Britvin, Murashko, Krzhizhanovskaya, Vapnik, Vlasenko, Vereshchagin, Pankin, and Vasiliev (2025) from heavily veined dark-colored fine-grained anorthite–diopside paralava blocks in a small abandoned building-stone quarry (31°21'52" N, 36°10'55" E) in the 300 km2 Daba-Siwaqa pyrometamorphic complex (Hatrurim Formation / "Mottled Zone"), ~80 km south-southeast of Amman, central Jordan (named after the ancient Kingdom of Moab; holotype polished section 5627/1 deposited in the Fersman Mineralogical Museum of the Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow, Russia, pp. 353–356). Occurs in millimeter-sized phosphate segregations as isometric to short prismatic euhedral crystals and anhedral grains up to 30 um across, formed by high-temperature (<= 1400 °C) pyrolytic oxidation of natural Fe–Ni phosphides and associated with diopside, anorthite, crocobelonite (CaFe3+2(PO4)2O, IMA 2020-005), yakubovichite (CaNi2Fe3+(PO4)3, IMA 2021-096), hematite, an unnamed alluaudite-group phosphate intermediate between NaNaCa(Fe3+Mg)(PO4)3 and []NaCa(Fe3+Fe3+)(PO4)3, native iron (alpha-Fe), and precursor phosphides negevite (NiP2), murashkoite (FeP), transjordanite (Ni2P), and halamishite (Ni5P4) (pp. 354–356, Figs. 1–2). Macroscopically deep-brown to very dark-brown/almost-black with vitreous lustre, semi-transparent red-brown in thin section (predicted Gladstone–Dale mean refractive index 1.99), Mohs hardness 4, no cleavage observed, Dcalc = 4.324 g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit-cell parameters (Abstract, p. 353; Table 5 on p. 358 reports Dx = 4.338 g/cm3 for ideal NiFe(PO4)O), and grey in reflected light with red-brown internal reflections, non-pleochroic, weak anisotropy and bireflectance (Rmax / Rmin in air, Table 2, p. 355: 14.1 / 14.0% at 470 nm, 13.5 / 13.3% at 546 nm, 13.1 / 12.9% at 589 nm, and 12.8 / 12.7% at 650 nm). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (632.8 nm He–Ne laser, Section 5, pp. 355–356, Fig. 3) confirms the absence of O–H/H2O bands and shows bands at 115, 130, 160, 179, 198, 255, 292sh, 307, 361, and 388 cm-1 ([MO6] octahedral and lattice modes), 410, 423, 449, and 469 cm-1 (nu2 symmetric PO4 bending), 545, 590, 628, and 650sh cm-1 (nu4 asymmetric PO4 bending), 843, 871, and 918 cm-1 (nu1 symmetric P–O stretching), and 988, 1019, 1090, and 1157 cm-1 (nu3 asymmetric P–O stretching). Mean of 5 WDS electron-microprobe analyses (WAVE 500 wavelength-dispersive spectrometer, Oxford Instruments, attached to a Hitachi S-3400 N scanning electron microscope, 20 kV, 15 nA, 2 um beam; Section 2, p. 354, and Section 6, p. 356, Table 3) yielded Fe2O3 36.04 wt% (range 34.70–37.11), P2O5 31.22 (30.47–32.55), NiO 29.75 (29.37–30.11), CuO 1.73 (1.58–1.92), V2O5 0.47 (0.42–0.51), MgO 0.45 (0.36–0.61), Al2O3 0.19 (0.00–0.38), Cr2O3 0.18 (0.00–0.32), total 100.03 wt%, corresponding on 5 O apfu to the empirical formula (Ni0.90Cu0.05Mg0.03)Sigma0.98(Fe3+1.01Al0.01Cr0.01)Sigma1.03(P0.99V5+0.01)Sigma1.00O5. Orthorhombic, space group Pnma (no. 62), Z = 4 (Section 2, p. 354, and Section 7, pp. 356–360, Tables 1, 4–8, Fig. 4): single-crystal MoKalpha XRD refinement on a 0.03 x 0.01 x 0.01 mm crystal (Bruker Kappa APEX DUO, 389 reflections with I > 2sigma(I) out of 499 unique, 1866 collected, Rint = 0.062, R1 = 0.033, wR2 = 0.071, GoF = 1.04, Table 5, p. 358) gives a = 7.2161(16) Å, b = 6.4064(15) Å, c = 7.4706(19) Å, V = 345.4(1) Å3, with zigzag [010] chains of alternating edge- and face-sharing [NiO6] octahedra (Ni1 at 4a, Ni1–O4 = 2.036(3) Å x 2, Ni1–O1 = 2.072(3) Å x 2, Ni1–O2 = 2.139(3) Å x 2, <Ni1–O> = 2.082 Å, BVS = 2.07 v.u., Table 8, p. 359) and [Fe3+O6] octahedra (Fe1 at 4c, Fe1–O1 = 1.886(5) and 2.081(5) Å, Fe1–O3 = 1.903(5) Å, Fe1–O4 = 2.014(3) Å x 2, Fe1–O2 = 2.374(5) Å, <Fe1–O> = 2.045 Å, BVS = 3.04 v.u.) cross-linked by [PO4] tetrahedra (P1 at 4c, P1–O3 = 1.511(5) Å, P1–O4 = 1.540(3) Å x 2, P1–O2 = 1.554(5) Å, <P1–O> = 1.536 Å, BVS = 5.08 v.u., pp. 359–360) and oxo anions O1 (4c, coordinated by 2 Ni1 and 2 Fe1); CoKalpha Debye–Scherrer powder XRD refinement (Rigaku RAXIS Rapid II diffractometer with semi-cylindrical imaging plate, r = 127.4 mm, 40 kV, 15 mA, Section 2, p. 354, and Section 7, p. 356, Table 4, p. 357) gives a = 7.2145(3) Å, b = 6.4031(3) Å, c = 7.4657(3) Å, V = 344.88(2) Å3, with seven strongest lines at 2.7262 (100)(121), 3.251 (83)(201), 5.20 (63)(101), 3.321 (37)(102) (printed with a decimal comma as 3,321(37)(102) in the Abstract on p. 353), 2.5946 (37)(202), 2.3542 (25)(103), and 2.3044 (24)(122) Å. Distinct from yakubovichite, crocobelonite, negevite, transjordanite, halamishite, and elemental nickel or phosphorus; no criticality designation for moabite itself, no microbial or biological mechanism, and no industrial recovery yield are asserted.

Monazite-(Ce)

Monazite-(Ce) is the cerium-dominant phosphate mineral species with ideal formula Ce(PO4), distinct from elemental cerium, other monazite species and mixed monazite-bearing ores. Ni, Hughes and Mariano (1995) characterized a natural crystal from the Kangankunde carbonatite, Malawi, using chemical analysis and single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Its monoclinic P2_1/n structure has nine-coordinate rare-earth sites. The natural crystal contains other rare-earth elements; the separately studied synthetic CePO4 crystal is not that specimen. Monazite-(Gd)

Monazite-(Gd) is the gadolinium-dominant monazite species with ideal formula Gd(PO4), approved as IMA 2022-055. It is distinct from elemental gadolinium, mixed rare-earth ores and tetragonal xenotime-(Gd), which shares its ideal formula. Ondrejka et al. (2023) characterized natural microscopic domains from the Zimna Voda quartz vein near Prakovce, Slovakia, using wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analysis, Raman spectroscopy and selected-area electron diffraction of a focused ion-beam lamella. These observations support monoclinic P21/n symmetry. The six analyses in Table 2 average 22.84 wt% Gd2O3 and contain substantial Sm and Nd; this is mixed mineral composition, not pure GdPO4, a bulk ore grade or a recovered gadolinium yield. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction was not performed because of crystal size. The unit-cell dimensions emphasized in the abstract and Table 3 are estimates from weighted synthetic end-members; they differ from the less precise electron-diffraction measurements. Density was calculated, while hardness and several other physical properties could not be determined. The proposed hydrothermal enrichment explanation is a geological interpretation, not a controlled formation or extraction experiment. This characterization does not establish microbial production, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Monazite-(Sm)

Monazite-(Sm) is the samarium-dominant monazite mineral species with ideal formula Sm(PO4), distinct from elemental samarium, hydrated samarium phosphates, other monazite species and mixed rare-earth ores. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list assigns approved status and number 2001-001. The original description instead prints 2000-001; the current authority is followed here while retaining that source discrepancy. Masau et al. (2002) characterized natural crystals from the Annie Claim #3 granitic pegmatite in southeastern Manitoba, Canada, by wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analysis, optical examination, single-crystal diffraction and Gandolfi powder diffraction. The diffraction data support monoclinic P21/n symmetry. The analyzed natural material contains substantial Gd, Ce, Th and Ca and is not a pure SmPO4 end-member. Table 1 reports 13.02 wt% Sm2O3 for the average of three grains used for physical, optical and crystal data; its 14.29 wt% maximum belongs to a different analysis, not one of those extracted grains. These are mineral oxide compositions, not a bulk ore grade or recovered samarium yield. Density and hardness could not be measured; the reported densities are calculated. Selective rare-earth complexation during pegmatite crystallization is a proposed geological explanation, not an experimentally demonstrated extraction or formation mechanism. This natural characterization does not establish microbial biomineralization, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Montebrasite

Montebrasite is the hydroxyl-dominant lithium aluminium phosphate mineral with ideal formula LiAl(PO4)(OH), distinct from fluorine-dominant amblygonite. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status and original-description year 1871. Groat2003 Methods (pages 197-199), Table 2 (page 198), Table 11 (page 206) and neutron/NMR figures establish the natural substituted series: the Dunton specimen has neutron-derived F/(F+OH)=0.04, whereas estimates for the near-boundary Tanco specimen differ by technique and are not treated as a pure endmember. Triclinic primitive P-1 and centered C-1 are alternative settings, not evidence for separate polymorphs. In the Shirose thesis, Figures 13-16 (printed pages 29-31, PDF pages 36-38) show co-oriented lacroixite patches and low-fluorine montebrasite in a natural host; Figure 12 (page 25, PDF page 32) shows secondary montebrasite veins without lacroixite. Section 5.3 and Figure 19 (pages 34-36) interpret an exsolution sequence, but do not reproduce that sequence by controlled synthesis. Figure 21 and Table 5 (pages 38 and 39) include gem-quality XS110 with no observed lacroixite, so the patch texture is not universal. Lithium and water in the thesis microprobe tables were calculated stoichiometrically. These are primary identity and natural-texture observations; no microbial mechanism, measured lithium extraction, isolated recovery yield or mineral criticality is asserted. The studies are also used in cmmmech:amblygonite and are not independent experiments for each owner; the ambiguous XN163 heating arm is not transferred here as a montebrasite-specific threshold.

Monteregianite-(Y)

Hydrated potassium-sodium-yttrium double-sheet silicate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula KNa2YSi8O19·5H2O, status Rn (renamed), and special-procedure tag 1987 s.p. (originally approved as monteregianite by the IMA Commission on New Minerals and Mineral Names prior to publication by Chao 1978, and suffixed Monteregianite-(Y) in 1987; listed under 1987 s.p. in the IMA Master List rather than a numbered CURIE). Chao (1978, pp. 561–562) described the holotype specimen (preserved at the National Museum of Natural Sciences, Ottawa, specimen 37130; formerly known as UK-6 in Chao et al. 1967) from miarolitic cavities, thermally metamorphosed inclusions, and rheomorphic breccias in nepheline syenite at Mont St-Hilaire, Quebec, Canada, where it is usually associated with calcite, pectolite, microcline, albite, aegirine, and arfvedsonite and minor amounts of phlogopite, fluorite, quartz, ekanite, sepiolite, ashcroftine, lorenzenite, narsarsukite, natrolite, harmotome, apophyllite, molybdenite, and pyrite. Chemical analysis performed by D.C. Mah on approximately one gram of hand-picked colorless material following the procedures of Hounslow & Moore (1966), combined with electron-microprobe analysis for Y2O3 and thermogravimetric/thermal analysis to 1000 °C for H2O (Chao 1978, Table 3 and prose, pp. 561, 563), gave SiO2 60.30, Al2O3 0.50, Y2O3 11.97, CaO 0.65, MgO 0.15, BaO 0.35, MnO n.d., FeO n.d., Na2O 9.14, K2O 5.36, H2O 11.40, total 99.82 wt%, corresponding to the empirical formula (Na4.50K1.80)(Y1.85Ca0.20Mg0.06Ba0.04)(Si15.87Al0.15)O38·10.02H2O (printed in the Abstract on p. 561 with minor rounding/typographical variants Na4.56K1.80, Ca0.19, and Al0.16), simplified to (Na,K)6Y2Si16O38·10H2O; a partial electron-microprobe analysis of a mauve variety reported in prose on p. 563 gave 10.67% Y2O3, 1.38% MnO, 5.89% K2O, and 9.37% Na2O. Physical, optical, and crystallographic determinations in Chao (1978, pp. 561–563, Table 1 on p. 562, and Table 2 on p. 563 comparing monteregianite with the macdonaldite-group minerals rhodesite, macdonaldite, and delhayelite) show needle-shaped crystals in irregular and radiating clusters (Fig. 1), elongate tabular crystals in parallel groups (Fig. 2), or irregular micaceous masses (0.05 to 3 mm, bounded by {010}, {001}, and {100} pinacoids and occasional {101} prisms), colorless, white, grey, or rarely mauve or pale green color, white streak, vitreous to silky lustre, perfect {010}, very good {001}, and good to fair {100} cleavages, Mohs hardness ~3½, Dmeas = 2.42(2) g/cm3 (determined by flotation in diluted bromoform and by use of a Berman balance), Dcalc = 2.391 g/cm3 (for Z = 4 of (Na,K)6Y2Si16O38·10H2O), ready etching by cold 1:1 HCl, HNO3, and H2SO4 along cleavage planes (pp. 561–562), and biaxial (+) optics (Na light, spindle stage) with alpha = 1.510(1), beta = 1.513(1), gamma = 1.517(1), 2Vmeas = 87(1)°, 2Vcalc = 82°, orientation X = c, Y = a, Z = b, optic plane perpendicular to the axis of elongation (a), and inconspicuous dispersion; Weissenberg, precession, and least-squares powder-diffraction refinement (Table 1, p. 562; 114.6 mm camera, CuKalpha radiation, lambda = 1.5418 Å, Si internal standard; strongest eight lines: 12.00 (100)(020), 7.03 (100)(200), 6.55 (40)(002), 6.02 (50)(220,040), 4.42 (100)(042), 3.405 (50)(062), 3.026 (50)(034,440), and 2.873 (80)(044) Å) initially indexed the mineral as orthorhombic Bmab or B2ab with a = 14.014(4), b = 23.910(5), c = 13.096(2) Å and a pronounced pseudocell with a and c halved in Pmmb, P2mb, or Pm2b. Ghose, Sen Gupta, and Campana (1987; spelled montregianite throughout their paper) determined and refined the crystal structure by single-crystal MoKalpha X-ray diffraction on a 0.34 x 0.32 x 0.34 mm Mont St. Hilaire cleavage fragment donated by G.Y. Chao (after an initial orthorhombic Cmca refinement on 2209 reflections to R = 0.066 showed anomalously large Si–O bond-length standard deviations, 13724 reflections were recollected on a Syntex P1 four-circle diffractometer to 2theta = 65°, yielding 5669 inequivalent and 4877 observed reflections refined to R = 0.059, Rw = 0.061; Tables 1–4, pp. 366–373), establishing true monoclinic (pseudo-orthorhombic, 2/m) symmetry in standard space group P21/n with a = 9.512(2), b = 23.956(4), c = 9.617(2) Å, beta = 93.85(1)°, V = 2186.5(6) Å3, Z = 2 for Na4K2Y2Si16O38·10H2O (Z = 4 for KNa2YSi8O19·5H2O), Dcalc = 2.41 g/cm3, and mu(MoKalpha) = 35.45 cm-1 (non-standard pseudo-orthorhombic setting C1121/a: a = 13.973(2), b = 13.064(2), c = 23.956(4) Å, gamma = 90.62(1)°, V = 4372.8(10) Å3, Z = 4, Table 1, p. 366). The structure consists of two types of layers alternating along [010] parallel to the (010) perfect cleavage (pp. 365, 370–373): (1) an open mixed octahedral sheet of isolated [YO6] octahedra (mean Y–O = 2.261(30) Å; octahedral Y site refined with 0.60 Y + 0.40 Ce in Table 2, p. 366, and prose, p. 370) and three distinct [NaO4(H2O)2] octahedra (Na(1) occupancy 0.95, mean Na–O = 2.493(32) Å for 6 bonds or 2.551 Å including a weak 7th O(5B) bond at 2.900(6) Å; Na(2A) occupancy 0.47, mean 2.416(30) Å; Na(2B) occupancy 0.45, mean 2.411(26) Å; Table 2, p. 366, Table 4, p. 368, and prose, p. 371) forming elliptical eight-membered octahedral rings, and (2) an apophyllite-type double silicate sheet with four- and eight-membered tetrahedral rings (bridging Si(1) and Si(4) tetrahedra with mean Si–O = 1.598 Å and Si(1)–O(1)–Si(4) = 176.5(3)°, and six other tetrahedra with three bridging and one nonbridging oxygen and mean Si–O = 1.613 Å; Table 4, pp. 368–369, and prose, pp. 371–373) housing split ten-coordinate [KO6(H2O)4] sites (K(1) occupancy 0.62, mean K–O = 2.978 Å; K(2) occupancy 0.38, mean K–O = 2.991 Å, separated by 0.34 Å; Table 2, p. 366, Table 4, p. 368, and prose, p. 372) and six independent water positions W(1)–W(6) (W(1) and W(2) fully occupied at 1.0 in the octahedral sheet; W(3) occupancy 0.95, W(4) 0.46, W(5) 0.35, and W(6) 0.37 in the channels; Table 2, p. 366, and prose, p. 372). The second reference listed in the IMA Master List (Journal of Physical Chemistry B 102 (1998), 4379) was not inspected in full text and no claims from that 1998 study are asserted here. Distinct from macdonaldite-group silicates (rhodesite, macdonaldite, delhayelite), apophyllite, ashcroftine-(Y), and elemental yttrium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Ash resulting from municipal-waste thermal treatment, a heterogeneous secondary resource distinct from coal fly ash and sewage-sludge incineration ash. The curated study calls its feed ash A without identifying whether it is fly ash, bottom ash, or a mixture; this record does not resolve that fraction by inference. Criticality of individual constituents does not designate the whole ash. The selected experiment is shared with the niobium element record, not an independent replication.

Natroboltwoodite

Natroboltwoodite is a sodium-bearing uranyl silicate hydrate mineral, distinct from potassium-bearing boltwoodite and elemental uranium. The September 2026 IMA list gives Na(UO2)(SiO3OH)(H2O), status Rn and the special-procedure entry 2007 s.p.; that entry records renaming, not an ordinary approval accession. Historical sodium boltwoodite and Na-boltwoodite terminology is retained for the experimental material below. Ilton and colleagues used synthetic material represented as Na(UO2)(SiO3OH)·1.5H2O. Its measured bulk U/Si and U/Na ratios were approximately one, but minor impurities could not be excluded and its hydration was not reconciled with the current IMA one-water formula. The laboratory dissolution results therefore describe that characterized synthetic preparation, not a universal composition or behavior of natural natroboltwoodite. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial recovery claim is inferred.

Natrojarosite

Natrojarosite is the sodium ferric hydroxysulfate mineral with ideal formula NaFe3(SO4)2(OH)6, all iron ferric. The September 2026 IMA list records the species as redefined, 1987 s.p. It is distinct from potassium jarosite, ammoniojarosite, hydroniumjarosite and a mixed industrial jarosite residue. Natural compositions can contain substitutions; the ideal formula is not an assay of every specimen. Gómez et al. (2024), sampling in May 2010, identified natrojarosite and quartz in an inner crust associated with a cyanobacteria-containing mixed microbial mat beneath a gypsum-rich outer layer at Río Tinto, Spain. Their field deposit measurements averaged pH 0.8, but pH across the thin cyanobacterial layer could not be measured. This is an association, without controlled evidence that the organisms precipitated or dissolved natrojarosite, without a verified cyanobacterial species or strain, and without an extraction or recovery measurement. No constituent-element criticality or industrial deployment is inferred.

Graphite of natural mineral origin considered as a commercial raw-material commodity. Navajoite

Navajoite is a hydrated vanadium-iron oxide mineral with formula (V5+,Fe3+)10O24·12H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, which assigns grandfathered status G and original-description year 1954. That year is not a numbered IMA approval. The complete 1955 description characterized selected natural material from the Monument No. 2 mine, Apache County, Arizona, with residual impurities and uncertain partitioning of iron and reduced vanadium; its tentative V2O5·3H2O formula and indexing are historical interpretations. Evans and Hughes later reindexed powder/fiber diffraction from USNM 106900, whose type status they marked uncertain, using a C-centered cell with C2/m indexing. They attributed two extra lines to probable bokite and found that some other specimens labeled navajoite were bokite or mixtures. Their revised empirical formula was fitted to Sherwood's original 1955 chemical analysis, not a new independent assay, and the diffraction work did not solve the atomic structure. The earlier proposed natural oxidation of corvusite and storage-related water loss do not establish controlled transformation kinetics or a microbial mechanism. Navajoite is distinct from associated corvusite, bokite, elemental vanadium and mixed uranium-vanadium ore. These sources establish no isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment, and the mineral does not inherit vanadium's criticality designations.

Niasite

IMA-approved anhydrous nickel arsenate mineral (IMA 2019-105; status A, Approved 2020) with ideal end-member formula Ni2+4.5(AsO4)3 (requiring NiO 49.37 wt%, As2O5 50.63 wt%, total 100 wt%), representing the tetragonal garnet-like (jeffbenite-type) dimorph of monoclinic unprotonated alluaudite-type johanngeorgenstadtite (IMA 2019-122) and the natural analogue of synthetic Ni4.35As3O11.7(OH)0.3 (Barbier, 1999; Kampf et al., 2020, European Journal of Mineralogy 32:373-385). Discovered on museum specimen AMNH 17956 from Johanngeorgenstadt, Erzgebirge, Saxony, Germany, where it occurs as a secondary oxidation product of primary nickeline associated with johanngeorgenstadtite, aerugite, bunsenite, quartz, rooseveltite, and xanthiosite; the holotype specimen is deposited at the American Museum of Natural History, New York (catalogue no. AMNH 17956, consisting of three major fragments and numerous smaller ones including 10 pieces mounted on two acrylic discs; also the holotype for johanngeorgenstadtite), and a cotype specimen of five fragments mounted on a glass slide is deposited at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (catalogue no. LACMNH 74203, ex-Mark Feinglos collection, originally from the matrix of AMNH 17956). Forms sugary aggregates of violet-red to red-orange irregular, rounded grains or short prisms ~50 um in diameter with a pale-pink streak, resinous to subadamantine lustre, transparent diaphaneity, Mohs hardness ~4, brittle tenacity, conchoidal fracture, no cleavage, non-fluorescence under long- or short-wave ultraviolet light, insolubility in concentrated HCl and concentrated H2SO4 at room temperature, and calculated density Dcalc = 5.222 g/cm3 for the empirical formula and 5.245 g/cm3 for the ideal formula from single-crystal unit-cell parameters (or Dx = 5.065 g/cm3 in Table 3 for the refined cell contents Ni4.10(AsO4)3). Optically uniaxial (-) in white light with omega = 1.925(5) and epsilon = 1.855(5), pleochroic with O beige and E deep pink (absorption O < E), and Gladstone-Dale compatibility index 1 - (Kp/Kc) = -0.021 (excellent) for the empirical formula and -0.017 (superior) for the ideal formula. Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser) is featureless from 4000 to 1000 cm-1 (confirming the absence of O-H and H2O) and exhibits a dominant doublet at 855 and 822 cm-1 (overlapping nu3 antisymmetric and nu1 symmetric AsO4 stretching vibrations, with a weak shoulder at 723 cm-1), bands at ~550, 507, and 491 cm-1 (nu4 AsO4 bending), overlapping bands at 438 and 432 cm-1 (nu2 AsO4 bending), a composite band at ~347 cm-1 (Ni3O4 stretching), and low-energy M-Ox and lattice modes at 270, 222, 192, 156, 147, and 130 cm-1. Electron microprobe analysis (5 points on 4 crystals, Cameca SX-50, 15 kV, 20 nA, 5 um beam; Table 1) yielded NiO 40.38 wt% (range 36.91-43.79, SD 3.10), CoO 7.26 wt% (5.42-8.54, SD 1.39), FeO 0.29 wt% (0.12-0.56, SD 0.21), Al2O3 0.15 wt% (0.01-0.35, SD 0.17), CuO 0.13 wt% (0.07-0.19, SD 0.04), Na2O 0.08 wt% (0.00-0.20, SD 0.10), Ag2O 0.06 wt% (0.00-0.15, SD 0.07), and As2O5 51.03 wt% (50.27-51.58, SD 0.48), total 99.38 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 12 O atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula (Ni2+3.69Co2+0.66Fe2+0.03Al0.02Na0.02Cu2+0.01)Sigma4.43As3.03O12 (with trace Ag2O 0.06 wt% below 0.005 apfu omitted from the rounded formula) and simplified formula (Ni2+,Co2+,Fe2+,Al,Na,Cu2+)4.5(AsO4)3 or (Ni2+,Co2+)4.5(AsO4)3. Crystallizes in the tetragonal system, space group I-42d (#122), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 6.8046(8) A, c = 18.6190(13) A, V = 862.1(2) A3, and Z = 4 (refined to R1 = 0.0226, wR2 = 0.0442, GoF = 1.089, and Flack parameter 0.03(3) for 471 reflections with Io > 2sigma(I) out of 499 unique reflections collected with MoKalpha radiation on a 35 x 30 x 20 um crystal, printed as "35 mm x 30 mm x 20 mm" in Table 3 via a mm-for-um unit typo). The dense garnet-like heteropolyhedral framework (isostructural with jeffbenite, Mg3Al2Si3O12) contains two fully occupied AsO4 tetrahedra (As1 with <As1-O> = 1.696 A, BVS = 4.88 v.u.; As2 with As2-O1 = 1.688(4) A x 4, BVS = 4.96 v.u.), two octahedra jointly occupied by Ni and Co (Ni1 with refined site occupancy 0.983(6), <Ni1-O> = 2.058 A, BVS = 2.08 v.u., sharing opposite edges with two As1O4 tetrahedra; Ni2 with refined site occupancy 0.971(5), <Ni2-O> = 2.091 A, BVS = 1.90 v.u.), and one partially occupied dodecahedral site (Ni3 with refined site occupancy 0.200(7), ideal occupancy 0.25, four shorter Ni3-O2 = 2.209(5) A and four longer Ni3-O3 = 2.707(4) A bonds, <Ni3-O> = 2.458 A, BVS = 1.08 v.u.; note that in Table 6a on p. 383 the O1 bond-valence contributions 0.39 + 0.35 + 1.24 sum to 1.98 v.u. whereas Table 6a prints 1.99 v.u. due to unrounded summation). The strongest observed Gandolfi powder X-ray diffraction lines (dobs in A (Iobs; hkl), MoKalpha, Table 2a) are 2.752 (100; 2 0 4, 2 1 3), 1.678 (28; 3 2 5, 4 0 2, 2 2 8), 3.008 (25; 2 1 1), 1.706 (21; 2 1 9, 4 0 0), 3.274 (18; 1 0 5), 1.446 (13; 4 2 4), 2.330 (10; 2 1 5, 0 0 8), 1.412 (10; 3 3 6, 2 0 12, 3 1 10, 1 0 13), and 4.644 (9; 0 0 4, 1 0 3) / 2.408 (9; 2 2 0) / 1.533 (9; 3 2 7, 3 0 9, 4 2 0). Nickel flotation tailings

Residual mixed solids from flotation in nickel-ore beneficiation, distinct from the recovered flotation concentrate, unprocessed ore, a pure sulfide mineral and downstream smelter slag. The curated case is the material called lama in a 2010 UNESP thesis, supplied by Votorantim Metais from flotation at its Serra de Fortaleza-MG nickel extraction operation in Brazil. Original particles were reported as 50-100 micrometres. XRD indicated a heterogeneous silicate/carbonate assemblage with pyrrhotite; no pure-pyrrhotite feed or quantitatively established sulfide-hosted nickel fraction is assigned. Table 7 gives total Ni 0.30%, Cu 0.03% and Co 0.01%, versus aqua-regia-soluble Ni 0.25%, Cu 0.03% and Co 0.01%. The digestion-defined soluble fraction is not water-soluble metal. These are feed-specific measurements, not a universal tailings composition or an inherited criticality claim.

Nickel laterite ore

Naturally occurring heterogeneous nickel-bearing regolith formed by intense weathering of ultramafic parent rocks, including oxide-rich limonitic, clay-rich and hydrous magnesium-silicate-rich horizons. The USGS deposit model grounds this geological resource identity; excavated or stockpiled unprocessed ore remains within its scope. It is distinct from nickel metal, a mineral species such as goethite, a product-grade commodity and processing-generated laterite tailings. Individual ore samples differ in mineralogy and nickel, cobalt and chromium distribution; their laboratory leaching outcomes do not apply to every laterite or establish extraction from a pure host mineral.

Nickel smelter slag

Mixed solid residue from pyrometallurgical smelting in nickel extraction, distinct from nickel ore, flotation concentrate, flotation tailings and an individual constituent mineral. The curated case is the flash-furnace slag supplied by Votorantim Metais from its Serra de Fortaleza-MG nickel extraction operation in Brazil for a 2010 doctoral thesis. The source reports original particles of 100-500 micrometres and a dominant fayalite/forsterite-type iron-magnesium silicate diffraction pattern; that assignment does not make the bulk slag a pure mineral. Table 7 reports total Ni 0.26%, Cu 0.27% and Co 0.06%, versus aqua-regia-soluble Ni 0.07%, Cu 0.06% and Co 0.06%. The latter is an operational digestion fraction, not water solubility. These feed-specific assays do not define every nickel slag. No constituent criticality status or industrial microbial deployment is inferred.

Nickel sulfate hexahydrate commodity

Manufactured crystalline nickel sulfate hexahydrate products with nominal formula NiSO4.6H2O. This commodity is distinct from nickel metal, other sulfate hydrates, aqueous nickel-bearing leachates and a naturally occurring mineral specimen. Primobius identifies a hexahydrate product for lithium-ion cathode precursors and publishes a minimum nickel content of 22.0 wt%; Coremax version 8 specifies more than 22.3 wt% Ni for its battery-labelled product and permits customer-specific requirements. These examples establish a traded product form, not one universal battery-grade composition or evidence that every nickel sulfate product meets cathode requirements. Coremax also lists electroplating use. No criticality designation or microbial production of qualified sulfate crystals is asserted here.

Nickeline-bearing ore

Natural heterogeneous nickel-arsenide-bearing ore containing nickeline with carbonate and quartz gangue. The present evidence concerns a low-grade sample collected approximately 2.5 km northwest of Patang village in eastern Iran and a high-grade sample from Talmesi mine in central Iran. These are distinct feed arms within one geological resource class, not processing wastes, pure nickeline, nickel metal or a standardized concentrate grade. Boroumand et al.'s supplementary Table S1 reports nickel and arsenic contents of 4.93% and 5% for the low-grade feed, and 33.4% and 50% for the high-grade feed. Those are source-reported bulk sample compositions, not mineral formulas or general specifications. XRD and reflected-light observations identify nickeline with carbonate/quartz phases; whole-ore results cannot establish pure-phase selectivity. No criticality-list status is inferred from nickel.

Oil and gas produced water

Water brought to the surface as a byproduct of hydrocarbon production and considered here as a secondary feed for constituent recovery. It can contain formation water, returned injected fluids, condensed water and mixtures of these; its composition and salinity vary by reservoir and operation. This record concerns the generated oil-and-gas production stream, not an untouched geological brine resource, geothermal extraction feed, individual dissolved element or mineral species. Some produced waters are investigated as sources of lithium and other constituents, without implying that every sample contains economically recoverable quantities. USGS resource research supplies context, not a criticality-list designation for this mixture. Microbial treatment and recovery mechanisms remain unasserted pending verification of full experimental methods, controls and outcomes; no deployment or product yield is claimed.

Parauranophane is the calcium uranyl silicate hydrate mineral Ca(UO2)2(SiO3OH)2(H2O)4·H2O listed by IMA in September 2026. It is the historical beta-uranophane or uranophane-beta, renamed by CNMNC in August 2022. Rn, 2022 s.p. denotes that nomenclature action, not a unique approval accession. Pascoite

Pascoite is a calcium decavanadate mineral with formula [Ca3(H2O)17]V5+10O28 in the September 2026 IMA list, which assigns grandfathered status G and original-description year 1914. That year is not a numbered IMA approval. Hughes and colleagues characterized a natural crystal from Harvard specimen 91449, Minasragra, Peru, and refined a disordered monoclinic C2/m structure containing [V10O28]6- units and hydrated calcium complexes. Disorder gives the Ca1 site possible local coordination by six, seven or eight oxygen atoms, averaging seven; hydrogen positions were located in difference maps but subsequently restrained, with residual disorder and partial occupancy. The 2005 paper supports this model over its tested ordered C2 alternative; it does not provide an unconstrained determination of every local hydrogen configuration. The 1966 predecessor's publisher title specifies 16H2O whereas the 2005 reference list prints 17H2O; the current identity follows the IMA formula and inspected 2005 original. The 1966 full text remains unavailable. The inspected 2005 depository files contain thermal parameters and observed/calculated diffraction intensities, but their Table 5/6 labels differ from the article's Table 4/5 deposit references; they belong to the same experiment. Pascoite is distinct from the decavanadate ion, the broader mineral group and elemental vanadium. These structural observations establish neither microbial extraction nor isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment; criticality is not inherited from vanadium.

Perovskite

Perovskite is the calcium titanate mineral species with ideal formula CaTiO3. The September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list gives grandfathered status G and original description year 1839, not an IMA approval number. This owner identifies the mineral species, not the broader perovskite structure class, halide photovoltaic materials, elemental titanium, or a perovskite-bearing concentrate. Keller and Buseck (1994) independently characterized natural perovskite grains from Ca-Al-rich inclusions in the Allende and Vigarano carbonaceous chondrites by transmission electron microscopy and electron diffraction, using the orthorhombic Pnma setting. Their energy-dispersive analyses detected Ca and Ti without other reported detectable elements; this is detection-limited cation evidence, not proof of absolute purity or a measured oxygen balance. The paper examined over 50 grains from six extracted regions. Its separately synthesized CaTiO3 cooling experiments are not natural-feed extraction or recovery studies. Twinning observations and inferred meteorite thermal histories are kept distinct; no universal high-temperature transition sequence or cooling-rate thermometer is asserted here. No microbial mechanism, processing performance, industrial deployment or criticality designation is inferred.

Pertlikite

Pertlikite is an approved tetragonal mineral of the voltaite group, IMA 2005-055, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as K2(Fe(II),Mg)2(Mg,Fe(III))4Fe(III)2Al(SO4)12(H2O)18. It is distinct from cubic voltaite and magnesiovoltaite, rather than a synonym for any magnesium-bearing voltaite-group material. Ertl et al. (2008) characterized natural type material from Madeni Zakh, Iran, using portions of a single crystal for diffraction, optical examination and electron-microprobe analysis, with additional grains for bulk hydrogen analysis. Tetragonal I41/acd symmetry and unequal Fe/Mg site occupancies distinguish the studied crystal from the cubic structural model. The formula combines microprobe chemistry, fitted Mossbauer spectral areas and structure refinement; it is not a direct assay of every site or oxidation state. Spectral areas were not corrected for different recoil-free fractions. Measured water was 15.3 wt.% with estimated 10% relative uncertainty, whereas 16.73 wt.% in the composition table was estimated from the structure. Powder and single-crystal cell dimensions differ beyond their stated precision, and hydrogen positions around disordered Al-bound waters were not located. A proposed origin through pyrite decomposition is geological interpretation, not an observed reaction or microbial mechanism. No extraction, recovery yield or criticality designation is curated.
