Indium- and tin-bearing copper-iron-zinc-silver sulfide mineral of the stannite group with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Cu,Ag)2(Fe,Zn)(Sn,In)S4 and approval number IMA 1985-052. Kissin and Owens (1989) characterized petrukite on cotype specimens (GSC 65049-65052, plus Herb claim metatypes AMNH T98797, BM 1987,94, Ecole des Mines T44352, and NMNH 163779) from three co-type localities: the Herb claim, Cassiar District, Turnagain River area, British Columbia, Canada; the Mount Pleasant mine, Charlotte County, New Brunswick, Canada; and the Ikuno mine, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan. Electron-microprobe analyses across the three localities (Table 5, p. 682) yielded a Herb claim mean empirical formula of (Cu1.85Fe0.95Zn0.24Ag0.03)Sigma3.07(Sn0.89In0.05)Sigma0.94S3.99 (0.05 apfu In), Mount Pleasant compositions with 0.02-0.04 apfu In, and Ikuno mine compositions spanning 0.07-0.21 apfu In via the coupled substitution Cu+ + Sn4+ <-> In3+ + Zn2+. Precession single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction on Herb claim, Mount Pleasant, and Ikuno grains indexed in orthorhombic space group Pmn21 (wurtzite-type superstructure, Table 7, pp. 680-683: Herb claim a = 7.6671(81), b = 6.4399(32), c = 6.2605(61) A; Ikuno a = 7.7050(27), b = 6.4462(14) [printed 6.4421(14) in text p. 680], c = 6.2757(26) A; Mount Pleasant a = 7.6858(101), b = 6.4395(60), c = 6.2947(23) A; Z = 2), where ordering of Cu, (Fe,Zn), and (Sn,In) lowers the symmetry from the hexagonal P63mc wurtzite subcell. No full atomic- coordinate refinement was performed in the 1989 study, and the compositional and structural boundary between Sn-dominant orthorhombic petrukite and indium-rich sakuraiite remained open to further single-crystal investigation. Distinct from sakuraiite, ferrokësterite, kësterite, stannite, and elemental indium or tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Phosphoferrite

Phosphoferrite is the ferrous phosphate mineral with ideal formula Fe2+3(PO4)2(H2O)3. The September 2026 IMA list records redefined status under the 1980 special procedure. It is distinct from the more hydrated species vivianite and ludlamite, the Mn-dominant related mineral reddingite, and ferric kryzhanovskite. The historical Hagendorf Sud specimen studied by Moore (1971) contained Mn and Ca and was not a pure synthetic Fe endmember. Laboratory heating produced a source-reported ferric crystalline product with diffraction similarities to the starting material. Later structural work by Moore, Araki and Kampf (1980) corrected substantial indexing and unit-cell errors in the earlier natural kryzhanovskite comparison; this record therefore retains the limited heating observation without treating the earlier cell dimensions, exact structural model or pure-product identity as established. These are abiotic laboratory observations, not microbial extraction or demonstrated industrial recovery. No criticality designation is inherited from iron or phosphorus.

Phosphophyllite

Phosphophyllite is a grandfathered monoclinic zinc-ferrous phosphate mineral, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as Zn2Fe(II)(PO4)2(H2O)4 with historical year 1920. It is a mineral species, distinct from elemental zinc, a zinc commodity and the related minerals hopeite and parahopeite. Hill (1977) refined the structure of a natural Potosi, Bolivia crystal in P21/c using three-dimensional X-ray data, resolving competing earlier structural models. Zinc/phosphate tetrahedral sheets are linked through Fe-bearing octahedra; the Potosi result is not a universal assay of every locality. Dunn and Norberg (1977) partially analyzed eleven Hagendorf and three Potosi specimens, finding variable Mn substitution for Fe in the Hagendorf material and very little Mn in the Potosi material. One borderline Hagendorf Mn:Fe weight ratio of 51:49 was explicitly insufficient, given analytical uncertainty, to establish a separate Mn-dominant species. Their unpublished specimen-by-specimen analytical table was not acquired. These natural-crystal studies support identity and composition variability, without establishing microbial extraction, a recovery yield or industrial deployment. No criticality designation is inherited from zinc, iron or phosphorus.

Distinct from adamsite-(Y), shomiokite-(Y), and elemental neodymium; no criticality designation or microbial mechanism is asserted.

Pilanesbergite

IMA-approved sodium-calcium-iron-titanium oxy-fluor-disilicate mineral of the wohlerite group (IMA 2023-007; symbol Pbg in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 173, and Pbt in Figure 2 of the type description; status A, Approved 2023; full description published January 2024) with ideal end-member formula Na2Ca2Fe2Ti2(Si2O7)2O2F2 (written Na2Ca2Fe2+2Ti2(Si2O7)2O2F2 in the IMA Master List; requiring Na2O 8.38 wt%, CaO 15.16 wt%, FeO 19.42 wt%, TiO2 21.60 wt%, SiO2 32.48 wt%, F 5.14 wt%, and -F=O 2.16 wt% for a printed total of 100 wt%, arithmetic sum 100.02 wt%; Dal Bo et al., 2024, European Journal of Mineralogy 36:73-85). Represents the Fe2+- and Ti4+-dominant member of the wohlerite group (isomorphic with lavenite Na2Ca2Mn2Zr2(Si2O7)2O2F2, normandite Na2Ca2Mn2Ti2(Si2O7)2O2F2, and madeiraite Na2Ca2Fe2Zr2(Si2O7)2O2F2 via the homovalent substitutions Mn2+ <-> Fe2+ on X3 and Zr4+ <-> Ti4+ on X1), and is named after its type locality in the 1395 +/- 10 Ma Pilanesberg Alkaline Complex (LA-ICP-MS U-Pb titanite age; Elburg and Cawthorn, 2017), North West Province, South Africa. Discovered in a river gulley near the southern margin of the Pilanesberg Complex (25.3463 deg S, 27.0658 deg E; sample MEPB62, (Na + K)/Al = 1.24, femic CIPW-normative minerals summing to 16.95 wt%), where it occurs as a late magmatic rock-forming mineral in medium-grained nepheline syenite (locally known as green foyaite) showing flow foliation defined by alkali feldspar crystals completely exsolved to end-member albite and microcline. Occurs interstitially to feldspar (post-dating alkali feldspar, nepheline, and sodalite) associated and partly intergrown with aegirine (sharing inclusions of euhedral nepheline, titanite, and minor sodalite) and in stable grain contacts with arfvedsonite, apatite, and lamprophyllite, accompanied by eudialyte, minor pyrrhotite and Fe-Mn-Ti oxide minerals, aenigmatite, scarce lorenzenite, late-crystallized natrolite, and an undescribed fibrous Ti-Zr silicate mineral; cotype specimens are deposited at the Natural History Museum, University of Oslo, Norway (catalogue number KNR 44406; sample used for EPMA, SCXRD structural refinement, and petrographic description) and the Laboratoire de Mineralogie, University of Liege, Belgium (catalogue number 21980; sample used for PXRD, optical properties, and density measurement). Forms translucent brown-orange grains and blocky crystals with a brownish streak, vitreous lustre, brittle tenacity, no observed cleavage, estimated Mohs hardness 5-6 (by comparison with lavenite), and measured density Dmeas = 3.47 g/cm3 (Berman balance in toluene) vs calculated density Dcalc = 3.40 g/cm3 in the Abstract and Section 3 (p. 74) and 3.49 g/cm3 in Table 3 (p. 79). Optically biaxial positive (+) with alpha = 1.743(3), beta = 1.768(3), gamma = 1.795(5) (determined by the immersion method in Cargille refractive index liquids under 589 nm sodium light) and a 2V angle close to 90 deg (2Vcalc = 88 deg; Table 8), with strong pleochroism in thin section between straw yellow and orange red and in immersion between light yellow (alpha) and yellowish orange (gamma); optical orientation was not determined because the crystals could not be oriented under the polarizing microscope due to the absence of cleavage planes, and the Gladstone-Dale compatibility index 1 - (Kp/Kc) = 0.037 corresponds to the excellent category (Mandarino, 1981). Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (n = 15 analyses, CAMECA SX100 with four spectrometers at the University of Johannesburg, 15 kV, 15 nA, 5 um beam diameter; Table 1) yielded SiO2 32.28 wt% (range 31.88-32.62, 2sigma SD 0.37), TiO2 18.33 wt% (17.63-19.12, SD 0.94), CaO 16.87 wt% (16.27-17.64, SD 0.79), FeO 9.70 wt% (8.54-10.26, SD 0.98), Na2O 9.43 wt% (9.23-9.60, SD 0.20), F 5.54 wt% (5.42-5.63, SD 0.11), MnO 4.96 wt% (4.62-5.52, SD 0.52), ZrO2 2.95 wt% (2.19-4.16, SD 1.10), Nb2O5 1.36 wt% (1.06-1.76, SD 0.39), MgO 0.49 wt% (0.39-0.63, SD 0.14), SrO 0.18 wt% (0.11-0.22, SD 0.06), Al2O3 0.03 wt% (0.01-0.04, SD 0.02), Ce2O3 0.02 wt% (0.00-0.08, SD 0.05), and K2O 0.01 wt% (0.00-0.02, SD 0.01), with Table 1 printing Total = 102.13 wt%, O=F = 2.33 wt%, and net Total = 99.80 wt% whereas the exact arithmetic sum of the 14 printed mean constituents is 102.15 wt% and 99.82 wt% after -O=F (a 0.02 wt% rounding difference). Pinnoite

Pinnoite is the magnesium hydroxyborate mineral MgB2O(OH)6 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its grandfathered status G and year 1884 describe its nomenclatural history, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from chloropinnoite, other magnesium borate species, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Frost and Xi (2014) examined natural material supplied as pinnoite from the Inder boron deposit and salt dome, Kazakhstan. Their institutional author manuscript reports Raman spectra from at least ten crystals using 633-nm excitation and nominal 2 cm-1 resolution, and diamond ATR-FTIR spectra from 128 scans at 4 cm-1 resolution. Figures 2a, 3a and 4a show prominent Raman bands at 900 and 745 cm-1 and OH-region bands at 3179, 3399, 3554 and 3579 cm-1. These are specimen-level spectroscopic observations, not extraction yields or a new chemical-purity assay. The manuscript does not establish a complete bulk composition or report a new diffraction refinement for these crystals. Interpretation is limited by internal inconsistencies: manuscript page 5 says the OH-stretching region provides no water-band evidence, whereas page 7 assigns bands at 1629, 1665 and 1696 cm-1 to water bending and considers strongly adsorbed surface water. These passages do not establish occupied structural-water sites or justify changing the accepted ideal formula. The 745 cm-1 assignment differs between the results and conclusion; the infrared 3543 cm-1 value in the results differs from 3513 cm-1 in Figure 4b, abstract and conclusion. Hydrogen-bond distances are estimates from an empirical spectral correlation, not directly measured interatomic distances. Proposed nanomaterial uses were not tested as material performance. This characterization does not establish a microbial mechanism, recovered boron product, industrial deployment or jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

The USGS platinum-group-elements category identifies these six related metals; Australia's 20 February 2024 Critical Minerals List explicitly includes the same six in its platinum-group-elements entry. This is a grouped commodity scope, overlapping the individual element records, rather than a single element, mineral species, fixed-composition alloy or waste feedstock. The dated designation below applies to Australia's explicitly enumerated six-member group. Identity and designation are curated here; no shared microbial recovery performance is asserted for all six metals.

Plumbogottlobite (IMA 2025-075) is an IMA-accepted hydrous lead–magnesium vanadate mineral of the adelite–descloizite group with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula PbMg(VO4)(OH) (PDF p. 174, status A; official IMA symbol Pgtb, whereas Section 1 on p. 209 lists "Warr symbol: Pgot"; ideal composition PbO 61.41 wt%, V2O5 25.02 wt%, MgO 11.09 wt%, H2O 2.48 wt%, total 100 wt%), representing the Pb2+ analogue of gottlobite (CaMg(VO4)(OH)), the Mg2+ analogue of descloizite (PbZn(VO4)(OH)), the V5+ analogue of duftite-alpha (Pb(Cu,Mg)(AsO4)(OH)), and the Mg-dominant analogue of mottramite (PbCu(VO4)(OH)) and cechite (Pb(Fe2+,Mn2+)(VO4)(OH)). Described by Kampf, Désor, and Ma (2026) from a single hydrothermal baryte-vein specimen collected on the dumps of the Glücksstern mine, Gottlob Hill, Friedrichroda, Gotha District, Thuringia, Germany (50°51'6" N, 10°34'10" E; holotype deposited in the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County under catalogue no. 77403, pp. 209–210). Occurs as subparallel intergrowths of orange-brown tablets flattened on {001} (bounded by observed crystal forms {100}, {010}, {001}, {110}, {011}, {101}, and {111}) up to ~0.2 mm across on fracture surfaces in baryte with hausmannite (Sections 2–3, p. 210, Figs. 1–2). Exhibits a light-orange-brown streak, transparent character with adamantine lustre, non-fluorescence under long- or short-wave UV, Mohs hardness 4–4.5, brittle tenacity with irregular to conchoidal fracture, no cleavage or twinning, rapid decomposition in dilute HCl at room temperature forming a white residue that slowly dissolves, and calculated density Dcalc = 5.359 g/cm3 for the empirical formula and 5.516 g/cm3 for the structural formula on the single-crystal cell (Section 3, p. 210, and Table 3, p. 212). Optically biaxial (–) with 2Vmeas = 84(1)°, optical orientation Y = c (whereas Section 3 on p. 210 erroneously writes "uniaxial (–)" in the sentence immediately preceding 2V = 84(1)° and Y = c), non-pleochroic in demonstrable orientations, and Gladstone–Dale predicted mean refractive index n_calc = 2.077 (exceeding available index liquids, Section 3, p. 210). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser, 2 mW, Section 5, pp. 210–212, Fig. 3) shows a broad weak O–H stretching band at ~3217 cm-1, a weak overtone at ~1550 cm-1, VO4 stretching bands at 847 (very strong), 781 (shoulder), and 732 (medium) cm-1, VO4 bending modes at 441, 381, and 325 cm-1, and external/lattice modes at 275, 198, and 138 cm-1. Polylithionite

Polylithionite is the lithium-bearing mica mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula KLi2AlSi4O10F2 and approved status (PDF page 175). Its 1998 s.p. entry denotes a special-procedure action, not a modern approval-number CURIE. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes monoclinic material and uses the generalized formula KLi2AlSi4O10(F,OH)2; its natural specimen analyses and hydroxyl substitution are not substituted for the current IMA formula. Documented geological occurrence includes late-stage segregations, veinlets and metasomatic replacement in syenite pegmatites of the Lovozero alkalic massif. This establishes a lithium-bearing geological host, not a universal ore grade, present mining status or recovery process. The IMA-approved mica nomenclature report defines lepidolite as a series name for trioctahedral micas on or near the trilithionite-polylithionite join. Lepidolite is therefore not used as an exact synonym for this endmember; a lepidolite-labelled mixed feed needs specimen-specific characterization before its behavior can be assigned to polylithionite. This species is distinct from elemental lithium and a bulk lithium concentrate. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.

The commodity category of mined and manufactured salts containing potassium in water-soluble form. In particular, potassium feldspar is not equated with a potash product. The named US 2025 designation applies to potash as a commodity. No microbial production or recovery mechanism is asserted.

Powellite

Powellite is the calcium molybdate mineral species Ca(MoO4), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental molybdenum, wulfenite and an uncharacterized calcium molybdate precipitate. Sidorenko and colleagues (2008) examined black Ca-Mo-rich grains from the Bota-Burum Mo-U deposit, South Kazakhstan. Powder diffraction and infrared spectroscopy supported crystalline powellite in the uranophane-beta-associated material. Chemically similar grains from the uramarsite-associated material were optically isotropic and X-ray amorphous, with no characteristic powellite infrared bands; the authors interpreted these as metamict powellite. That interpretation is kept distinct from the directly characterized crystalline material. Radiation-induced alteration and the origin of the black colour were inferred, without a controlled irradiation test. The article's page 29 discussion is internally inconsistent about retention versus loss of anisotropy and diffraction in the silicate assemblage; the explicit characterization on pages 23-27 anchors this limited record. These observations establish neither a microbial transformation nor a mineral recovery yield. Criticality is unrecorded.

Preobrazhenskite

Preobrazhenskite is the grandfathered magnesium borate species Mg3B11O15(OH)9 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Its 1956 entry is an original-description year, not an approval identifier. Burns and Hawthorne refined a natural crystal from the Inder borate deposit, Kazakhstan, in orthorhombic Pbcn symmetry, with a = 16.291(4), b = 9.181(2) and c = 10.571(2) angstrom. Complex borate sheets parallel to (010) are linked through two octahedrally coordinated magnesium sites. Hydrogen positions were located from difference-Fourier maps; a crystallographically symmetric H site is an average structural model whose true local symmetry the authors explicitly left uncertain. Possible off-centre disorder and a high-temperature transition were suggestions, not experimentally demonstrated transformations. The study reported no new bulk chemical analysis or microbial experiment. This magnesium borate is distinct from potassium-bearing kaliborite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. No criticality designation, extraction mechanism or industrial recovery is inferred.

Priceite

Priceite is the Ca2B5O7(OH)5(H2O) mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original- description year 1873, not an approval number. Pandermite is a historical name for the same species. It is distinct from colemanite, gowerite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Wallwork et al. determined a monoclinic P21/c structure from synchrotron powder diffraction of natural Sultancayir material, South Australian Museum specimen G3769. The model has four tetrahedral and one triangular boron sites per formula unit; boron positions were assigned geometrically and not refined, and hydrogen positions were not located. Hydroxyl and water assignments were supported by bond-valence analysis. The paper's abstract and body disagree on the borate-chain direction, so no direction is selected here. A separate Fuka, Japan, study reports eight electron-probe analyses averaging 49.95 wt% B2O3 and 32.35 wt% CaO. Its 17.56 wt% H2O was calculated by difference because pure material was insufficient for direct determination; its 2.486 g/cm3 density was calculated, not measured. The proposed natural alteration of shimazakiite and its inferred temperature range are geological interpretations, not a controlled synthesis experiment. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial extraction performance is inferred from these observations.

Probertite

Probertite is the NaCaB5O7(OH)4(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1929, not a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from ulexite, elemental boron, the borates commodity and mixed ores containing probertite. Gatta et al. studied natural Kramer Deposit material from collection specimen 11717, using separate crystals for X-ray diffraction at 293 K and neutron diffraction at 20 K. Both refinements used monoclinic P21/c; the model contains pentaborate chains with three tetrahedral and two triangular boron sites, four hydroxyl groups and three water molecules per formula unit. Ten hydrogen sites were first located using neutron data and then incorporated into the X-ray refinement. Chemical analyses are specimen-specific: electron-probe results give CaO 15.8(2) and Na2O 8.6(3) wt%, while the separate trace-element table reports a mean lithium concentration of 0.392 wt ppm from ten analyses. Near-ideal major-cation composition does not mean zero trace elements or establish purity for every deposit. The paper reports limitations of its neutron extinction correction; the deposited CIFs and final publisher version were not acquired. This identity and characterization record makes no criticality, microbial extraction, isolated-product recovery or demonstrated radiation-shielding deployment claim.

Quenstedtite

Quenstedtite is a triclinic ferric sulfate mineral, represented in the September 2026 IMA list as Fe(III)2(SO4)3(H2O)9·2H2O. It is distinct from other ferric-sulfate hydrates and from mixed-valence romerite. Thomas et al. (1974) refined a natural Chilean crystal of unknown exact locality in P-1, locating nine iron-coordinated water sites and two additional interlayer water sites. Eleven waters fit that specimen; earlier analyses indicating less water were retained as possible occupancy variability, with the lower limit untested. A separate 2012 MSc thesis refined a natural Alcaparrosa specimen and modeled hydrogen positions at 180 K. Its calcium-bearing surface grains were attributed to gypsum, rather than accepted as calcium intrinsic to quenstedtite. The thesis contains inconsistent comparison table angles, instrument descriptions and water-bonding prose; its CIF records mixed hydrogen treatment and geometrical H-site location. These qualifications prevent treating all hydrogen positions as direct unconstrained measurements or its proposed romerite conversion as an observed reaction. This is an identity and structure record, without a curated extraction, microbial mechanism, recovery yield or criticality designation.

Regerite

Regerite is a hydrated potassium ferric phosphate mineral with ideal formula KFe6(PO4)4(OH)7(H2O)6·4H2O, approved as IMA 2023-028 and retained in the September 2026 IMA list. Rewitzer et al. (2023) characterized crystals from a historical Kreuzberg pegmatite specimen from Pleystein, Germany. The natural material contains titanium; wavelength-dispersive analyses of 15 crystals are not independent occurrences or a synthesis experiment. Water was calculated from the structural model and an assumed charge-compensating substitution, rather than directly measured. Single-crystal synchrotron diffraction at 100 K supports monoclinic P21/c symmetry and a framework of iron-centred octahedra and phosphate tetrahedra with potassium and water in channels. Bond-valence sums support the ferric assignment, rather than a separate direct iron-valence assay. Twenty-five of the 27 ideal hydrogen positions were located and refined with restraints; H22 and H30b remained unresolved. The deposited all-Fe model and ideal formula do not represent the full measured titanium-bearing composition. The proposed titanium distribution, displacement and charge-compensation scheme remain interpretations, with displaced Ti not unambiguously confirmed. The text's O18-to-O33 water-site range overlaps its hydroxyl assignment; Table 4 and the deposited hydrogen model instead distinguish O17-to-O23 hydroxyl sites from O24-to-O33 water sites. Natural occurrence and crystal structure do not establish a formation, microbial extraction or recovery mechanism. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

Richetite

Grandfathered hydrated lead-iron-magnesium uranyl oxide hydroxide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Fe3+,Mg)xPb2+8.6(UO2)36O36(OH)24(H2O)41, status G, and original-description year 1947 (not a numbered IMA approval CURIE). Originally described by Vaes (1947) from the Shinkolobwe mine, Katanga (Haut-Katanga), Democratic Republic of the Congo, richetite was structurally solved for the first time by Burns (1998) on a Shinkolobwe crystal provided by William Pinch. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (5 points, Table 2, p. 188) detected UO3 (77.02-77.83 wt%, mean 77.43 wt%) and PbO (16.76-17.37 wt%, mean 17.06 wt%), corresponding to a U:Pb atomic ratio of 1:0.282 (10.15 Pb2+ per 36 U), whereas Fe and Mg were below the microprobe detection limit on that thin flake (~0.25 wt% FeO/MgO inferred from structure). Single-crystal SMART CCD X-ray diffraction refined in triclinic space group P1 (a = 20.9391(3), b = 12.1000(2), c = 16.3450(3) A, alpha = 103.87(1), beta = 115.37(1), gamma = 90.27(1) degrees, V = 3605.2 A3, Z = 1, R = 8.9%, S = 1.79 for 12,383 unique observed reflections with |Fo| > 4sigma_F; attempts to refine in P-1 failed) established alpha-U3O8-type uranyl oxide hydroxy-hydrate sheets [(UO2)18O18(OH)12] stacked with 13 partially occupied interlayer Pb2+ sites (8.74 Pb pfu), two octahedral M(1)/M(2) sites (modeled with 0.47(5) Fe2+ + 0.53(5) Mg2+ at M(1) and 0.30(5) Mg2+ at M(2), x = 1.30), and 41 H2O sites, yielding the 1998 structural formula MxPb8.74[(UO2)18O18(OH)12]2(H2O)41. Hydrogen positions were not directly refined, and only U and Pb atoms were modeled anisotropically. The subsequent 2017 refinement cited in the IMA Master List (American Mineralogist 102 (2017), 1771, specifying (Fe3+,Mg)x and Pb2+8.6) is behind a paywall and was not independently acquired at curation. Distinct from masuyite, fourmarierite, vandendriesscheite, curite, and elemental uranium or lead; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Romanèchite

Romanèchite is a barium-bearing manganese oxide mineral with the IMA formula (Ba,H2O)2(Mn4+,Mn3+)5O10. The September 2026 list marks it approved (A), with "1982 s.p." in the number/year column; special-procedure notation is not a YYYY-NNN accession. The Handbook describes its monoclinic crystal structure. Romanèchite is a mineral species, distinct from barium or manganese elements, cryptomelane, and mixed manganese ores. The historical collective term psilomelane is not treated as an exact synonym for a pure mineral species. No constituent commodity's criticality is inherited. Pracejus's September 1989 thesis supplies mixed-ore experimental context rather than an accepted romanèchite-specific microbial mechanism. Section 5.5 correlates calculated normative mineral proportions of Groote Eylandt cemented pisolites with results from an Enterobacter-species leaching series. Appendix I.3.2 describes 1.89 g heat-sterilized ore, 8 mL 1% w/v molasses, incubation at 32 degrees C, and weekly concentrated H2SO4 addition before centrifugation and supernatant AAS, followed by fresh molasses and bacteria for a 21-week series. The normative romanèchite calculation allocates barium to this phase and neglects its variable potassium, intergrowths and other potential hosts; it is not a direct time-resolved phase abundance measurement. Figures 5.12-5.13 therefore cannot establish a pure-romanèchite bacterial dissolution yield. Matched uninoculated and acid-only results are not presented in the inspected leaching methods, figures or Appendix V.2. The record retains this experimental relevance without assigning a species/strain CURIE, microbial necessity, mineral-specific rate, isolated recovery, or industrial use.

Roquesite is the copper-indium sulfide mineral species CuInS2, listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with renamed status (Rn) and IMA number 1962-001. Picot and Pierrot's original description concerns natural material from Charrier, Allier, France, observed as inclusions in bornite. Powder diffraction, reflected-light microscopy and electron-microprobe observations support its distinction from the associated host minerals. The paper compares this natural material with a separately supplied synthetic CuInS2 specimen; that comparator is not the natural mineral specimen or a microbial product. The synthetic powder pattern contains additional broad central lines whose origin the authors could not test because material was scarce. The natural specimen has reported traces of iron and zinc, so qualitative element-map contrast is not evidence of absolute chemical purity. Both natural and synthetic microprobe analyses total above 100 percent; the authors attribute the excess mainly to sulfur-standard and correction difficulties and also discuss possible reference-metal surface oxidation. Those analyses support the mineral assignment without establishing a closed recovery balance. This record identifies the mineral species, not elemental indium, the entire polymetallic ore or every manufactured material of nominal CuInS2 composition. No microbial mechanism, isolated-metal yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is asserted.

The September 2026 IMA list recognizes it as a redefined species. The accepted primary experiment follows rozenite as a transient phase during laboratory heating of a natural melanterite sample. Phase fractions are diffraction-refinement results, not isolated-product recoveries or universal environmental stability limits. No microbial transformation is established by this experiment.

Rutherfordine

Rutherfordine is the uranyl carbonate mineral with the ideal formula (UO2)(CO3), distinct from elemental uranium, aqueous uranyl-carbonate complexes and uranium commodities. The September 2026 IMA list gives approved status A and the special procedure token 1962 s.p.; it is not listed as grandfathered. A natural Shinkolobwe crystal was refined in orthorhombic Imm2 in 1999, with neutral uranyl-carbonate sheets. That specimen's carbonate-sheet orientation is not assigned automatically to synthetic products. The structural paper discusses possible OH/H2O variability and absorption-correction limitations, so the ideal formula is not proof that every preparation is chemically identical. No criticality designation, microbial mechanism or industrial deployment is inferred.

Rutile

Rutile is the mineral species with IMA-approved formula TiO2. The September 2026 IMA list gives grandfathered status G and original description year 1803; the year is not an IMA approval identifier. This mineral is distinct from elemental titanium, traded titanium products, rutile-bearing concentrates and other TiO2 polymorphs or manufactured TiO2 nanoparticles. Sabinaite

Anhydrous sodium-zirconium-titanium oxycarbonate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula Na4TiZr2O4(CO3)4, status A, and approval number IMA 1978-071. Jambor, Sturman, and Weatherly (1980) originally described the cotype specimens (NMC 61017-61024 and ROM M35902) from dawsonite-bearing silicocarbonatite sills at the Francon (St-Michel) quarry, Montreal Island, and from Mont Saint-Hilaire, Quebec, Canada. Combined electron-microprobe, atomic-absorption, and thermal-decomposition analysis on the Francon quarry type material (Table 2, p. 27) yielded Na2O 20.7, CaO 0.2, ZrO2 39.1, HfO2 0.47, TiO2 12.0, CO2 27.1 (mean of 28.1 wt% by TGA and 26.2 wt% by evolution), total 99.57 wt%, from which Jambor et al. (1980) proposed the provisional formula Na9Zr4Ti2O9(CO3)8 and a pseudo-orthorhombic/monoclinic subcell. McDonald (1996) solved the crystal structure on an untwinned crystal from Mont Saint-Hilaire in monoclinic space group C2/c (a = 10.196(1), b = 6.616(1), c = 17.958(3) A, beta = 94.14(1) degrees, V = 1208.2(3) A3, Z = 4, R = 2.1%, wR2 = 5.7% for 1564 observed reflections with F > 4sigma(F) out of 1759 unique reflections; WDS composition Na2O 19.01, ZrO2 39.20, TiO2 10.50, Nb2O5 2.02, HfO2 0.56, CO2 28.08 calc, total 99.37 wt%), proving complete ordering of 6-coordinated Ti4+ and 8-coordinated Zr4+ in polyhedral [Zr2TiO4(CO3)4]4- sheets interleaved with Na+ layers and establishing the ideal stoichiometric formula Na4Zr2TiO4(CO3)4 ( noting also that the IMA Master List misprints the 1980 Canadian Mineralogist volume as 19 instead of 18). Distinct from weloganite, dresserite, and elemental zirconium or titanium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Sabugalite

Sabugalite is the aluminium uranyl phosphate hydrate mineral H0.5Al0.5(UO2)2(PO4)2·8H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. Sakuraiite

Indium-dominant copper-zinc-iron-indium-tin sulfide mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 and approval number IMA 1965-017. Originally described by Kato (1965) from the Kanagase vein group of the Ikuno mine, Asago-cho, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan, with a tetragonal or pseudotetragonal subcell (a = 5.455, c = 10.91 A, Z = 2) and an Ag-rich formula (Cu,Zn,Fe,Ag)3(In,Sn)S4, type material from the Ikuno mine (including Kato's 1965 holotype and specimen NSM M-15843 from the Senju-hon vein) was chemically re-examined by Shimizu, Kato, and Shiozawa (1986). Electron-microprobe analyses (Table 1: 5 sakuraiite analyses SK 1-5, 3 coexisting indium-bearing stannite/petrukite analyses ST 1-3, and 2 indium- bearing kësterite analyses KS 1-2, plus step-scan traverses across zoned grains in Figure 3) showed that Kato's 1965 elevated Ag values (3.5-4 wt%) were erroneous (actual Ag 0.10-0.15 wt% in sakuraiite) and established the revised formula (Cu,Zn,Fe)3(In,Sn)S4 with In:Sn atomic ratios reaching 89:11 (analysis SK 2: Cu 1.221, Ag 0.004, Fe 0.436, Zn 1.302, Mn 0.001, Cd 0.032, Sn 0.189, In 0.817, S 3.987 on an 8-atom basis) via coupled (Zn,Fe)In-for-CuSn substitution toward a hypothetical (Zn,Fe)2CuInS4 end-member. Shimizu et al. (1986) did not report new X-ray diffraction measurements, and Kissin and Owens (1989, pp. 684-686) subsequently examined Ikuno mine specimens, identified orthorhombic Pmn21 petrukite and an unindexed Zn > Fe phase, and noted that holotype sakuraiite still required definitive X-ray diffraction characterization to resolve its crystal symmetry and structural relationship to petrukite. Distinct from petrukite, roquesite, stannite, kësterite, and elemental indium or tin; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or extraction yield is asserted.

Saléeite

Saléeite is the magnesium uranyl phosphate decahydrate mineral Mg(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)10 in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1932 denotes its original description, not a numbered IMA approval. It is distinct from lower-hydration metasaléeite, arsenate-bearing nováčekite, aluminium-bearing sabugalite, and elemental magnesium or uranium. Dal Bo and colleagues examined natural saléeite from Shinkolobwe, Democratic Republic of Congo, with associated torbernite. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 293(2) K supports a monoclinic P21/n structure with uranyl-phosphate sheets and hydrated interlayer magnesium. The refined saléeite cell is a = 6.9516(3), b = 19.942(1), c = 6.9667(3) angstrom and beta = 90.586(4) degrees; R1 is 0.0307 for 1990 observed reflections after the reported twin treatment. Qualitative EDS detected U, P, Mg and O but no Fe or As, whereas the crystallographic occupancy model refined 0.97(1) Mg and 0.03(1) Fe at the interlayer cation site. These are different analytical results, not proof of a chemically pure endmember. Hydrogen positions used restrained O-H distances and constrained displacement parameters. This identity and structure evidence does not establish a microbial transformation, an extraction yield, an industrial process or a universal dehydration threshold. No criticality claim is inferred from the mineral's constituents. Deposited reflection data CSD-430599 were not acquired or independently re-refined, and the separate bassetite oxidation discussion is not a saléeite experiment.

Schoepite is a uranyl oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral with the current IMA formula (UO2)4O(OH)6·6H2O, distinct from metaschoepite, elemental uranium and products historically called dehydrated schoepite. Seafloor massive sulfides

Naturally occurring polymetallic sulfide deposit material formed at or beneath the seafloor by hydrothermal mineralization. This resource includes heterogeneous sulfide-bearing ore and associated gangue, rather than a single mineral species, constituent element, finished metal commodity, or processing residue. USGS distinguishes this hydrothermal resource from polymetallic nodules and cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts. The curated experiment used collected Japanese marine hydrothermal ores, not seawater alone or pure synthetic sulfides. Their compositions are sample-specific and do not define a universal resource grade. Collection, grinding and washing leave the feed a primary resource. No constituent criticality designation is inherited; the laboratory mechanism does not establish seafloor extraction or industrial deployment.

Sheldrickite

Hydrated sodium-calcium fluorocarbonate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula NaCa3(CO3)2F3(H2O), status A, and approval number IMA 1996-019. Grice, Gault, and Van Velthuizen (1997) described the cotype specimens (CMNMI 81530, 81537, 81538, and 81539) from thermally metamorphosed marble xenoliths at the Poudrette quarry, Mont Saint-Hilaire, Rouville County, Quebec, Canada, where it occurs on fluorite and calcite with leucophanite, pectolite, microcline, arfvedsonite, and schorlomite. Electron-microprobe WDS analysis (mean of 3 points, p. 182) combined with thermogravimetric H2O measurement and stoichiometric CO2 calculation yielded Na2O 9.16, CaO 48.84, SrO 0.36, F 16.17, CO2 25.81 (calc), H2O 5.61, less O=F 6.81, total 99.14 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 2 C atoms (10 anions) to the empirical formula Na1.01(Ca2.97Sr0.01)Sigma2.98(CO3)2[F2.90(OH)0.07]Sigma2.97·H2O. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction refined in acentric trigonal space group P32 (single-crystal cell a = 6.726(2), c = 15.044(4) A, V = 589.7(3) A3, Table 2; Debye-Scherrer powder XRD cell a = 6.718(3), c = 15.050(4) A, V = 588.3(3) A3, Z = 3, R = 4.6%, wR = 4.2% for 867 observed reflections with Fo > 5sigma(Fo) out of 965 unique reflections) established a three-layer c-repeat sequence of [CaF]-, [(CO3)2]4-, and [Na(H2O)]+ structural slabs. Thermogravimetric analysis under dry nitrogen recorded a single continuous 5.61 wt% dehydration step between 160 and 265 degrees C. Distinct from fluorite, shortite, rouvilleite, and commercial fluorspar; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Skogbyite

IMA-approved zirconium-magnesium-manganese oxy-orthosilicate mineral of the braunite group (IMA 2023-085; symbol Skb in the primary description and Skg in the IMA Master List; status A, Approved 2024; full description published April 2025) with ideal end-member formula Zr(Mg2Mn3+4)SiO12 (written Zr(Mg2Mn3+4)O8(SiO4) in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 201; requiring Mn2O3 54.46 wt%, ZrO2 21.26 wt%, MgO 13.91 wt%, SiO2 10.37 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Jonsson et al., 2025, European Journal of Mineralogy 37:269-277). Represents the Mg-dominant analogue of gatedalite, Zr(Mn2+2Mn3+4)SiO12, via the homovalent substitution Mn2+ <-> Mg2+, and is named after Swedish mineralogist Henrik Skogby (b. 1956) of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, Stockholm. Discovered in a complex regionally metamorphosed (Svecokarelian, ca. 1.87-1.80 Ga, 3-4 kbar, 550-600 degC) carbonate-silicate assemblage collected from the mine dumps of the Langban Fe-Mn oxide deposit, Filipstad Municipality, Varmland County, Bergslagen ore province, Sweden (59.86 deg N, 14.27 deg E), where it occurs as isolated microblasts in a Mn-bearing phlogopite, calcite, and dolomite groundmass and as inclusions within poikiloblastic pinakiolite, associated with hausmannite, jacobsite, macedonite, sparse baddeleyite, and late fracture-filling native lead, litharge, and hedyphane; holotype material (rock sample, polished thick and thin sections, and the mounted single crystal) is deposited at the Swedish Museum of Natural History (Naturhistoriska riksmuseet), Stockholm, Sweden, under catalogue number GEO-NRM20230033. Forms sparse, variably zoned, rounded to subhedral bluish-grey crystals mostly <=60 um (up to ~120 um) with a brownish-grey streak, sub-metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, brittle tenacity, no observed cleavage, parting, or twinning, estimated Mohs hardness 6-6.5 (by analogy with braunite and relative polishing hardness), calculated density Dcalc = 4.821 g/cm3 from the empirical formula and single-crystal unit cell, and axial ratio reported on p. 271 as "c : a = 0.4999" (which is the inverted ratio a : c = 9.4914 / 18.9875 = 0.49988, whereas true c : a = 2.0005). In plane-polarized reflected light it is bluish-grey with moderate reflectance (estimated ~17-21% in air by analogy with gatedalite), weak bireflectance, weak anisotropy, no pleochroism, and no internal reflections. Attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR-ATR) spectroscopy (650-4000 cm-1; Figure 2) displays a strong Si-O stretching band at 904 cm-1 (shifted to lower energy compared with ~945 cm-1 in braunite due to Zr4+ replacing Mn2+ at M(1)). Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (19 point analyses, JEOL JXA-8530F Hyperprobe, 15 kV, 20 nA, 1 um beam; Table 1) yielded Mn2O3 56.02(212) wt% (range 54.80-62.52), ZrO2 14.24(91) wt% (11.43-15.88), SiO2 10.51(59) wt% (10.27-11.15), MgO 9.86(146) wt% (7.79-11.02), Fe2O3 3.78(26) wt% (3.52-5.57), Ce2O3 2.80(113) wt% (0.51-4.39), Al2O3 0.79(19) wt% (0.65-1.08), ZnO 0.09(3) wt% (0.05-0.14), CaO 0.06(7) wt% (with printed range 0.02-0.05 wt% below the printed mean 0.06 wt%), PbO 0.04(5) wt% (0-0.17), La2O3 0.01(1) wt% (0-0.08), and Na2O 0.01(1) wt% (0.00-0.02), with Table 1 printing Total = 98.42 wt% whereas the arithmetic sum of the 12 printed mean oxides is 98.21 wt% (a 0.21 wt% tabulation discrepancy). Combined with single-crystal site-scattering optimization on the basis of 12 O atoms per formula unit, the empirical crystal-chemical formula is M(1)(Zr4+0.69Ce3+0.10Mg0.06Ca0.01Zn0.01Pb0.01)Sigma0.87M(2)(Mn3+1.56Mg0.35Al0.09)Sigma2.00M(3)(Mn3+1.17Mg0.55Fe3+0.28)Sigma2.00M(4)(Mn3+1.50Mg0.50)Sigma2.00Si1.04O12 (or merged as (Zr4+0.69Ce3+0.10Mg0.06Ca0.01Zn0.01Pb0.01)Sigma0.87(Mn3+4.23Mg1.40Fe3+0.28Al0.09)Sigma6.00Si1.04O12, where the rounded M(1) cation subscripts sum to 0.88 apfu vs printed Sigma0.87). Crystallizes in the tetragonal system, space group I41/acd (#142), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters a = 9.4914(4) A, c = 18.9875(10) A, V = 1710.52(17) A3, and Z = 8 (refined to R1 = 0.0460, R1(all) = 0.0675, wR2 = 0.1154, and GoF = 1.110 out of 903 unique reflections from 10,422 measured on a 0.08 x 0.08 x 0.09 mm crystal with MoKalpha radiation, with the Abstract on p. 269 stating 648 unique reflections with I > 2sigma(I) whereas Section 6.2 on p. 273 and Table 3 on p. 274 report 658 unique reflections with I > 2sigma(I)). The braunite-type structure (Tables 4-6) consists of eight-coordinated M(1) distorted cubes (<M(1)-O> = 2.292 A, refined s.o. Zr0.944(7), BVS = 2.97 v.u.), three Jahn-Teller-distorted octahedra M(2) (<M(2)-O> = 2.056 A, BVS = 2.58 v.u.), M(3) (<M(3)-O> = 2.079 A, BVS printed as 2.34 v.u. vs unrounded sum 2.32 v.u.), and M(4) (<M(4)-O> = 2.068 A, BVS printed as 2.43 v.u. vs unrounded sum 2.44 v.u.), and regular SiO4 tetrahedra (Si-O(3) = 1.636(3) A x 4, BVS = 3.88 v.u.). The seven strongest simulated powder X-ray diffraction lines (dcalc in A (Icalc; hkl), CuKalpha, Table 2) are 2.740 (100; 2 2 4), 1.678 (31; 0 4 8), 1.431 (16; 2 6 4), 1.678 (13; 4 4 0), 5.480 (12; 1 1 2), 2.373 (11; 0 4 0), and 1.431 (10; 2 2 12). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Skutterudite

Skutterudite is the cobalt arsenide mineral species listed as CoAs3 with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1845 in the September 2026 IMA compilation. The year is not an approval identifier. The Handbook describes cubic Im-3 symmetry and natural nickel and iron substitution. This species is distinct from nickelskutterudite, cobaltite, elemental cobalt and engineered skutterudite-type materials. Accepted microbial evidence concerns a phase-characterized, mixed Bou Azzer concentrate dominated by skutterudite; it does not establish a pure-endmember extraction rate or transfer constituent-element criticality to this mineral.

Smithsonite

Smithsonite is the zinc carbonate mineral Zn(CO3), listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1832. That year is not a numbered mineral approval. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes it as a calcite-group mineral formed in oxidized zinc deposits, sometimes replacing carbonate rocks and constituting zinc ore. This mineral owner is distinct from elemental zinc, dissolved zinc chloride, hydrozincite and mixed oxidized zinc ore. The experiment below concerns a laboratory precipitate assigned to smithsonite after drying; it does not demonstrate microbial extraction from natural smithsonite ore. No criticality designation is inherited from zinc, and no isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment is asserted.

Soddyite

Soddyite is the uranyl silicate hydrate mineral (UO2)2(SiO4)(H2O)2, with orthorhombic Fddd symmetry and U:Si = 2:1. The September 2026 IMA list records grandfathered status G and original-description year 1922; that year is not an IMA approval accession. Plášil's 2018 study provides new single-crystal diffraction data for natural museum material. The separate Giammar and Hering experiments used synthetic powder and demonstrate abiotic dissolution, silicon-dependent uranium release and precipitation of an incompletely resolved secondary uranium phase. These laboratory observations do not establish a microbial mechanism, a criticality-list designation, recovered uranium product or industrial use.

Sodium compounds

The source-defined industrial commodity category called Sodium (Na) (compounds) in the BGS/CMIC UK 2024 assessment. Section 2.6.3 defines its coverage as predominantly sodium carbonate, with some sodium nitrate and minor sodium metal; the category name is therefore not a chemical claim that metallic sodium is a compound. The assessment treats industrial salt separately. This record does not cover all sodium-containing substances, dissolved sodium ions or elemental sodium as a chemical-element concept. Its criticality entry uses corrected report OR/24/059, whose cover explicitly says it does not constitute government policy. No microbial extraction, transformation or recovery mechanism is asserted.

Spaltiite

IMA-approved thallium-copper-arsenic sulfosalt mineral (IMA 2014-012; status A, Approved 2014; full description published January 2026; symbol Spti in Section 1, p. 28, and Figure 3b caption, p. 30, and Spli in Figure 3a caption, p. 30, of the primary paper; no separate symbol column is printed in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 203) with ideal end-member formula Tl2Cu2As2S5 (printed as Tl2Cu2As2S5 in the September 2026 IMA Master List, p. 203, and in the Title, Abstract, and Section 1, pp. 27-28, as Cu2Tl2As2S5 in Section 5, p. 30, and as Cu2As2Tl2S5 in Table 4, p. 33, requiring Cu 15.02 wt%, As 17.71 wt%, Tl 48.32 wt%, S 18.95 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Graeser, Topa, Effenberger, Makovicky, Paar, and Dinca, 2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:27-37). Named from the laboratory nickname "spalti", derived from the German verb "spalten" ("cleave" in the Abstract, p. 27; "splitting" in Section 1, p. 28), in allusion to its extremely well-developed cleavage parallel to {100}. Found in 2009 by Walter Gabriel (a member of Forschungs-Gemeinschaft Lengenbach, FGL / FLG) on one of the dumps of the Lengenbach quarry, located southeast of the village of Faeld at ~1660 m altitude in the Binn Valley (Binntal), Canton Valais, Switzerland (660.171/135.176 in Swiss grid system CH903/LV03, i.e. latitude 46 deg 21 min 54 sec N, longitude 8 deg 13 min 15 sec E; hosted in a ~240 m thick bank of pure white Triassic dolostone of the Penninic Monte Leone Nappe metamorphosed to upper greenschist-lower amphibolite facies at up to 4 kb and 400-500 deg C during the Alpine orogeny and mineralized by late-stage hydrothermal solutions mainly enriched with As and Tl, inferred from its composition and mineral assemblage to originate from "Zone 1" of Graeser et al., 2008; Sections 1-2, pp. 28-29); the type specimen that contained the only three known crystals of spaltiite is deposited in the mineral collection of the Natural History Museum in Basel, Switzerland (catalogue no. S210), and one of the three crystals, which served for electron-microprobe, optical, and structural investigations, is deposited in the mineral collection of the Natural History Museum Vienna (catalogue no. N 9528) (Section 1, p. 28). Occurs in a ~30 x 30 x 20 mm3 piece of pure white Triassic dolostone as three euhedral long prismatic to lath-like crystals, each ~2 mm long and only ~0.2 mm thin (the crystal in Figure 2 measures 2.1 x 0.5 x 0.2 mm3), with point symmetry 2/m, elongated along the c axis [001] with the pinacoid {100} as the most prominent crystal form, numerous small {hk0} forms along the c axis, and a rounded top (Figure 2, p. 29), associated in the hand specimen and at the crystal base with small quantities of pyrite, drechslerite (Tl4(Pb,Sb,As)4S8; Topa et al., 2019), and hatchite (TlPbAgAs2S5) (Abstract, p. 27; Section 3, pp. 29-30; Figure 3, p. 30; and Table 2, p. 31). Crystals are greyish or lead-grey to black in colour and extremely soft with a metallic lustre and perfect cleavage parallel to {100} that produces minute and plastic slabs (all attempts to separate a small fragment for X-ray analysis yielded only extremely fine lamellae <1 um in diameter that could not be pulverised; Abstract, p. 27, and Section 3, p. 30). Mohs hardness is 1.5-2, corresponding to Vickers micro-indentation hardness VHN15 = 30-65 with a mean of 47 kg mm-2 (printed as "kg mm-2" in the Abstract, p. 27, and as "kg mm2" in Section 3, p. 30), and calculated density is Dcalc = 5.70 g cm-3 (Table 4, p. 33). In the ore microscope, a polished section appears white under plane-polarised incident light with common red internal reflections; neither pleochroism nor bireflectance is discernible; anisotropy is weak in air, with a reddish-brown to greenish tint, and more distinct in oil, with a violet to greenish rotation tint (Section 4, p. 30). Reflectance values (Rmin, Rmax in %) measured in air using a WTiC standard and a Leitz MPV-SP microscope photometer (Abstract, p. 27, and Section 4 and Table 1, p. 30) at the four COM standard wavelengths are 27.0, 32.6 (470 nm), 26.8, 32.1 (546 nm), 26.0, 31.1 (589 nm), and 24.8, 29.3 (650 nm) (full spectrum reported from 28.2, 33.2 at 400 nm to 23.8, 27.9 at 700 nm in 20 nm steps in Table 1, p. 30). After initial qualitative EDS analyses on an unpolished surface with a JEOL "Superprobe" JXA 8600F, quantitative wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses (JEOL "Hyperprobe" JXA 8530F FE-EPMA at the Central Research Laboratories of the Natural History Museum, Vienna; 25 kV, 20 nA, 2 um beam diameter, 10 s peak and 5 s background count times; standards lorandite TlAsS2 for AsLalpha, TlLalpha, and SKalpha, galena for PbMalpha, Ag metal for AgLalpha, chalcopyrite for CuKalpha, and stibnite for SbLalpha; n = 10 points on the main grain in the polished section parallel to the a axis; Section 5, p. 30, and Table 2, p. 31) yielded mean Cu 15.46(12) wt%, Ag 0.15(6) wt%, As 17.36(14) wt%, Sb 0.41(5) wt%, Tl 47.41(19) wt%, Pb not detected, S 19.20(8) wt%, total 99.99(32) wt% (charge balance ch = -1.2%), corresponding on the basis of 11 atoms per formula unit (Z = 4) in Table 2 (p. 31) to Cu 2.04(1), Ag 0.01(0), As 1.94(1), Sb 0.03(0), Tl 1.95(1), S 5.03(1) apfu (note that the Abstract on p. 27 and Section 5 on p. 30 print the empirical formula as Tl1.94Cu2.04Ag0.01As1.95Sb0.03S5.03 and Cu2.04Ag0.01Tl1.94As1.95Sb0.03S5.03, respectively, swapping the Table 2 apfu coefficients of Tl = 1.95(1) and As = 1.94(1), where 47.41 wt% Tl / 204.383 = 0.23197 and 17.36 wt% As / 74.9216 = 0.23171 confirm Tl1.95 and As1.94 apfu). Crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group P21/c (#14), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters (four-circle Nonius Kappa CCD diffractometer, 300 um capillary optics collimator, monochromated MoKalpha radiation, lambda = 0.71073 A, T = 293 K; Section 6.2, p. 31, and Table 4, p. 33) a = 15.791(8) A, b = 10.000(5) A, c = 6.323(3) A, beta = 99.25(8) deg, V = 985.5(8) A3, Z = 4, and axial ratio a:b:c = 1.579:1:0.632 (Gandolfi powder X-ray diffraction with FeKalpha radiation on a 114.6 mm camera, Section 6.1, p. 31, and Table 3 footnote b, p. 32, gave a = 15.821(9) A, b = 10.023(6) A, c = 6.334(4) A, beta = 99.21(6) deg). Data collection, structure solution by charge flipping, and refinements on F2 used COLLECT, JANA, and SHELXL-97 (Section 6.2, p. 31), converging to R1 = 0.1218 for 4753 observed reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo) and R1 = 0.1408 for all 6057 unique reflections out of 19,790 measured reflections, with GooF = 1.51 for 101 parameters (CSD-2505991; note that Table 4 on p. 33 prints the row label "R1(F): all, observed" alongside the values "12.18 %, 14.08 %", transposing the "all" and "observed" labels relative to the Abstract on p. 27, which confirms R1 = 12.18 % for the 4753 observed reflections with Fo > 4sigma(Fo)). The asymmetric unit (Table 5, p. 33, and Tables 6-7, p. 34) contains 11 independent fully occupied sites: two Tl1+ cations with stereoactive lone-electron pairs, Tl1[7] in a distorted pentagonal bipyramid (Tl1-S = 3.122(4)-3.517(4) A, BVS = 0.968 vu, effective charge / charge distribution CD = 0.998) and Tl2[8] in a bicapped pentagonal bipyramid (Tl2-S = 3.006(4)-3.519(4) A in Table 6, p. 34, cited as 3.007-3.521 A on p. 32; BVS = 0.965 vu, CD = 1.012); two As3+ cations with stereoactive lone pairs forming trigonal AsS3 pyramids, As1 (As1-S11 = 2.210(4) A, As1-S12 = 2.296(4) and 2.340(4) A, average S-As1-S = 97.9 deg, plus two long contacts As1-S22 = 3.731(4) A and As1-S23 = 3.846(4) A; BVS = 2.938 vu, CD = 2.960) whose As1S3 pyramids share S12 corners to form infinite chains along [001], and As2 (As2-S21 = 2.253(4) A, As2-S22 = 2.262(4) A, As2-S23 = 2.287(4) A, average S-As2-S = 100.7 deg, plus two long contacts As2-S11 = 3.462(4) A and As2-S12 = 3.659(5) A; BVS = 3.091 vu, CD = 3.014) whose As2S3 pyramids are not connected to each other; two Cu1+ cations, Cu1 in slightly pyramidal [3S] coordination (Cu1-S23 = 2.267(5) and 2.336(4) A, Cu1-S22 = 2.290(5) A, sum of S-Cu1-S angles 346.4 deg; BVS = 0.784 vu, CD = 0.983) shifted toward As1 with a short Cu1-As1 contact of 2.635(4) A (Table 7, p. 34; printed as 2.635 A on p. 32), and Cu2 in distorted Cu2S4 tetrahedra (Cu2-S21 = 2.308(5) and 2.337(4) A, Cu2-S22 = 2.381(4) A, Cu2-S11 = 2.392(5) A, average S-Cu2-S = 109.3 deg; BVS = 0.900 vu, CD = 1.034); and five S2- anions (S11, S12, S21, S22, S23). Corner-linked Cu1S3 and AsS3 pyramids form CuAs2S5 slabs along [001] that are connected by Cu2S4 tetrahedra into two inversion-related polar Cu2As2S5 layers (layer symmetry pc) parallel to {100} at (1/4 y z) and (3/4 y z), alternating with two topologically and crystallographically distinct centrosymmetric Tl layers (layer symmetry p21/c) centred at (0 y z) and (1/2 y z) and interlinked via S21 (Tl1-S21-Tl2 = 171.03(11) deg; Section 7, pp. 32-35). The seven strongest powder X-ray diffraction lines highlighted in bold in the Gandolfi pattern [dobs in A (Irel, Icalc, dcalc in A) hkl; Table 3, p. 32] are 3.907 (100, 100, 3.914) (021), 3.643 (80, 34, 3.646) (-221), 3.484 (30, 45, 3.496) (311), 2.980 (50, 63, 2.988) (510), 2.862 (30, 45, 2.869) (-511), 2.647 (60, 36, 2.652) (-331), and 2.506 (50, 29, 2.506) (040) (note that the Abstract on p. 27 lists eight strong lines using dcalc and Icalc values from Table 3 while printing intensity 40 instead of 100 for 021 and omitting minus signs on hkl: 3.914 (40) 021; 2.988 (63) 510; 3.496 (45) 311; 2.869 (45) 511; 2.652 (36) 331; 3.646 (34) 221; 2.506 (29) 040; and 2.762 (26) 202, where 202 has dobs = 2.749 A and Irel = 30 in Table 3). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Used vanadia-tungsta/titania catalysts from coal-fired power-plant flue-gas denitrification, represented by separately characterized laboratory feeds. Niu and colleagues studied an arsenic-contaminated honeycomb catalyst from a Xinjiang plant; Su and colleagues separately studied gray and yellow regions of three spent honeycomb catalysts, S3–S5. Their ideal Mg3[B(OH)4]2(SO4)(OH)F formula and absence of molecular water are conclusions from that structure; they did not chemically analyze the measured crystal. The current species formula's variable OH/F notation is retained rather than replaced with a universally fixed composition. Svanbergite

Svanbergite is the strontium aluminium sulfate-phosphate mineral SrAl3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from calcium-dominant woodhouseite, strontium aluminium phosphate goyazite and strontium as an element. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Kato and Miura (1977) refined a natural crystal from Dover Andalusite Mine, Nevada, British Museum specimen BM 17702. Single-crystal diffraction used 283 reflections and supported R-3m symmetry, a=6.992(2) and c=16.567(5) angstrom, with R=0.085. This specimen-specific structure contains disordered phosphorus/sulfur tetrahedral sites; the paper does not provide a new chemical analysis of that exact crystal or locate all hydrogen atoms directly. Its separate jarosite specimen and comparisons with earlier structures are not svanbergite synthesis experiments. Stoffregen and Alpers (1987) measured variable natural aluminium phosphate-sulfate grains in three hydrothermal ore deposits. Svanbergite-rich grains accompany alunite or kaolinite in shallower Summitville material, while La Escondida includes intermediate Ca/Sr compositions assigned probable hypogene or supergene origins from textures. Figure 1 shows a grain with subequal Ca and Sr rather than a pure svanbergite endmember; Table 3 and Figure 2 retain compositional variation and calculated water. Replacement or dissolution of apatite in acidic, sulfate-rich alteration is a geological interpretation, not a time-resolved transformation assay or demonstrated microbial mechanism. The 250 degrees C stability diagram in Figure 3 is a calcium-system woodhouseite inference and must not be treated as an experimentally measured svanbergite stability field. The companion woodhouseite record uses the same field-study lineage. Mineral identity and qualified natural alteration context are supported; microbial formation, strontium recovery yield, industrial deployment and mineral-specific criticality are not asserted.

Synchysite-(Ce)

A calcium-cerium fluorcarbonate mineral with the ideal IMA-CNMNC September 2026 formula CaCe(CO3)2F. The authority lists renamed status and identifier 1982-030; these identify this species, not the Nd- or Y-dominant synchysite species, bastnäsite, a rare-earth element or a mixed ore concentrate. Conconi et al. (2025) examined five natural crystals from miarolitic cavities in the Cuasso al Monte granophyre, Italy. Four crystals (FCBN1–FCBN4) supplied monoclinic C2/c average-structure refinements; Raman and SEM–EDS characterization used a subset, and TEM–EDS/electron diffraction used two lamellae from the separate FCBN5 crystal, as specified in Table A1. The crystals show chemical zoning, stacking disorder and inclusions. For FCBN3, Table 3 reports mean Ce contents of 0.44 atoms per formula unit in the core (13 spots) and 0.30 in the outer rim (11 spots), normalized to two cations; these are local composition averages, not recovery measurements or a uniform species formula. Low measured fluorine may reflect beam-induced loss. Fictitious scattering-site occupancies and calculated densities from the diffraction refinements do not directly represent measured chemistry. The proposed screw-dislocation growth sequence and Th-related loss of crystallinity are interpretations of natural microstructure; beam damage and other defects limit causal attribution. No controlled microbial, extraction, or recovery experiment is curated here. Underlying FCF diffraction files were available only upon request and were not acquired; published tables and Appendix A were inspected. No criticality designation is transferred from contained rare-earth elements.

USGS 2021 Minerals Yearbook (Graphite chapter, printed pp. 32.1-32.16) and USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 (Graphite (Natural) chapter, printed pp. 92-93) distinguish synthetic graphite from natural flake, amorphous, and vein/lump graphite (cmmmech:natural-graphite and mineral species cmmmech:graphite) and track synthetic graphite across electric-arc-furnace electrodes, unmachined shapes, motor brushes, steelmaking carbon raisers, and lithium-ion battery active anode material (HTS 3801.10, 3801.20, 3801.90, 6903.10, and 8545.11). In the 2023 US Department of Energy Final Critical Materials List (88 FR 51792-51798), DOE evaluated 'Graphite (natural and synthetic)' and 'Graphite--synthetic' in Table 1 (p. 51796, where synthetic graphite alone was scored 'Not Critical' in both short and medium terms) while explicitly noting in Footnote 6 (p. 51796) that the 2022 DOI/USGS Final List of Critical Minerals defined 'graphite' to include both natural and synthetic graphite. This record captures the manufactured synthetic-graphite commodity and its explicit authority scope boundaries without asserting a standalone mineral species identity or microbial mechanism.

Tancaite-(Ce)

IMA-approved iron-cerium hydrated molybdate mineral (IMA 2009-097; symbol Tnc-Ce in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 211; status A, Approved 2010; full description published June 2020) with ideal end-member formula FeCe(MoO4)3*3H2O (requiring MoO3 59.16 wt%, Ce2O3 22.49 wt%, Fe2O3 10.94 wt%, H2O 7.41 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Bonaccorsi and Orlandi, 2020, European Journal of Mineralogy 32:347-354). Displays a novel expanded- perovskite-like framework molybdate structure type (Nickel-Strunz class 7.GB; Dana class 49) related to synthetic orthorhombic Fe2(MoO4)3, and is named after Italian amateur mineralogist Giuseppe Tanca (b. 1943) who discovered the mineral, with the Levinson suffix -(Ce) indicating dominance of Ce3+ among the rare-earth elements. Discovered as a secondary mineral in the oxidation zone of a sulfide ore vein within cavities of quartz veins cutting granite at Su Seinargiu, Sarroch, Metropolitan City of Cagliari (CA), Sardinia, Italy, associated with quartz, muscovite, molybdenite, pyrite, and a mendozavilite-like phase; the holotype specimen is deposited in the Natural History Museum, University of Pisa, Italy, under catalogue number 18911. Forms small red to pale-brown transparent truncated octahedra up to 0.2 mm in size (Figure 1) with a yellow streak, vitreous to adamantine lustre, brittle tenacity, conchoidal fracture, no observed cleavage or parting, non-fluorescent behaviour, Mohs hardness 4-4.5, weak birefringence with calculated mean refractive index ncalc = 1.90, and calculated density Dcalc = 3.834 g/cm3 from the empirical formula (Abstract and Section 2, p. 348) vs 3.738 g/cm3 (Mg/m3) from the ideal formula in Table 4 (p. 352). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (Figure 2) confirms MoO4 stretching and bending modes below 1000 cm-1 together with H2O bending (~1620 cm-1) and O-H stretching (~3430 cm-1) bands. Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analysis (10 analyses, ARL-SEMQ, 15 kV, 20 nA, 20 um beam; Table 1) yielded MoO3 58.62 wt% (range 57.50-59.59), Fe2O3 11.29 wt% (11.04-11.71), Ce2O3 10.35 wt% (9.47-11.15), La2O3 5.04 wt% (4.66-5.53), Nd2O3 3.66 wt% (2.50-4.19), ThO2 2.58 wt% (1.97-3.44), Pr2O3 1.07 wt% (0.88-1.35), SiO2 0.34 wt% (0.02-1.56), Sm2O3 0.19 wt% (0.08-0.34), UO2 0.17 wt% (0.00-0.29), CaO 0.09 wt% (0.03-0.14), SrO 0.02 wt% (0.00-0.07), and stoichiometric H2O 7.43 wt% (3 H2O pfu from crystal-structure analysis), total 100.85 wt%, corresponding on the basis of 15 O atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula Fe3+1.03(Ce0.46La0.23Nd0.16Pr0.05Sm0.01U0.01Th0.07)Sigma0.99(Mo2.96Si0.04)Sigma3.00O12*3H2O. Single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction reveal a strong cubic subcell in space group Pm-3m (#221) with a = 6.870(1) A, V = 324.2(1) A3, and Z = 1 (average structure refined to R1 = 0.0387, wR2 = 0.0792 for 192 reflections with I > 2sigma(I) and R1 = 0.0424, wR2 = 0.0815, GoF = 1.261 for all 200 independent reflections from 3757 collected on a 0.1 x 0.08 x 0.08 mm crystal with MoKalpha radiation, Tables 4-6; note that the Abstract on p. 347 rounds R1 to 0.038 for 192 unique reflections with I > 2sigma(I) whereas Section 5 on p. 350 states R1 = 0.038 for 200 unique reflections), accompanied by weak superstructure reflections indexed on a 48-fold trigonal rhombohedral supercell in space group R-3 (#148) with single-crystal parameters a = 19.2901(3) A, c = 47.2510(5) A, V = 15,226.9(7) A3, and Z = 48 (reported in Section 4 on p. 349 and in the third column of Table 4 on p. 352, whose caption mistakenly attributes the third-column values to X-ray powder diffraction data) and Gandolfi CuKalpha powder-diffraction refined parameters a = 19.305(1) A, c = 47.438(5) A, and V = 15,311(3) A3 (Section 4 and Table 3, p. 350). In the average Pm-3m structure (Tables 5-6), corner-sharing FeO6 octahedra at the origin (Fe-O2 = 1.993(7) A x 6) are bridged by 1/4-occupied orientationally disordered MoO4 tetrahedra (Mo-O2 = 1.724(6) A x 2, Mo-O1 = 1.799(17) A x 2) around a central [6+3]-coordinated Ce/REE cage (Ce-O1 = 2.553(17) A x 6, Ce-H2O = 2.561(17) A x 3). The eight strongest observed powder X-ray diffraction lines indexed on the R-3 supercell (dobs in A (Irel; hkl), CuKalpha, Table 3) are 3.42 (100; 0 4 8), 3.93 (75; 4 0 4), 4.84 (45; 2 2 0), 1.825 (15; 2 8 0), 1.340 (12; 2 10 16), 2.785 (10; 0 6 0), 1.610 (10; 6 6 0), and 4.12 (8; 0 4 2). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Tennantite-(In)

Tennantite-(In) is the approved tetrahedrite-group mineral species with ideal formula Cu6(Cu5In)As4S13 and IMA number 2023-011. It is distinct from elemental indium, other members of the tennantite series and the entire polymetallic ore. Voudouris and colleagues describe natural anhedral grains from the Pefka epithermal deposit in Greece, associated with roquesite, galena and tennantite-(Fe) in quartz. Their study reuses the sample investigated by Voudouris and colleagues in 2022, rather than establishing an independent occurrence. Backscattered-electron imaging, wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses and single-crystal X-ray diffraction support the mineral assignment. The seven selected chemical spot analyses near the extracted crystal are part of 86 analyses of the zoned specimen, not seven independent deposits or a bulk ore grade. The refined structural model supports indium at the tetrahedrally coordinated M(1) site; its formal trivalent state is interpreted from chemical and structural constraints rather than measured by a separate valence-sensitive assay. The natural compositions include substitutions and do not equal the ideal end-member formula. Possible intergrowths with lead-bearing phases limit interpretation of minor lead as lattice substitution. The reported powder diffraction pattern and density are calculated; powder diffraction and hardness were not measured on this scarce material. The proposed crystallization sequence and changing fluid conditions are geological interpretations, not controlled reaction experiments. Abstract and Table 3 uncertainties for lead and arsenic differ, so those conflicting uncertainties are not adopted as precise measurements here. No microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality is assigned.

IMA-approved copper-cadmium antimony sulfosalt mineral of the tetrahedrite series within the tetrahedrite group (IMA 2022-115; symbol Ttr-Cd; status A, Approved 2023; full description published November 2023) with ideal end-member formula Cu6(Cu4Cd2)Sb4S13 (requiring Cu 36.02 wt%, Sb 27.61 wt%, S 23.63 wt%, Cd 12.74 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Sejkora et al., 2023, European Journal of Mineralogy 35:897-907). Represents the Cd-dominant C-site member of the tetrahedrite series and the Sb-isotype of tennantite-(Cd) and Cu-isotype of argentotetrahedrite-(Cd). Discovered in low-temperature hydrothermal quartz and (Pb-Mn)-rich calcite gangue from the 7th and 8th levels of the S-1 vein at the Radetice shaft, 300 m east of Radetice and 5 km southeast of Pribram, central Bohemia, Czech Republic (49 deg 38 min 20.44 sec N, 14 deg 05 min 13.66 sec E), hosted in Carboniferous coarse- grained granodiorite of the central Bohemian plutonic complex and associated with galena, bournonite, sphalerite, pyrite, geocronite, native silver, stromeyerite, tetrahedrite-(Zn), tetrahedrite-(Fe), Pb- and Cd-rich tetrahedrite-(Cu), and an unknown Pb-rich tetrahedrite- like phase (with a second documented occurrence in 1930 museum specimen MH-00683 from the Zmeinogorsk Mine, Altai Krai, Western Siberia, Russia); the holotype polished section is deposited in the Department of Mineralogy and Petrology, National Museum in Prague, Czech Republic (catalogue number P1P 43/2022), and the single-crystal X-ray diffraction grain is deposited in the Museo di Storia Naturale of the Universita di Pisa, Calci (PI), Italy (catalogue number 20025). Forms black metallic anhedral grains up to 200 um in size (or up to 50 x 50 um domains in Zmeinogorsk tetrahedrite-(Zn)) with a black streak, metallic lustre, opaque diaphaneity, estimated Mohs hardness ~4, brittle tenacity, conchoidal fracture, indistinct cleavage, and calculated density Dcalc = 5.094 g/cm3 from the holotype empirical formula and single-crystal unit cell. In reflected light it is isotropic and grey with greenish tints (Radetice) or greenish-brownish tints (Zmeinogorsk) without internal reflections; Commission on Ore Mineralogy (COM) reflectance values in air for the Radetice holotype (and Zmeinogorsk sample; Table 1) are 30.8% (30.3%) at 470 nm, 31.1% (31.2%) at 546 nm, 31.1% (31.6%) at 589 nm, and 28.8% (29.7%) at 650 nm. CHEBI:30440
Theisen sludge

Fine-grained flue-dust residue from top-gas scrubbing during copper-shale smelting in a blast furnace, also called Theisenschlamm. The resource scope here is the historical processing waste represented by the Helbra mono-landfill in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. It is distinct from unprocessed copper shale, a mineral species, an elemental commodity and a prepared leaching solution. Meschke et al. (2016) sampled material at a depth of 4 m in May 2015. They measured Cu, Mo, Pb, Sn, Sb and Zn by energy-dispersive X-ray fluorescence and Ag, Co, Ge and Re in an aqua-regia extract by ICP-MS. Their Figure 5A identifies zinc and lead as major measured components and reports other measured constituents; the two analytical fractions are not interchangeable measures of complete extractability. This sampled-feed characterization does not establish uniform composition throughout the landfill or a recoverable reserve. The same paper's membrane experiments used prepared Ge/Mo/Re solutions, rather than the sampled sludge or its actual leachate, and its Figure 2 reproduces bioleaching-solution information attributed to Klink et al. (2016). Those distinct evidence streams do not establish a newly verified microbial mechanism, isolated-metal yield or industrial recovery process for this record. No criticality designation is inherited from constituent elements.

IMA-approved hydrous molybdenum trioxide ("molybdic acid") mineral (IMA 2022-081; status A, Approved 2022; full description published January 2026; no mineral symbol is printed in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 217, or in the primary type description) with ideal end-member formula (MoO3)3*H2O (equivalently MoO3*1/3H2O, requiring MoO3 96.00 wt%, H2O 4.00 wt%, total 100.00 wt%; Gu, Yang, Gibbs, and Liu, 2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:39-52). Co-described with zhenruite ((MoO3)2*H2O, IMA 2022-050) and named in honour of the late Chinese mineralogist Prof. Huixin Tian (1933-2015) at Chengdu University of Technology, Sichuan Province, China, who graduated from the Changchun Institute of Geology in 1956 and from 1960 until her retirement taught crystallography and mineralogy, rare metal element mineralogy, and genetic mineralogy, making significant contributions to ore mineralogy, ore genesis, and exploration mineralogy (especially Ti- and V-bearing magnetite deposits and tin deposits in Sichuan Province and gold-tin deposits in Xinjiang Province; Section 1, p. 40). Found on specimens collected from an unnamed short adit of the Summit group of claims (latitude 32 deg 33 min 47 sec N, longitude 107 deg 43 min 48 sec W) near Cookes Peak, at the southern end of the Cookes Range, Luna County, New Mexico, USA (hosted in oxidized, silicified limestone-jasperoid fluorite-Pb-Zn-Ag ore bodies localized in limestone units beneath impermeable shale beds above a late Eocene-early Oligocene granodiorite stock; co-type locality for raydemarkite, virgilluethite, and stunorthropite, associated with barite, fluorite, ilsemannite, jordisite, powellite, pyrite, quartz, raydemarkite, sidwillite, and virgilluethite; Abstract, p. 39, and Section 2.1, pp. 40-41); parts of the cotype samples are deposited at the University of Arizona Alfie Norville Gem and Mineral Museum, Tucson, Arizona, USA (catalogue no. 22072), and the RRUFF Project (deposition no. 220024 in Section 1, p. 40, printed as R220024 in the Figure 2 caption, p. 41). Occurs as dark blue-green (or yellow-green in intergrowths, Figure 4, p. 42) nanometric crystal aggregates (10-70 um in size) intergrown with platy virgilluethite on a quartz matrix, showing microcleavages in backscattered-electron images (Figures 2, 4, and 5d, pp. 41-43; single-crystal X-ray diffraction data were collected from a 10 x 8 x 5 um aggregate fragment, Section 2.4, p. 45); crystals are translucent in transmitted light with lower transparency than virgilluethite, raydemarkite, or sidwillite, are insoluble in water or hydrochloric acid at room temperature, and have a white streak, vitreous lustre, brittle tenacity, Mohs hardness ~2, no observed macroscopic cleavage or twinning, Gladstone-Dale calculated average refractive index n_calc = 1.996 (optical properties could not be measured directly because the refractive indices exceed those of available immersion liquids), and calculated density Dcalc = 4.131 g cm-3 based on the empirical formula and powder X-ray diffraction unit-cell volume V = 361.74(2) A3 (Abstract, p. 39, and Section 2.2, pp. 41-42), or rho_cal = 4.11 g cm-3 in Table 3 (p. 47) based on the single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell volume V = 361.88(9) A3 with Z = 2 (density could not be measured directly owing to small crystal size and limited sample). Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses (Shimadzu EPMA-1720 at 15 kV, 10 nA, 2 um beam diameter, pure Mo metal standard, n = 8 spot analyses; Section 2.2, pp. 41-42, and Table 1, p. 41) yielded mean MoO3 96.81 wt% (SD 2.4 wt%), with stoichiometric H2O* = 4.04 wt% added in ideal proportion to measured MoO3, giving a total of 100.85 wt% and an empirical formula of (Mo1.00O3)3*H2O on the basis of 10 O atoms per formula unit (note that Table 1 footnote * on p. 41 labels H2O* = 4.04 wt% as "Added in ideal value", whereas Section 2.2 on p. 42 states that ideal (MoO3)3*H2O requires MoO3 96.00 wt% and H2O 4.00 wt%; 4.04 wt% is the stoichiometric H2O corresponding to 96.81 wt% MoO3, since 96.81 x (4.00 / 96.00) = 4.034 wt%). Tincalconite

Tincalconite is the Na2B4O5(OH)4(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1878 rather than a sequential approval identifier. It is distinct from borax, kernite, elemental boron and the borates commodity. Pabst and Sawyer characterized clear natural crystals from a Searles Lake drill core at about 116 feet depth; direct crystallization from brine was their interpretation of the occurrence, not an observed formation experiment. Giacovazzo et al. refined synthetic crystals grown from aqueous borax near 80 degrees C in trigonal R32. Luck and Wang later refined at 291(2) K a synthetic crystal obtained from layered aqueous sodium borohydride and tetraheptylammonium iodide in acetone, also in R32. Their partially occupied water-oxygen model favored Na6[B4O5(OH)4]3·8H2O, equivalent to 2.667 waters per Na2B4O5(OH)4 unit, rather than the three waters retained in the current IMA formula. Their freely refined O12 occupancy was 0.337(5); this is a crystallographic model result, not a measured water extraction yield or a new accepted mineral species. The 2002 Table 1 formula H28B12Na6O27 omits oxygen relative to the article's stated hydrated formula; its formula mass is therefore not adopted. Natural species identity, synthetic structural models and experimentally transformed mixed material remain separate. No commodity criticality, microbial activity or industrial recovery claim is inherited.

Todorokite

Todorokite is the hydrous manganese oxide species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula (Na,Ca,K,Ba,Sr)1-x(Mn,Mg,Al)6O12·3-4H2O (PDF page 218). Its status is approved; the accompanying 1962 s.p. entry identifies action by special procedure, not a modern approval-number CURIE. The Handbook of Mineralogy describes monoclinic material with variable cation composition and hydration in analyzed natural specimens. Its older generalized formula and specimen analyses are not substituted for the current IMA formula. Documented occurrence includes weathering or hydrothermal alteration of manganese-bearing minerals and deep-sea manganese nodules; these contexts do not specify a universal abundance or ore grade. The Handbook's geological term secondary mineral describes formation by alteration, not a material generated by industrial processing. This species is distinct from elemental manganese, a bulk manganese ore or nodule, and a manganese oxalate product. No microbial mechanism or criticality designation is assigned here.
