Torbernite

Torbernite is a copper uranyl phosphate mineral with formula Cu(UO2)2(PO4)2(H2O)4·8H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, which gives status A and the designation 1980 s.p.; this special-procedure designation is not a numbered mineral approval identifier. Locock and Burns grew synthetic torbernite crystals at approximately 5 degrees C over two months by diffusion of phosphate and uranyl nitrate into copper-bearing silica gel, then measured an epoxy-coated crystal by room-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction. They refined a tetragonal P4/nnc structure with twelve water groups per formula unit and uranyl-phosphate sheets. Copper has four short bonds to coordinating water groups and two longer contacts to uranyl oxygen atoms, interpreted as Jahn-Teller-distorted (4+2) coordination. The remaining water groups form square-planar sets above and below the copper plane. The proposed hydrogen-bond network uses difference-map hydrogen positions constrained to O-H bond lengths and fixed displacement parameters. The paper presumes equivalence to natural torbernite from agreement of unit-cell dimensions; it did not analyze a natural torbernite crystal. Its separate metatorbernite, zeunerite and metazeunerite arms have different preparations and structures. In particular, eight-water metatorbernite, its twinning and 88.3(6)% copper occupancy are not torbernite results. Structural comparison with the separately prepared eight-water phase supports a distinction between hydration states but is not a direct time-resolved dehydration experiment or recovery measurement. The article references deposited observed/calculated structure factors that were not acquired in this investigation; no independent diffraction re-refinement is claimed. Torbernite is distinct from metatorbernite, the autunite group, uranyl ions and elemental uranium or copper. This laboratory structural evidence establishes neither microbial extraction nor isolated-product recovery, industrial deployment or criticality inherited from either element.

Traction-battery hydrometallurgical residue

Residual solids from acid leaching in wet recovery of nickel or cobalt from waste traction-battery cathode materials and other recycled wastes. The curated study used separate nickel-line and cobalt-line residues from an unnamed Chinese enterprise; their compositions are not pooled. The source calls these residues slags, but does not establish molten-slag origin. They are downstream processing residues, distinct from mechanically prepared battery black mass, intact batteries, a pure cathode compound and isolated nickel or cobalt products. Exact incoming battery chemistries and the contribution of other wastes are unspecified. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Triphylite

Triphylite is the lithium iron(II) phosphate mineral LiFe2+(PO4), listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 as grandfathered, with original-description year 1834 rather than an approval identifier. It is distinct from Mn2+-dominant lithiophilite and oxidized, lithium-deficient members of the group. Losey2004 characterized natural pegmatite crystals by electron microprobe and single-crystal diffraction in the Pbnm setting of orthorhombic space group 62; Pmnb in the Handbook is another setting. The natural samples are solid solutions, including Mg substitution, not all pure LiFePO4. Lithium was not independently measured in that study: Li2O was assumed for matrix correction and Li-site occupancy fixed during refinement. The accepted transformation study uses a separately characterized natural triphylite specimen with minor sarcopsides visible microscopically, and demonstrates abiotic oxidation with spatially resolved lithium depletion, not microbial weathering or a recovered lithium product. The historical ferrisicklerite product name in the 2013 original is discredited under the 2022-approved nomenclature published in 2023; that publication classifies the studied Tri-77 and Tri-87 products as heterosite. No constituent-element criticality designation is inherited.

Tunellite

Tunellite is the SrB6O9(OH)2(H2O)3 mineral species in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with approved status A and special-procedure notation 1967 s.p., not a unique approval identifier. It is distinct from veatchite, elemental boron and strontium, and mixed borate ores. The monoclinic P21/a structure contains hexaborate units with three boron triangles and three tetrahedra, polymerized into sheets. The 1994 refinement of California specimen CMN 57614 located eight hydrogen sites using X-ray difference-Fourier maps with soft O-H distance constraints; seven sites participate in interpreted hydrogen bonds, five between sheets. This superseded the 1964 geometrical proposal, which had not located hydrogen sites. Separate Turkish material supplied the historical heating experiments below. No criticality, microbial mechanism or industrial deployment is inferred.

Tungsten skarn-processing tailings

Residual mineral solids generated by processing tungsten-bearing skarn ore. The curated case is historical tailings in the Smaltjärnen repository at the closed Yxsjöberg tungsten, copper and fluorspar mine in Sweden. The processing plant used gravity separation, magnetic separation and flotation. The characterized layered material contains scheelite among mixed silicate, carbonate, sulfide and other minerals; composition and particle liberation vary by sampled layer. This resource is distinct from tungsten as an element, pure scheelite, unprocessed ore, waste rock and a saleable concentrate. Hällström et al. document scheelite alteration, hydrous ferric oxide associations and tungsten transport in a field investigation of this repository; those geochemical observations do not establish microbial causation. No criticality designation is inherited from constituents, and the laboratory results below do not characterize all tungsten tailings.

Uranophane

Uranophane is the calcium uranyl silicate hydrate mineral Ca(UO2)2(SiO3OH)2(H2O)4·H2O in the September 2026 IMA list. Uranopilite

Uranopilite is the uranyl sulfate oxide hydroxide hydrate mineral with the September 2026 IMA formula (UO2)6(SO4)O2(OH)6(H2O)6·8H2O. Its grandfathered status G and original-description year 1882 are not a numbered approval accession. It is distinct from elemental uranium, a uranium commodity, zippeite and phases historically called metauranopilite. Burns determined the triclinic P-1 structure from a natural Joachimsthal, Bohemia specimen in Harvard Museum collection 89612. The structure contains uranyl sulfate chains with six coordinated and eight interstitial water groups per formula unit. Hydrogen positions were not directly located; the hydrogen-bond model and hydroxyl/water assignments used crystal-chemical and bond-valence arguments. The historical (UO2)6(SO4)(OH)10·12H2O formulation has the same total elemental composition but a different partition of hydroxyl and molecular water. The later natural Cervena-vein study confirmed the structure with substantial twinning and refinement limitations. Its Table 15 water content was calculated from the assumed fourteen-water structure, not independently measured. Natural crystals in ore fractures support occurrence in an alteration assemblage; they do not establish a controlled formation rate, exact formation pH or microbial causation. This record accepts natural identity and structural evidence, with thermal transformations deferred. No criticality designation, extraction yield or industrial recovery is inferred.

Veatchite

Veatchite is the strontium borate mineral species with ideal formula Sr2B11O16(OH)5·H2O in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list, with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1938. That year is not a sequential approval identifier. Its three named polytypes are veatchite-1A, veatchite-1M and veatchite-2M, historically called veatchite-A, p-veatchite and veatchite, respectively. These are not three separate species owners. Veatchite is distinct from elemental strontium or boron, the borates commodity, and the Ca-Sr-ordered species calcioveatchite, SrCaB11O16(OH)5·H2O. Grice and Pring (2012) determined the structures of separate natural specimens using single-crystal X-ray diffraction: NMNH 145911 from Emet, Turkey, for triclinic 1A with space group P-1; NMNH 113264 from Reyershausen, Germany, for monoclinic 1M with P21; and RG701/1 from Sussex, New Brunswick, for monoclinic 2M with Cc. The last specimen replaced the preserved California type crystal and must not be attributed to that type locality. Borate layers and their stacking distinguish the polytypes; the authors caution that their powder patterns alone do not satisfactorily distinguish them. Hydrogen positions were located by difference Fourier maps and refined, but no new chemical analyses were performed on the two type specimens. The paper's 2M Sr/Ca refinement has a slightly Ca-dominant smaller cation site and is explicitly discussed as potentially a new species; it is not a pure Sr end-member measurement. Pekov et al. (2024) subsequently establish the distinct calcioveatchite species and emphasize site occupancy in the boundary with veatchite. They do not directly reanalyse the 2012 RG701/1 crystal, so its exact modern species assignment remains a specimen-level qualification here. The 2012 temperature/pressure associations are geological interpretations with unknown precise parameters, not controlled polytype-transition experiments. Natural mineral characterization and geological occurrence do not establish microbial activity, boron recovery, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Vielleaureite-(Ce) (IMA 2022-134, symbol Vlr-Ce; formerly reported as UM2006-15-SiO:AlFHMgMnREE after Cenki-Tok et al. 2006) is an IMA-accepted manganese-cerium-magnesium-aluminium fluor-hydroxy disilicate-orthosilicate mineral of the dollaseite group within the epidote supergroup with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula Mn2+Ce(MgAlMn2+)(Si2O7)(SiO4)F(OH) (PDF p. 228, status A), representing the A1 = Mn2+ analogue of khristovite-(Ce) CaCe(MgAlMn2+)(Si2O7)(SiO4)F(OH) and the (A1 = Mn2+, M3 = Mn2+) analogue of dollaseite-(Ce) CaCe(MgAlMg)(Si2O7)(SiO4)F(OH), stabilized by the coupled heterovalent substitution M1Me3+ + O4O2- = M1Mg2+ + O4F-. Described by Ragu, Bindi, Bonazzi, Remusat, and Chopin (2025) from millimeter-thick rhodochrosite–sulfide–quartz veinlets crosscutting massive microcrystalline rhodochrosite ore in Lower Carboniferous greenschist-facies siliceous metasediments (~4 km from the 302–305 Ma Néouvielle granite pluton) collected ~10 m from the adit entrance at the Coustou manganese mine above the village of Vielle-Aure, Aure valley, Hautes-Pyrénées, France (holotype sample VA2016-5 and X-rayed crystal deposited at the Musée de Minéralogie, École des Mines de Paris, catalogue no. ENSMP 83943; cotype deposited at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle, Paris, catalogue no. MNHN_MIN_223.001, pp. 627–629). Occurs as scarce dark-brown to dark reddish-brown anhedral to subhedral prismatic grains elongated along [010] up to 200 um across, patchily zoned from F-poor, V-rich vanadoandrosite-(Ce)/vanadoakasakaite-(Ce) cores to near-endmember vielleaureite-(Ce) overgrowths, associated with rhodochrosite, quartz, chalcopyrite, vanadian spessartine (up to 1.7 wt% F in crystal cores), friedelite, Mn2+-dominant hellandite-(Y) relics (Mn/(Mn + Ca) = 0.49–0.61), monazite-(Ce), baryte, vanadian pyrophanite, minor hübnerite, galena, pyrite, ZnS, alabandite, cobaltite, chalcocite, rare skinnerite(?), helvite, welinite, manganhumite, and armoured relict inclusions of parisite-(La), fluorite, an unidentified Y-silicate, and a BaFCl phase (likely zhangpeishanite) (pp. 628–630, Fig. 1). Exhibits a reddish-brown streak, translucent diaphaneity, vitreous to adamantine lustre, brittle tenacity with uneven fracture, no cleavage or parting, no fluorescence under the electron beam, Mohs hardness ~6 (by analogy with allanite-group minerals), Dcalc = 4.33 g/cm3, and biaxial optics (589 nm) with alpha > 1.74 (Gladstone–Dale calculated n = 1.79) and strong pleochroism (very light yellow < light brown < brown // b, pp. 629–630). Voltaite

Voltaite is a cubic mixed-valence iron sulfate mineral with the September 2026 IMA ideal formula K2Fe(II)5Fe(III)3Al(SO4)12(H2O)18. This species is distinct from the voltaite mineral group, tetragonal pertlikite and the magnesium-, zinc- or ammonium-dominant analogues. Zhitova et al. (2023) characterized two samples labelled voltaite: Ni4225 from a coal-fire pseudofumarole in Nikitovka and SCCIII-14-20s from the Bolshoi Semiachik geothermal field. Their selected crystals were refined in cubic Fd-3c at 293 K, without clear evidence of lowered symmetry. The surrounding assemblages include other sulfates and are not pure voltaite feeds. Composition was measured by EDS on beam-sensitive hydrated grains; Fe(II)/Fe(III) proportions were calculated by charge balance, water was assigned from stoichiometry, and totals for these unpolished samples were normalized. Table 4 gives approximately one monovalent cation per formula unit for these samples, whereas the ideal formula and fully occupied structural A site imply two; this unresolved analytical/refinement discrepancy is not silently corrected. SCCIII-14-20s is also close to the Fe/Mg species boundary. These observations support a qualified natural-specimen identity record, without transferring every sample composition to ideal voltaite or treating geological occurrence as a controlled formation experiment. No microbial mechanism, extraction, recovery yield, industrial deployment or criticality designation is curated.

Weeksite

Potassium uranyl silicate hydrate mineral with current September 2026 IMA-CNMNC approved formula (K)2(UO2)2(Si5O13)(H2O)2·2H2O, status A, and special-procedure approval year 1962 s.p. (not a numbered IMA-XXXX-YYY accession). Outerbridge, Staatz, Meyrowitz, and Pommer (1960) described the holotype from opal-fluorite-calcite veinlets in porphyritic rhyolite at the Autunite No. 8 claim, east side of the Thomas Range, Juab County, Utah, USA, and documented nine additional occurrences in Utah, California, New Mexico, Wyoming, Pennsylvania, Texas, Arizona, and Chihuahua, Mexico. Microchemical analysis of ~100 mg of purified Thomas Range type material (Table 3, p. 46: SiO2 33.6, UO3 51.5, K2O 5.5, BaO 1.4, CaO 1.1, Na2O 0.7, Al2O3 0.6, CO2 0.3, H2O 6.6, Fe2O3 <0.1, sum 101.3 wt%) and single-crystal precession / powder X-ray diffraction led the 1960 authors to propose the orthorhombic Pnnb formula K2(UO2)2(Si2O5)3·4H2O (a = 14.26(2), b = 35.88(10), c = 14.20(2) A, Z = 16). Later structural studies cited in the IMA Master List (including the paywalled second reference Mineralogical Magazine 90 (2026), 653, which was not acquired at curation) revised the silicate-sheet stoichiometry from (Si2O5)3 (6 Si per 2 U) to (Si5O13) (5 Si per 2 U); both the 1960 analytical formula and the current IMA formula are retained with explicit attribution. Outerbridge et al. (1960) also demonstrated laboratory hydrothermal synthesis of weeksite and its Na analogue in sealed Pyrex tubes at 150 degrees C. Distinct from haiweeite, boltwoodite, uranophane, and elemental uranium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Sabina, Jambor, and Plant (1968) originally described weloganite from an alkaline dawsonite-bearing sill at the Francon quarry, St-Michel, Montreal Island, Quebec, Canada, initially proposing the Na-free trigonal formula Sr5Zr2(CO3)9·4H2O based on a partial analysis that overlooked essential sodium (Table 1, p. 471: SrO 41.0, ZrO2 19.4, CO2 32.2, H2O 6.6, sum 99.2 wt%). Following Chen and Chao's (1975) discovery of essential Na and triclinic symmetry, Grice and Perrault (1975) performed a complete chemical re-analysis on 2.0 g of pure Francon quarry weloganite (Table 1, p. 210: SrO 36.18, CaO 1.14, ZrO2 15.26, Na2O 7.75, K2O 0.02, CO2 30.70, H2O+ 7.65, H2O- 0.11, SiO2 0.25, Fe2O3 0.03, MgO <0.02, total 99.20 wt%, empirical formula (Sr2.8Ca0.2)ZrNa2(CO3)6·3H2O) and solved the crystal structure in non-centrosymmetric triclinic space group P1 (a = 8.966(1), b = 8.980(2), c = 6.730(1) A, alpha = 102.72(2), beta = 116.65(1), gamma = 60.06(1) degrees, V = 419.60 A3, Z = 1, R = 0.043 for 2354 observed reflections), showing ordered 9-coordinated [Zr(CO3)3O3] (3m symmetry), 6-coordinated [NaO4(H2O)2] and [NaO2(H2O)4] octahedra, and three 10-coordinated Sr2+ polyhedra. Distinct from mckelveyite-(Y), donnayite-(Y), bainbridgeite-(NdCe), strontianite, and elemental strontium or zirconium; no criticality designation, microbial mechanism, or industrial recovery yield is asserted.

Woodhouseite

Woodhouseite is the calcium aluminium sulfate-phosphate mineral CaAl3(SO4)(PO4)(OH)6, distinct from strontium-dominant svanbergite, calcium aluminium phosphate crandallite and calcium as an element. The September 2026 IMA list records its redefinition by special procedure in 1987. Lemmon (1937) described natural crystals from quartz veins adjoining and penetrating andalusite deposits on White Mountain, Mono County, California. Geometrical crystallography, optical observations and wet chemical analysis of hand-sorted crystals supported the new mineral. Its analysis contains minor substituents and a phosphate-sulfate imbalance; Lemmon explicitly considered a single analysis insufficient to prove the proposed substitution. This historical description is not a modern single-crystal refinement. Stoffregen and Alpers (1987) subsequently measured natural aluminium phosphate-sulfate grains by electron microprobe at Summitville, La Granja and La Escondida. Calcium-rich grains approaching woodhouseite occur at depth in Summitville and at La Granja, where small grains appear to replace apatite and contact pyrophyllite. Variable Ca/Sr and phosphate/sulfate ratios, minor additional cations and calculated rather than measured water distinguish these grains from pure ideal endmembers. Figure 1 depicts an approximately equal Ca/Sr grain, not pure woodhouseite. Apatite dissolution or replacement during advanced argillic alteration is the authors' field-textural interpretation; there was no controlled formation experiment, reaction time series or microbial assay. Their 250 degrees C, 40-bar stability diagram uses assumed aqueous compositions and an inferred woodhouseite boundary because direct thermodynamic data were unavailable to that study. It is not a measured formation threshold, and its hydroxyapatite model omits fluoride/chloride effects. The companion svanbergite record uses the same field study. These sources establish mineral identity and qualified natural alteration context, not microbial formation, elemental extraction yield, isolated-product recovery or industrial deployment. No constituent-element criticality is inherited.

Wulfenite

Wulfenite is the lead molybdate mineral species PbMoO4, distinct from elemental lead or molybdenum, the tungstate endmember stolzite and an unspecified lead-bearing ore or precipitate. The Handbook of Mineralogy identifies its tetragonal structure and documents W-bearing compositions. Gracanin and colleagues (2024) characterized natural tabular and bipyramidal crystals from Mezica, Slovenia: single-crystal diffraction assigned both examined forms to I41/a, while microscopy showed inclusions within the otherwise compositionally wulfenite host. Their environmental growth reconstruction is an inference, not a monitored precipitation experiment. The publisher correction repairs the legends of Figures 1-6; the updated figures and Tables 1-4 are used here. The separately studied Xinjiang material underwent abiotic sodium-sulfide treatment in the laboratory. This record does not establish a microbial mechanism, an isolated-metal recovery yield or industrial deployment. Criticality is unrecorded.

Wumuite

Wumuite (IMA 2017-067a) is an IMA-accepted potassium-aluminium-tungsten oxide mineral with a hexagonal tungsten bronze (HTB)-type structure (Strunz 04.E, Dana 07 AB3O9) and September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula KAl0.33W2.67O9 (PDF p. 236, status A; also written K(W2.67Al0.33)O9 or K(W2.67Al0.33)Sigma3O9 in Xue, Li, and Xie 2020). Described by Xue, Li, and Xie (2020) from a lightly weathered yellowish-gray aplitic Neoproterozoic Sinian (800 Ma zircon age) biotite–quartz monzonite body near the contact zone of Permian mafic rocks and ~300 m northeast of a fault-controlled pyrite-quartz-vein gold deposit in gabbro, near Nanyang village, Huaping County, Lijiang City, Yunnan Province, adjacent to northwestern Panzhihua City on the Sichuan–Yunnan boundary in the Panzhihua–Xichang (Pan–Xi) region, southwestern China (note coordinate discrepancy between the Abstract on p. 483, 26°46'8.21" N, 101°27'13.86" E, and Section 2 on p. 484, 26°46'18.21" N, 101°27'13.86" E; named after the Wumu River; holotype M13782 at the Geological Museum of China, Beijing, and cotype NY-6-2Z at the Crystal Structure Laboratory, China University of Geosciences, Beijing, pp. 483–485). Occurs as light green, transparent, hexagonal tabular crystals up to 0.3 mm across dominated by {0001} pinacoids with {10-10}, {01-10}, and {1-100} prism forms, associated with major quartz, orthoclase, albite, biotite, hornblende, and kaolinite, minor/accessory ilmenite, goethite, hematite, zircon, zoisite, tourmaline, monazite-(Ce), and allanite-(Ce), and W–Te mineralization comprising earlier automorphic scheelite inclusions, tellurite, later allotriomorphic rims and intergrowths of tewite (K1.5(Te,W)1.5W5O19, IMA 2014-053), and unnamed natural WO3 (pp. 483–485, Figs. 1–3). Exhibits a white streak, vitreous to adamantine lustre, brittle tenacity, good {10-10} and {0001} cleavage, Mohs hardness ~5–6, Dcalc = 6.52 g/cm3 (measured density not determined due to small crystal size), uniaxial (+) optics with Gladstone–Dale calculated refractive index n = 2.13, and reflection FTIR bands (Bruker HYPERION 1000, 4000–400 cm-1, Section 5, pp. 485–486, Fig. 4) at 816 cm-1 (WO6 octahedral stretching) and 523, 475, 446, and 424 cm-1 (W–O bending). Ten-point WDS electron-microprobe analysis on a single grain (JEOL JXA-8100, 20 kV, 10 nA, 2 um beam; Section 4, p. 485, Table 1) yielded WO3 91.16 wt% (range 88.45–92.35, SD 1.10, scheelite standard), K2O 5.55 (5.16–5.85, SD 0.28, microcline standard), Al2O3 2.52 (2.40–2.68, SD 0.04, albite standard), TeO2 0.59 (0.54–0.75, SD 0.08, Sb2Te3 standard), total 99.82 wt%, corresponding on 9 O apfu to the empirical formula K0.80(W2.68Al0.34Te0.03)Sigma3.05O9 within the nonstoichiometric HTB solid-solution series Kx(W3-x/3Alx/3)Sigma3O9 (x <= 1, coupled substitution 3[] + W6+ = 3K+ + Al3+). Hexagonal, space group P6/mmm, Z = 1 (Sections 6.1–6.2, pp. 485–492, Tables 2–8, Figs. 5–8): primary single-crystal MoKalpha XRD refinement on a 0.07 x 0.07 x 0.05 mm crystal (Bruker Apex-CCD, 162 reflections with I > 2sigma(I) out of 164 independent, 777 measured, Rint = 0.01, R1 = 0.025, wR2 = 0.072, GoF = 1.05, Table 3, p. 488) gives a = 7.2952(5) Å, c = 3.7711(3) Å (printed as 3.7713 Å in the Abstract on p. 483 and Section 6.2 prose on p. 487), V = 173.81(2) Å3, with corner-sharing (W0.89Al0.11)O6 octahedra at 3f ((W1,Al1)–O2 = 1.886(0) Å x 2, (W1,Al1)–O1 = 1.891(3) Å x 4, W site BVS = 6.019 v.u. in Tables 6–7, p. 489) forming hexagonal tunnels along c partially occupied by 18-coordinated K1 at 1b (occupancy 0.8, Ueq = 0.120(11) Å2, K1–O1 = 3.261(1) Å x 12, K1–O2 = 3.648(3) Å x 6, BVS = 0.51 v.u. in Tables 4–7, pp. 488–489); a second SCXRD measurement on another grain (Rigaku Oxford Diffraction XtaLAB PRO-007HF rotating-anode microfocus MoKalpha source, Section 6.2, pp. 486–487, Fig. 5) gave a = 7.2904(2) Å, c = 3.7686(2) Å, V = 173.47(1) Å3, Z = 1, and observed only 38 very weak superlattice diffraction points (average intensity ~1/1000 of strong reflections) in the lower layer, insufficient to index a doubled c ≈ 7.4 Å superstructure or P63/mcm symmetry (unlike synthetic KAl0.33W2.67O9 in P63/mcm, reported with a = 7.23072 Å, c = 7.5462 Å on p. 486 and a = 7.3072 Å, c = 7.5462 Å in Table 8 on p. 491); CHECKCELL powder XRD refinement (MoKalpha, Section 6.1, p. 485, Table 2, p. 487) gave a = 7.285(5) Å, c = 3.767(1) Å, V = 173.1(3) Å3, with four strongest lines at 3.161 (100)(020), 2.413 (40)(021), 6.261 (36)(010), and 3.727 (30)(001) Å. In abiotic solid-state synthesis experiments (Section 7, pp. 492–493, Fig. 9), heating pure WO3 with natural granite orthoclase (KAlSi3O8) at 700 °C and 1 atm yielded synthetic wumuite, and heating synthetic wumuite with WO3 and TeO2 for 10 h at 650 °C and 1 atm yielded synthetic tewite. Distinct from tewite, liguowuite, scheelite, tellurite, and elemental tungsten; no criticality designation for wumuite itself, no microbial or biological mechanism, and no industrial recovery yield are asserted.

Xenotime-(Gd)

Xenotime-(Gd) is the gadolinium-dominant xenotime species with ideal formula Gd(PO4), approved as IMA 2023-091. Its tetragonal I41/amd structure distinguishes it from monoclinic monazite-(Gd), despite their shared ideal formula. Ondrejka et al. (2024) characterized natural domains up to 20 micrometres across within xenotime-(Y) from the Zimna Voda quartz vein near Prakovce, Slovakia. Electron microprobe analyses at and near the holotype lamella average 29.16 wt% Gd2O3 across six points in Table 2, with substantial Y and Dy; these are mixed mineral compositions, not pure GdPO4, bulk ore grade or recovered gadolinium yield. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, Fourier-transform patterns and Raman observations support xenotime-type identity. Single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction were not obtained; Table 3 is a calculated powder pattern. The cell parameters from 25 Fourier-transform reflections and those estimated from weighted end-members are separate results. Density and refractive index are calculated, and several physical properties remain unmeasured. The 2026 corrigendum replaces Figure 4 because the black Raman traces for xenotime-(Y) and xenotime-(Gd) were interchanged; its authors retain the original text and interpretations. The proposed hydrothermal origin does not establish a controlled formation mechanism, microbial activity, recovery performance, industrial deployment or a jurisdiction-specific criticality designation.

Xenotime-(Yb)

Xenotime-(Yb) is the ytterbium-dominant xenotime mineral with ideal formula Yb(PO4), approved as IMA 1998-049. It is distinct from elemental ytterbium, xenotime-(Y), xenotime-(Gd) and mixed xenotime concentrates. Buck et al. (1999) described microscopic natural grains in ferrian muscovite aggregates from the SHE-5 pegmatite of the Shatford Lake group, southeastern Manitoba, Canada. Wavelength-dispersive electron microprobe analyses show substantial Y and other rare-earth substitution. The mean of three spots on the diffraction-analyzed grain contains 36.37 wt% Yb2O3 and totals 95.75 wt%; a separate embedded grain contains 32.27 wt% Yb2O3 and totals 98.27 wt%. The authors attribute the low first total mainly to charging in nonconductive epoxy; this explanation was not independently established and the values are not corrected here. These are grain compositions, not ore grades or extraction yields. Powder diffraction of three grains supports a tetragonal xenotime pattern consistent with I41/amd and refined cell dimensions a = 6.866(2) and c = 6.004(3) angstrom. Suitable material for single-crystal structure refinement was unavailable. Powder intensities were estimated visually, without an internal standard or film-shrinkage correction. The reported density of 5.85 g/cm3 was calculated, not measured. Geological discussion of fluoride complexing does not establish a controlled formation, microbial extraction or recovery process. No industrial deployment or jurisdiction-specific criticality designation is asserted.

Xianhuaite-(Ce) (IMA 2024-091, symbol Xhu-Ce) is an IMA-accepted potassium-cerium-niobium oxide mineral with September 2026 IMA-CNMNC Master List ideal formula K2CeNb5O15 (PDF p. 236, status A), representing the first naturally occurring mineral with a tetragonal tungsten bronze (TTB)-type framework structure and the natural analogue of room-temperature centrosymmetric synthetic K2CeNb5O15. Described by Yang, Xue, Yang, Sun, Li, Yu, Yan, Liu, Zhao, Meng, Chen, Chen, Liu, Yan, Hou, Ao, and Wang (2026) from two specimens in the giant Bayan Obo REE–Nb–Fe deposit, Baotou, Inner Mongolia, China (named in honor of Academician Xianhua Li; holotype specimen GMCTM2024012 deposited in the Geological Museum of China, Beijing, and cotype specimen BYEB-3 deposited at the Crystal Structure Laboratory, China University of Geosciences, Beijing, pp. 449–450): (1) sample BY-E2024-103 from the East Orebody (41°48'01" N, 109°59'39" E), occurring as black-brown megacrystalline aggregates at the contact between aegirine-type and dolomite-type Nb–REE–Fe ores in association with fersmite and fergusonite-(Ce); and (2) sample BY-EC2024-14 from the East Contact Zone (41°48'47" N, 110°01'27" E), occurring in dolomite-type Nb–REE–Fe ore quantified by TIMA as dolomite (71.89 vol%), magnetite (12.19 vol%), fersmite (8.00 vol%), calcite (2.69 vol%), columbite-(Fe) (1.72 vol%), xianhuaite-(Ce) (0.40 vol%), aeschynite (0.37 vol%), fergusonite-(Ce) (0.28 vol%), kinoshitalite (0.21 vol%), pyrochlore (0.19 vol%, preserved as relict inclusions within fersmite and xianhuaite-(Ce)), phlogopite (0.18 vol%), barite (0.15 vol%), apatite (0.10 vol%), chlorite (0.09 vol%), biotite (0.05 vol%), forsterite (0.02 vol%), and other minerals (1.47 vol%), recording fluid-mediated Nb remobilization during Permian granitic skarnization (pp. 450–451, 453–454, Fig. 1). Occurs as irregular granules or tetragonal prisms from 0.03 x 0.03 x 0.1 mm to 0.4 x 0.4 x 0.6 mm; dark brown to black-brown in hand specimen and pale yellow-brown to brownish-red in transmitted-light thin fragments, with white streak, adamantine lustre, non-fluorescence under 365 nm UV, no magnetism, brittle tenacity with conchoidal fracture, perfect {001} cleavage (no parting), Mohs hardness 5–6 (VHN200 = 469.5 kg/mm2 mean, range 448.7–490.2 kg/mm2), Dcalc = 5.23 g/cm3, Gladstone–Dale calculated refractive index Ncalc = 2.22, and grey reflected-light color with air reflectance Rmin–Rmax (CRAIC 20/30PV Pro, 6 spots across 6 grains, p. 450, Fig. 2) of 17.6–18.5% (470 nm), 17.4–18.5% (546 nm), 17.3–18.3% (589 nm), and 17.2–18.4% (650 nm). Micro-Raman spectroscopy (532 nm laser, WITec 300R, 50–4000 cm-1, Section 5, pp. 452–453, Fig. 3) shows no peaks above 1000 cm-1 and exhibits diagnostic TTB modes at ~853 cm-1 (NbO6 octahedral vibrations), 645 and 537 cm-1 (Nb–O stretching), 175 cm-1 (internal NbO6 mode), and 135 and 81 cm-1 (external cation modes). Mean of 10 WDS spot analyses on a single grain (JEOL JXA-iHP200F, 15 kV, 20 nA; Section 4, pp. 450, 452, Table 1) yielded Nb2O5 65.45 wt% (range 64.38–66.47, SD 0.65, KNbO3 standard), BaO 11.19 (8.96–12.28, SD 1.02, barite), Ce2O3 6.65 (6.33–7.07, SD 0.28, H2CeO5P), K2O 6.28 (5.97–7.03, SD 0.32, KNbO3), La2O3 5.26 (4.78–5.82, SD 0.32, H2LaO5P), Fe2O3 1.18 (0.67–1.74, SD 0.33, magnetite), CaO 0.91 (0.67–1.13, SD 0.14, apatite), Nd2O3 0.75 (0.63–0.83, SD 0.07, H2NdO5P), TiO2 0.63 (0.44–1.21, SD 0.25, rutile), Na2O 0.31 (0.26–0.35, SD 0.02, jadeite), Pr2O3 0.28 (printed range 0.00–0.23, where the printed mean 0.28 wt% exceeds the printed upper range bound 0.23 wt%, SD 0.14, H2PrO5P), MgO 0.17 (0.09–0.27, SD 0.06, forsterite), SrO 0.16 (0.09–0.23, SD 0.04, celestite), Ta2O5 0.08 (0.00–0.20, SD 0.09, LiTaO3; rounds to 0.003 apfu on 15 O and is omitted from the printed empirical formula), total 99.30 wt% (ideal K2CeNb5O15 requires Nb2O5 72.01, Ce2O3 17.78, K2O 10.21, total 100 wt%), giving on 15 O apfu the empirical formula A1(K1.30Ba0.69Sr0.02)Sigma2.01 A2(Ce0.39La0.31Nd0.04Pr0.02Ca0.15Na0.09)Sigma1.00 B(Nb4.75Fe3+0.13Ti0.09Mg0.04)Sigma5.01 O15 and simplified formula (K,Ba)2(Ce,La)(Nb,Fe)5O15. Tetragonal, space group P4/mbm (#127, mean |E2 - 1| = 0.925; non-centrosymmetric P4bm refinement gave R1 = 0.0197 without improving the model), Z = 2 (Sections 6 and 7.2, pp. 449, 452–458, Tables 2–7, Fig. 4): single-crystal MoKalpha XRD refinement on a 0.02 x 0.02 x 0.01 mm crystal fragment (Rigaku XtaLAB PRO-007HF, 293 K, 427 reflections with I > 2sigma(I) out of 480 independent and 4897 measured, Rint = 0.036, R1 = 0.0189, wR(F2) = 0.042, S = 1.11, SREF formula K1.285Ba0.715Ce0.812Ca0.188Nb4.947Fe0.053O15, Mr = 972.07, Table 3, p. 455) gives a = 12.5355(4) Å, c = 3.9213(2) Å, V = 616.19(5) Å3, with corner-sharing NbO6 octahedra at B1 (2c, Nb0.947(15)Fe0.053(15), <B1–O> = 1.964 Å, BVS = 5.17 v.u.) and B2 (8j, Nb1.00, <B2–O> = 1.975 Å, BVS = 5.15 v.u.) forming c-axis tunnels with five-membered rings hosting 9-coordinated A1 sites (4g, K0.642(3)Ba0.358(3), <A1–O> = 2.949 Å, BVS = 1.21 v.u.) and four-membered rings hosting 12-coordinated A2 sites (2a, Ce0.812(4)Ca0.188(4), <A2–O> = 2.678 Å, BVS = 2.63 v.u.); MoKalpha rotation-mode powder XRD refinement (Rigaku XtaLAB PRO-007HF, Chekcell, Section 6.1, pp. 452–453, Table 2, p. 454) gives a = 12.5458(8) Å, c = 3.9279(1) Å, V = 618.24(9) Å3, with seven strongest observed lines at 2.785 (100)(420, 311), 3.208 (61)(211), 3.034 (53)(410), 1.960 (44)(620, 002, 441), 2.931 (40)(330, 221), 3.469 (28)(320), and 3.915 (25)(001) Å. IMA:2024-091
Yanomamite

Yanomamite is the hydrated indium arsenate mineral species In(AsO4)(H2O)2, approved as IMA 1990-052 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. Botelho and colleagues (1994) characterized natural crystals from quartz-topaz greisen at the Mangabeira tin deposit, Goiás, Brazil, using microscopy, electron-microprobe analysis and single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction. The orthorhombic Pbca assignment is supported by natural specimens and a separate synthetic comparator; a matching chemical formula alone does not identify the mineral. Natural crystals contain minor Fe and Al and occur intergrown with or coated by indium-bearing scorodite. Even the three selected single crystals retained minor scorodite, whereas the selected powder material showed no significant scorodite reflections. Water in the reported empirical composition was calculated rather than directly measured because of these impurities. The authors considered both supergene and hydrothermal origins, favoring a hydrothermal association with the main cassiterite stage while explicitly describing the origin discussion as speculative. The actual indium source and transport were not established. These natural alteration associations do not constitute a microbial transformation experiment. This mineral is distinct from elemental indium, scorodite, mixed greisen feed and industrial secondary resources; geological replacement does not make it processing waste. The characterized grains establish neither a bulk resource grade nor extraction performance. No microbial mechanism, industrial recovery or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

WDS electron-microprobe analysis (n = 17 points on a JEOL JXA-8200 at 15 kV, 5 nA, 3 um beam; Table 1, p. 376) gave WO3 73.40 (range 71.58–74.79, SD 0.90), Nd2O3 9.37 (8.90–9.66, SD 0.21), Sm2O3 3.56 (2.39–4.24, SD 0.48), Ce2O3 3.17 (2.35–4.49, SD 0.58), Pr2O3 2.10 (1.61–2.64, SD 0.27), Gd2O3 1.74 (1.04–2.28, SD 0.36), La2O3 1.44 (0.68–2.77, SD 0.59), Y2O3 0.91 (0.36–1.45, SD 0.30), Dy2O3 0.81 (0.57–1.30, SD 0.19), Yb2O3 0.71 (0.46–0.90, SD 0.12), P2O5 0.18 (0.08–0.27, SD 0.06), CaO 0.09 (0.01–0.28, SD 0.09), Er2O3 0.09 (0.00–0.25, SD 0.10), MoO3 0.07 (0.00–0.26, SD 0.08), Eu2O3 0.07 (0.00–0.36, SD 0.12), Tb2O3 0.07 (0.00–0.33, SD 0.10), As2O5 0.04 (0.00–0.14, SD 0.04), TiO2 0.03 (0.00–0.09, SD 0.03), SiO2 0.02 (0.00–0.05, SD 0.02), Al2O3 0.01 (0.00–0.02, SD 0.01), K2O 0.01 (0.00–0.05, SD 0.01), stoichiometric H2Ocalc 4.24 (based on 1 OH- and 1 H2O pfu from structure refinement), total 102.13 wt% (Mg, Mn, Fe, Ho, Tm, Lu, Pb, Th, U, Nb, Ta, Sn, F, Cl, and Na below detection limits). Occurs in honeycomb-textured oxidation zones after "reinite" (ferberite pseudomorphs after primary scheelite) as yellow-orange platy/tabular crystals flattened on {010} and fibrous radial aggregates up to 100 um in diameter closely associated with white fine-grained anthoinite (AlWO3(OH)3) and microcrystalline yellowish hydrokenoelsmoreite ([]2W2O6(H2O)) octahedra (within a wider oxidation assemblage containing ferberite, meymacite, raspite, yttrotungstite-(Ce), and iron oxides; pp. 374–375, Fig. 2); also corresponds to the previously reported unnamed Nd-dominant mineral UM2004-//-O:CeHNdSmW from the Clara Mine, Wolfach, Germany (Kolitsch et al. 2004; p. 375). Exhibits twinning parallel to (001), white streak, vitreous lustre, no UV fluorescence, Mohs hardness 1, brittle tenacity, perfect cleavage on (010) and excellent cleavage on (100) and (001), Dcalc = 6.25 g/cm3 (for the empirical formula and single-crystal cell; 6.331 g/cm3 for the ideal structural model in Table 3, p. 378), biaxial optics with alpha = 1.90(2) and gamma = 2.10(2) at 589 nm, optical plane parallel to (010) with X ^ c = 6° and Z ^ a = 9° (Fig. 3), pleochroism from light yellow (X) to yellow (Z), and Gladstone–Dale compatibility index 1 - (KP/KC) = 0.0583 (good; p. 375). IMA:2023-064
Yusupovite

Yusupovite is the sodium-zirconium silicate mineral species with ideal formula Na2Zr(Si6O15)(H2O)3, approved as IMA 2014-022. It is a monoclinic C2/m dimorph of orthorhombic elpidite, rather than another name for elpidite or elemental zirconium. Agakhanov and colleagues (2015) characterized natural grains in pegmatitic rock samples collected from the Darai-Pioz glacier moraine in Tajikistan. The grains occur within reedmergnerite-bearing material with quartz and other associated minerals; this is not a pure bulk ore or an in-place deposit survey. Powder and single-crystal diffraction, electron-microprobe analyses, microscopy and infrared spectroscopy support the assignment. The mean of ten point analyses and the refined site populations describe a compositionally substituted specimen containing K, Cs, Y and minor Hf, not an exact realization of the ideal end-member. Its water content was calculated from the structure refinement, yielding about 2.52 H2O per formula unit; it was not an independent direct water measurement. The authors' structural comparison with elpidite does not demonstrate a time-resolved transformation between the minerals. Their discussion of ion exchange and radionuclide containment is prospective and draws on separate, earlier elpidite experiments. No yusupovite exchange capacity, microbial mechanism, metal recovery, industrial deployment or constituent-derived criticality designation is assigned.

IMA:1976-034
Zeunerite

Zeunerite is the copper uranyl arsenate mineral Cu(UO2)2(AsO4)2(H2O)4·8H2O in the September 2026 IMA list, with grandfathered status G. The year 1872 denotes its original description, not a numbered IMA approval. Its ideal twelve-water composition is distinct from eight-water metazeunerite, phosphate torbernite, calcium meta-autunite and elemental uranium, copper or arsenic. Synthetic-crystal X-ray diffraction and a later partially deuterated synthetic-powder neutron study support P4/nnc models under their respective conditions. Hydrogen positions and disorder are model-dependent; these experiments do not establish natural-specimen homogeneity, long-term containment, a universal dehydration threshold or an extraction yield. No criticality or microbial activity is inferred from composition.

IMA-approved hydrous molybdenum trioxide ("molybdic acid" hemihydrate) mineral (IMA 2022-050; status A, Approved 2022; full description published January 2026; no mineral symbol is printed in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 240, or in the primary type description) with ideal end-member formula (MoO3)2(H2O) in the September 2026 IMA Master List (PDF p. 240) and (MoO3)2*H2O (equivalently MoO3*1/2H2O, requiring MoO3 94.11 wt%, H2O 5.89 wt%, total 100.00 wt%) in Gu, Yang, Gibbs, and Liu (2026, European Journal of Mineralogy 38:39-52). Co-described with tianhuixinite ((MoO3)3*H2O, IMA 2022-081) and named in honour of the late Chinese mineralogist Prof. Zhenru Zhang (1930-2002) at Central South University, Changsha, Hunan Province, China, who graduated from the Department of Geology of Nanjing University in 1952, taught crystallography and mineralogy, ore geology, and modern analytical techniques at the Department of Geology, Central South University, and made important contributions to clay mineralogy in ceramics and ore mineralogy in nonferrous metals and gold deposits with over 44 articles and 3 books (Section 1, p. 40). Found on specimens (Figure 1, p. 40) collected from the Freedom #2 mine in the Central Mining Area (latitude 38 deg 29 min 43 sec N, longitude 112 deg 12 min 55 sec W), ~5.6 km north-northeast of the town of Marysvale in the central part of the Marysvale volcanic field, Utah, USA (weathered product of primary molybdenum ores in an epithermal U-Mo vein system hosted in a 23-18 Ma volcanic/hypabyssal complex of porphyritic quartz monzonite, fine-grained granite, and glassy alkali rhyolite; co-type locality for umohoite, liangjunite, wangpuite, downsite, vanpeltite, and fanguangite, associated with alunogen, anhydrite, coquimbite, fluorite, liangjunite, quartz, and raydemarkite; Abstract, p. 39, and Section 2.1, pp. 40-41); parts of the cotype samples are deposited at the University of Arizona Alfie Norville Gem and Mineral Museum, Tucson, Arizona, USA (catalogue no. 22720), and the RRUFF Project (deposition no. R220010) (Section 1, p. 40, and Figure 1 caption, p. 40). Occurs as acicular or prismatic crystals up to 60 x 10 x 10 um elongated along [010] (Figures 1 and 3, pp. 40-42; single-crystal X-ray diffraction data were collected from a 25 x 6 x 6 um crystal, Section 2.4, p. 43); crystals are colourless in transmitted light and transparent, are insoluble in water or hydrochloric acid at room temperature, and have a white streak, vitreous lustre, brittle tenacity, Mohs hardness 1.5-2, perfect cleavage on {001}, no observed twinning, Gladstone-Dale calculated average refractive index n_calc = 1.990 (optical properties could not be measured directly because the refractive indices exceed those of available immersion liquids), and calculated density Dcalc = 4.081 g cm-3 based on the empirical formula and single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell volume V = 248.89(2) A3 with Z = 2 (Abstract, p. 39; Section 2.2, pp. 41-42; and Table 3, p. 47; density could not be measured directly owing to small crystal size and limited sample). Wavelength-dispersive electron-microprobe analyses (Shimadzu EPMA-1720 at 15 kV, 10 nA, 2 um beam diameter, pure Mo metal standard, n = 7 spot analyses; Section 2.2, pp. 41-42, and Table 1, p. 41) yielded mean MoO3 93.24 wt% (SD 1.81 wt%), with ideal H2O* = 5.89 wt% added, giving a total of 99.13 wt% and an empirical formula of (Mo1.00O3)2*H2O on the basis of 7 O atoms per formula unit. Micro-Raman spectroscopy (Horiba ARAMIS micro-Raman system, 532 nm solid-state laser, thermoelectrically cooled CCD detector, 2 cm-1 resolution, 1 um spot size; Section 2.3, p. 42, and Figure 6, p. 44) showed a band at 3460 cm-1 assigned to O-H stretching vibrations in H2O, bands at 907, 925, 980, and 984 cm-1 attributed to Mo-O stretching vibrations, bands between 280 and 700 cm-1 ascribable to Mo-O-Mo and O-Mo-O bending vibrations, and bands below 280 cm-1 associated with rotational and translational modes of MoO6 octahedra and H2O groups as well as lattice vibrational modes. Crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group P21/m (#11), as the natural counterpart of synthetic monoclinic P21/m (MoO3)2*H2O ("alpha-MoO3*1/2H2O" of Fellows et al., 1983, and Benard et al., 1994), with single-crystal X-ray diffraction unit-cell parameters (Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy D/S four-circle diffractometer, CuKalpha radiation, lambda = 1.54184 A, at room temperature on a 25 x 6 x 6 um crystal; Section 2.4, p. 43, and Table 3, p. 47) a = 9.6790(6) A, b = 3.70653(19) A, c = 7.1029(4) A, beta = 102.391(5) deg, V = 248.89(2) A3, Z = 2, and axial ratio a:b:c = 2.6113:1:1.9163 (powder X-ray diffraction on the Rigaku XtaLAB Synergy D/S four-circle diffractometer with CuKalpha radiation, lambda = 1.54184 A, in Gandolfi mode at 50 kV and 1 mA, refined using Holland and Redfern, 1997, gave unit-cell parameters a = 9.6760(5) A, b = 3.708(18) A, c = 7.101(2) A, beta = 102.372(1) deg, and V = 248.92(5) A3; Section 2.4, p. 43; note that Table 3 on p. 47 prints Z = 2 for natural zhenruite alongside Z = 4 for synthetic (MoO3)2*H2O from Benard et al., 1994, where V = 248.4 A3 and Z = 4 correspond to the hemihydrate formula unit MoO3*1/2H2O rather than (MoO3)2*H2O). The crystal structure was solved and refined using SHELX2019 (Section 2.4, pp. 43-44) to R1 = 0.032 and wR2 = 0.091 for 582 observed reflections with I > 2sigma(I) (out of 609 independent and 5069 collected reflections, Rint = 0.054, GooF = 1.073 for 55 parameters; Table 3, p. 47). The asymmetric unit (Table 4, p. 47, Table 6, p. 48, and Table 7a, p. 50) contains two independent Mo6+ cations at 2e special positions with y = 1/4, Mo1 (BVS = 5.98 v.u. in Table 7a, p. 50) and Mo2 (BVS = 5.84 v.u. in Table 7a, p. 50), and seven O sites (O1-O7 at 2e; O1 is the coordinated H2O oxygen with BVS = 0.36 v.u., and hydrogen-bond-corrected oxygen BVS sums are O2 = 2.07, O3 = 2.14, O4 = 1.95, O5 = 2.08, O6 = 1.95, and O7 = 1.94 v.u.), forming two topologically identical double chains of edge-sharing octahedra along [010] with Mo-O bond distances varying from 1.684 to 2.428 A (Section 3.1, p. 47, and Table 6, p. 48): a type-A chain of Mo1O6 octahedra (Mo1-O4 = 1.688(6) A, Mo1-O2 = 1.696(7) A, Mo1-O3 x 2 = 1.9590(14) A, Mo1-O3 = 2.240(5) A, Mo1-O6 = 2.428(6) A; mean <Mo1-O> = 1.995 A) and a type-B chain of Mo2O5(H2O) octahedra (Mo2-O7 = 1.684(7) A, Mo2-O6 = 1.736(6) A, Mo2-O5 x 2 = 1.9569(18) A, Mo2-O1 = 2.276(6) A, Mo2-O5 = 2.318(6) A; mean <Mo2-O> = 1.988 A) that alternate via shared O6 corners to build corrugated layers parallel to (001) linked along [001] by interlayer hydrogen bonds from O1 (O1...O2 = 2.920 A x 2, O1...O4 = 2.936 A, O1...O6 = 3.160 A, O1...O7 = 3.050 A), topologically identical in layer geometry to anhydrous molybdite (MoO3) and raydemarkite (MoO3*H2O) (Sections 3.1 and 3.3, pp. 47-51). The seven strongest powder X-ray diffraction lines [dmeas in A (Imeas, Ical) (hkl); Abstract, p. 39, and Table 2, p. 46] are 6.932 (68.0, 72.6) (001), 4.729 (47.2, 75.3) (200), 3.565 (24.0, 35.7) (201), 3.183 (100.0, 100.0) (11-1), 3.139 (43.2, 33.4) (20-2), 3.003 (31.2, 35.3) (111), and 2.281 (20.0, 20.2) (20-3). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Zhiqinite

IMA-approved super-reduced titanium disilicide mineral (IMA 2019-077; status A, Approved 2019; full description published November 2020; no mineral symbol assigned in the September 2026 IMA Master List, PDF p. 240, or in the type description) with ideal end-member formula TiSi2 (requiring Ti 46.01 wt%, Si 53.99 wt%, total 100 wt%; Xiong et al., 2020, European Journal of Mineralogy 32:557-574). Isostructural with synthetic orthorhombic C54-type TiSi2 (Laves and Wallbaum, 1939; Jeitschko, 1977) and named in honour of Professor Xu Zhiqin (b. 1941, Shanghai), structural geologist, graduate of Peking University (1964) with a PhD from the University of Montpellier (1987), former deputy dean of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences (CAGS) and director of the Institute of Geology, and Academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (1995), under whose leadership the Continental Dynamics Key Laboratory of the Ministry of Land and Resources was established and discovered a large number of deep mantle minerals (Section 2, p. 558). Discovered together with badengzhuite (TiP, IMA 2019-076) and a mixture of the potentially new ternary intermetallic minerals Ti10(Si,P,[])7 (isostructural with Mn5Si3) and Ti11(Si,P)10 (containing up to 2 wt% V, 3 wt% Cr, 2 wt% Mn, and 2 wt% Fe in the two ternary phases) inside a single 20 um intermetallic melt-droplet spheroid enclosed in a translucent-to-transparent corundum grain (>200 um) separated from the Cr-11 podiform chromitite orebody, Luobusa ophiolite, Yarlung Zangbo suture zone, ~200 km east-southeast of Lhasa, Tibet, China (inferred to have crystallized along the peritectic path Ti10(Si,P,[])7 -> Ti11(Si,P)10 -> TiSi2 + TiP over 2130-1330 deg C in the Ti-Si binary and 2100-1600 deg C in the Ti-P binary from trapped Ti-Si-P alloy melts formed by interaction of mantle-derived CH4 + H2 fluids with basaltic magmas in the shallow lithosphere at ~30-100 km depth under oxygen fugacities more than 6 log units below the iron-wustite buffer, partly surrounded by a halo of a dmisteinbergite-like mineral KCa3(Al7Si9)O32; note that Section 4.1 on pp. 560-563 and Section 6.2 on pp. 568-569 address the controversy raised by Litasov et al., 2019a,b alleging that the Cr-11 corundum grains and enclosed ultra-reduced phases are anthropogenic brown fused alumina abrasive, concluding that mineralogical and textural differences between the Cr-11 inclusions and fused alumina favour a natural origin); the holotype specimen (catalogue number M13817, source of focused-ion-beam TEM foil no. 5358) and FIB foil no. 5358 are deposited in the Chinese Geological Museum, Xisiyangrouhutong 15th, Xicheng District, Beijing, China. Occurs in foil no. 5358 as mostly tabular grains mostly 1 to 2 um long (with tabular habit possibly resulting from flattening parallel to (110)), enclosing globules up to ~0.5 um across and an oval grain nearly 1 um long of badengzhuite (TiP), plus a possible second occurrence constituting the entirety of a 25 x 30 um inclusion (Si/Ti ~ 2 by EDX) in another corundum grain (Section 5.1, p. 565); owing to the sub-micrometre to micrometre grain size, direct physical, optical, and experimental powder X-ray diffraction measurements could not be performed (both minerals are presumably opaque), and zhiqinite is compared with synthetic TiSi2, which is white to gray in colour with a metallic lustre (Laves and Wallbaum, 1939; Cotter et al., 1956), Mohs hardness 4-5 (Honigschmid, 1906), Vickers hardness VHN load 1 kPa (HV1) = 870 +/- 15 kg/mm2, and measured density 4.07 g/cm3 (Frommeyer and Rosenkranz, 2004), while the density calculated from the ab initio 3D electron diffraction structure solution is Dcalc = 4.136 g/cm3 (compared with 3.85 g/cm3 calculated for the metastable 8-coordinated C49 polymorph of TiSi2; Section 5.2, p. 565, and Section 5.4, p. 566). Standardless energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX, Cliff-Lorimer thin-specimen approximation on a Zeiss Libra 120 TEM at 120 kV with a Bruker XFlash6T-60 detector; Table 3, p. 564, n = 4 analyses at points 428, 429, 430, and 431 in foil no. 5358, after excluding Cu from the FIB foil support grid; only a few net counts of C (19-50) and O (8-47) were detected alongside Si (1784-2788) and Ti (1187-1839), confirming the absence of structural O, H2O, and CO2) yielded: Analysis 428: Si 57.69(1.40) wt% (69.92 at.%), Ti 42.31(1.85) wt% (30.08 at.%); Analysis 429: Si 55.21(1.36) wt% (67.75 at.%), Ti 44.79(1.92) wt% (32.25 at.%); Analysis 430: Si 60.42(1.35) wt% (72.24 at.%), Ti 39.58(1.71) wt% (27.76 at.%); Analysis 431: Si 57.13(1.31) wt% (69.44 at.%), Ti 42.87(1.70) wt% (30.56 at.%); with average (n = 4) Si 57.61 wt% (SD 2.15, range 55.21-60.42 wt%; 69.84 at.%, SD 1.85) and Ti 42.39 wt% (SD 2.15, range 39.58-44.79 wt%; 30.16 at.%, SD 1.85), sum 100 wt% (100 at.%), corresponding on the basis of 3 cations/atoms per formula unit to the empirical formula Ti0.905Si2.095 (Abstract, p. 557, and Section 5.3, p. 565). Crystallizes in the orthorhombic system, space group Fddd (#70), with three-dimensional electron diffraction (3D ED; 1 deg beam precession via Nanomegas Digistar P1000, ASI Timepix single-electron camera, 150 nm beam diameter, 180 mm camera length, 0.8 A theoretical resolution, 1 deg angular steps over a total tilt range of 80 deg, PETS data reduction, SIR2014 direct methods, and JANA2006 dynamical refinement using 65 out of 81 diffraction patterns across an estimated 30-50 nm lamella thickness at 0 deg tilt to final residual R(3sigma) = 0.1015 at point 428, Section 4.4, p. 564, and Section 5.4, p. 566) unit-cell parameters a = 8.18(16) A, b = 4.85(10) A, c = 8.42(17) A, V = 334(12) A3, and Z = 8 (note that the Abstract on p. 557 misstates the lattice type as "a primitive orthorhombic cell", whereas Section 5.4 and Figure 6 on p. 566 confirm that space group Fddd has an F-centered orthorhombic lattice with characteristic chess-board extinctions and hk0: h + k = 4n d-glide conditions). In the crystal structure (Table 5 and Figure 7, pp. 566-567; essentially identical to C54-type synthetic TiSi2 of Jeitschko, 1977 and Li et al., 2013), Ti1 at (0.125, 0.125, 0.125) (multiplicity 8, occupancy 1, Uiso = -0.0032(16) A2) and Si1 at (0.4528(14), 0.125, 0.125) (multiplicity 16, occupancy 1, Uiso = 0.0028(20) A2) have Ti atoms coordinated with 10 Si atoms at Ti-Si interatomic distances ranging from 2.51(8) to 2.80(5) A, while 3D ED at point 429 (Figure 8) revealed (110) twin lamellae rotated around c* exchanging (110) and (1-10) (simulated CuKalpha powder X-ray diffraction pattern calculated from the 3D ED structure is reported in Supplement Table S2 and Figure S6). No biological or microbial interaction data are reported in the type mineralogical description.

Zinc leach residue

Mixed residual solids from acid leaching in zinc hydrometallurgy, including zinc retained in ferrite, sulfide and other specimen-dependent phases. The accepted studies used separate industrial residues from Hunan and Yunnan, China; their compositions and treatment outcomes are not interchangeable. This processing-generated resource is distinct from elemental zinc, a pure zinc-ferrite phase, zinc calcine before leaching, and zinc-purification waste. Two laboratory abiotic treatments are documented. No criticality designation, microbial mechanism, isolated zinc-product yield or deployment of these particular experimental protocols is inferred.

Zinc purification hot filter cake

Mixed precipitated solids removed during the hot purification of zinc leach liquor, before the subsequent zinc-powder cementation stage. The accepted specimen is hot filter press cake (HFC) from the National Iranian Lead and Zinc Company in Zandjan, Iran, containing zinc, cobalt and manganese. This processing residue is distinct from zinc leach residue, cold purification filter cake, a pure oxide mineral, or elemental zinc. Its laboratory chemical leaching does not establish a microbial mechanism, a criticality designation, purified-metal production or industrial deployment of the tested treatment.

The United States designation maps the listed zinc commodity to this element; it does not designate every zinc-bearing mineral or waste. Zincite

Zincite is the hexagonal ZnO mineral species listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with grandfathered status G and original-description year 1845, not a numbered approval. The Handbook documents natural Zn-dominant oxide with possible Mn substitution. This owner is distinct from elemental zinc, hydrozincite, zinc oxalate and mixed zinc-bearing wastes. Evidence below concerns commercial zincite-structured ZnO in fungal experiments and a separate source-described natural zincite specimen in an abiotic dissolution experiment. Commercial particles are synthetic analogues, not natural ore. No criticality designation, phase-specific recovery yield or industrial deployment is asserted.

Zincobriartite

Zincobriartite is the natural copper-zinc-germanium sulfide mineral Cu2ZnGeS4, listed as approved IMA 2015-094 in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. The original announcement in CNMNC Newsletter 29, published in February 2016, places it among proposals approved in January 2016 and describes it as the zinc analogue of briartite from the Kipushi mine, Democratic Republic of the Congo. The proposal identifier's 2015 prefix is retained without treating it as the publication or approval month. The announcement reports the historical formula Cu2(Zn,Fe)(Ge,Ga)S4 and type material at the Natural History Museum, London, catalogue BM 1967,271. That broader formula is distinguished from the current listed endmember and is not a measured composition of every specimen. Newsletter 90, published in April 2026, still lists zincobriartite among approved minerals lacking a published full description. The announcement therefore supports bounded identity and provenance, not unavailable analytical methods, specimen assays or independently reproducible structure refinement. Historical briartite grains are not automatically reassigned to this species. No extraction mechanism, recovery yield or inherited constituent-element criticality is asserted.

IMA:2015-094
Zippeite

Zippeite is the potassium uranyl sulfate hydroxide hydrate mineral with the September 2026 IMA formula K2[(UO2)4(SO4)2O2(OH)2](H2O)4, redefined status Rd and entry 1971-029a. It is a mineral species, distinct from the zippeite group, other cation-dominant group members, elemental uranium and a uranium commodity. The natural species must not be equated without qualification to the K3, three-water synthetic compound called zippeite by Burns and colleagues in 2003. The latter was refined in C2; the natural material discussed by Plasil and colleagues in 2014 was indexed in C2/m. Their original powder-XRD result for fine-grained zippeite II from the Cervena vein, Jachymov, Czech Republic gave a = 8.844(1), b = 14.115(2), c = 8.856(1) angstrom, beta = 104.785(8) degrees and V = 1068.9(3) cubic angstrom (Table 29). This is distinct from the zippeite I single-crystal values reproduced from their earlier 2011 study. Figures 13-14 show crystalline aggregates and powdery coatings in the natural weathering assemblage. The proposed later precipitation of the powdery material is a petrographic interpretation, not a timed or controlled conversion. Formation pH, temperature, aqueous composition and uranium mass balance were not directly established for that event. This record accepts natural identity and occurrence evidence; no criticality designation, microbial process, extraction yield or industrial recovery is inferred.

Zircon

Zircon is the zirconium silicate mineral species Zr(SiO4), listed as grandfathered in the September 2026 IMA-CNMNC list. It is distinct from elemental zirconium, zirconia (ZrO2), zircon-bearing sand or concentrates, and other ZrSiO4 polymorphs. Hazen and Finger (1979) characterized two fragments of one natural, nonmetamict, gem-quality crystal from the Finsch Pipe kimberlite near Kimberley, South Africa, using single-crystal X-ray diffraction under pressure. Their specimen description reports nearly pure zircon with 1.2 weight percent HfO2 and 26 ppm uranium; these are specimen-specific values, not universal mineral composition or a resource grade. The refinements support a tetragonal I41/amd structure with four formula units per unit cell. Measurements extended to 48.1 kbar; higher-pressure phase transitions discussed in that paper are predictions or references to other studies, not transformations observed in this experiment. The two fragments are not independent geological occurrences. This identity and structural evidence does not establish microbial transformation, recovery, industrial deployment or a criticality designation for the mineral.

Zirconium

The element Zr, distinct from zirconium salts, zirconia phases, zircon mineral and zirconium-metal commodities. The United States 2025 Zirconium designation is mapped to this element without extending it to every host mineral or compound. The curated laboratory preparation combines microbial culture with subsequent thermal processing and does not establish isolated zirconium-metal recovery.

Zirconolite

Zirconolite is a zirconium-bearing oxide mineral listed by IMA-CNMNC in September 2026 with formula (Ca,Y)Zr(Ti,Mg,Al)2O7 and redefined status. Its 1989 special-procedure entry is not a numbered new-mineral approval. CaZrTi2O7 is the simplified composition used in the cited nomenclature and natural-specimen study, not the measured formula of every grain. The IMA-approved nomenclature published by Bayliss et al. (1989) uses the unsuffixed name for metamict or undetermined-polytypoid material and distinguishes the 2M, 3T and 3O layered variants from cubic zirkelite. This record does not assign a particular polytypoid, space group or synthetic ceramic composition to an uncharacterized natural specimen. Bellatreccia et al. (1999) studied a natural polycrystalline aggregate collected at Jacupiranga, São Paulo, Brazil, from the locality historically associated with the name zirkelite. It was explicitly a different specimen from the historical type specimen. One hand-picked grain yielded no diffraction pattern after 48 hours in a Gandolfi camera; the authors assigned zirconolite using the metamict state and chemical composition. Three crystals examined by electron microscopy and electron microprobe showed oscillatory, sector or irregular compositional zoning. Their zirconium-bearing chemistry also included niobium, thorium, uranium, hafnium and rare-earth elements; this is specimen chemistry rather than a bulk resource grade. Table 3 separates new zirconolite analyses from the chemically distinct intergrown calzirtite. Point analyses and images support the natural occurrence, but no structure refinement of the unheated metamict specimen establishes a 2M identity. Historical heat-treated lattice parameters in Table 2 are reused from other studies, not newly measured natural-crystal structures in this investigation. The specimen's reported heavy-mineral sand provenance and carbonatitic chemical affinity do not resolve its original host rock unambiguously. Fine lamellae approach the microprobe spot size, so intermediate analyses can mix adjacent zones. The seven-oxygen cation formulae and inferred substitutions are calculations from chemistry, not direct site-occupancy or oxidation-state measurements. Figure 5 and Figure 6 captions disagree with plotted expressions or axis labels; no substitution regression is recalculated here. Tables 1-2 compile older data and do not add independent sampling. This identity and natural-specimen record makes no microbial mechanism, extraction yield, industrial deployment or inherited elemental criticality claim.
